1	# Chezmoi integration
2	
3	The recommended chezmoi contract is intentionally narrow: let chezmoi maintain
4	a read-only external checkout at `~/.local/share/pi-agents` (the same path
5	below the Windows user profile), and add that checkout's `bin/` directory to
6	`PATH` only when the platform launcher exists. `pia` writes runtime state
7	elsewhere, so no agent credentials or sessions enter the external checkout.
8	
9	This repository does not edit a dotfiles repository. The following snippets are
10	an integration recipe to apply there.
11	
12	## External checkout
13	
14	Add an entry like this to the dotfiles source `.chezmoiexternal.toml.tmpl`
15	(adjust the URL if the repository remote differs):
16	
17	```toml
18	[".local/share/pi-agents"]
19	    type = "git-repo"
20	    url = "https://github.com/daviddwlee84/pi-agents.git"
21	    refreshPeriod = "168h"
22	    [".local/share/pi-agents".clone]
23	        args = ["--depth", "1"]
24	    [".local/share/pi-agents".pull]
25	        args = ["--ff-only"]
26	```
27	
28	Treat this checkout as an immutable deployment mirror. `--ff-only` refreshes
29	will stop on local edits instead of overwriting them. Author combos in a normal
30	development checkout, commit and push them, then refresh the external.
31	
32	## Presence-gated PATH on macOS and Linux
33	
34	Add this to the shared shell environment template used by zsh/bash:
35	
36	```sh
37	PIA_EXTERNAL_ROOT="$HOME/.local/share/pi-agents"
38	if [ -x "$PIA_EXTERNAL_ROOT/bin/pia" ]; then
39	  export PATH="$PIA_EXTERNAL_ROOT/bin:$PATH"
40	fi
41	unset PIA_EXTERNAL_ROOT
42	```
43	
44	The guard keeps a first bootstrap or failed network clone from adding a dead
45	PATH entry. Because `bin/pia` derives its source root from its own checkout,
46	`PIA_SOURCE_ROOT` is unnecessary for this deployment.
47	
48	No `npm install` or generated `dist/` tree is required in the external mirror:
49	Node 22.19+ executes the repository's erasable TypeScript sources directly.
50	
51	## Windows launchers and PATH
52	
53	The same external entry checks out to
54	`%USERPROFILE%\.local\share\pi-agents`. Add its `bin` directory through the
55	dotfiles repository's managed user-PATH mechanism, gated on the cmd launcher:
56	
57	```powershell
58	$piaRoot = Join-Path $HOME ".local\share\pi-agents"
59	$piaBin = Join-Path $piaRoot "bin"
60	if (Test-Path (Join-Path $piaBin "pia.cmd")) {
61	    $env:Path = "$piaBin;$env:Path"
62	}
63	```
64	
65	The snippet demonstrates the presence gate for the current process. Persist
66	the same directory through the dotfiles repository's canonical Windows PATH
67	surface instead of appending it from `$PROFILE` on every shell start.
68	
69	PowerShell resolves `pia` to `bin\pia.ps1`; cmd.exe resolves it to
70	`bin\pia.cmd`. Both call the checkout's extensionless Node launcher, so the
71	CLI and combos remain tied to one Git revision. The PowerShell launcher keeps
72	literal argv boundaries; the cmd launcher follows normal cmd.exe quoting and
73	is intended for trusted interactive commands. Programmatic callers with
74	arbitrary input should use the PowerShell launcher. `.gitattributes` keeps the
75	two Windows launchers on CRLF checkouts.
76	
77	Node 22.19+ remains required on Windows. Pi's npm package normally exposes
78	`pi.ps1` and `pi.cmd`, while the OMP binary installer exposes `omp.exe`; `pia`
79	resolves the PowerShell shim without `shell: true` and launches the native OMP
80	executable directly.
81	
82	## Shell completion
83	
84	`pia completion zsh`, `pia completion bash`, and
85	`pia completion powershell` emit sourceable native completion scripts. The
86	generated adapters complete commands and flags, and scan the checkout's local
87	`combos/pi` and `combos/omp` directories for combo positions such as
88	`pia use <Tab>`. A runtime `PIA_SOURCE_ROOT` override is honoured immediately.
89	
90	On macOS/Linux, add `pia` to the existing post-apply completion generator so it
91	writes `~/.zfunc/_pia` and the bash-completion user file. Resolve the launcher
92	from `~/.local/share/pi-agents/bin/pia` explicitly: on a first apply the parent
93	shell may not yet have the new PATH. Use the external checkout's Git revision
94	as the freshness stamp because `bin/pia` itself may be unchanged while its
95	TypeScript or completion assets change.
96	
97	On Windows, cache `pia completion powershell` through the profile's normal
98	generated-init mechanism and use the same checkout revision as an additional
99	cache stamp. This avoids paying the Node/TypeScript startup cost on every new
100	PowerShell process. The generated completer scans combo manifests directly on
101	each Tab press, so combo additions do not require regeneration.
102	
103	Preview and apply from the dotfiles workflow:
104	
105	```sh
106	chezmoi diff
107	chezmoi apply
108	chezmoi apply --refresh-externals   # force a refresh before 168h
109	pia doctor
110	pia list --tree
111	```
112	
113	The same commands work in PowerShell after the managed user PATH is visible in
114	a new process. For a one-off checkout test, use `bin\pia.ps1 doctor` or
115	`bin\pia.cmd doctor` before changing PATH.
116	
117	On this machine, edit the chezmoi source returned by `chezmoi source-path`, not
118	rendered files under `$HOME`. The natural locations are
119	`.chezmoiexternal.toml.tmpl` and the shared shell exports template.
120	
121	## Boundaries
122	
123	- Do not copy combo `agent/` files directly into `~/.pi`, `~/.omp`, or the
124	  dotfiles repository; use `pia apply`.
125	- Do not store auth, sessions, generated manifests, or handoffs in chezmoi.
126	- Do not run `pia derive` or `pia lineage --ack` against the external mirror;
127	  those are source-authoring operations.
128	- Use `PIA_SOURCE_ROOT=/path/to/dev/checkout` temporarily when testing
129	  uncommitted combo work with the installed CLI.
130	- In PowerShell, the equivalent is
131	  `$env:PIA_SOURCE_ROOT = "C:\path\to\dev\checkout"`.
132	- Keep chezmoi responsible only for checkout availability and PATH wiring.
133	
134	This preserves a clean ownership boundary: chezmoi deploys the tool, Git tracks
135	combo intent, and `pia` owns private runtime synchronisation.
136
```

2	
3	**Status**: P?

5	**Related**: `TODO.md` · `docs/architecture.md` · `docs/combos.md`
6	
7	## Context
8	
9	Deferred on 2026-08-30 in favor of complete copied configs with lineage
10	metadata. Inheritance looks attractive for `base -> language -> domain`
11	families, but defining merge, deletion, ordering, validation, and conflict rules
12	before real usage would add a second configuration language without evidence it
13	is needed.
14	
15	## Current findings
16	
17	- `pia derive` copies a complete parent and records `derivedFrom` plus a parent
18	  digest. Parent changes warn; the child never changes until a human reviews it.
19	- `pia diff --parent` and `pia lineage --ack` provide a deliberately manual
20	  update loop with no hidden launch-time composition.
21	- OMP has native layers, while Pi and individual resource types expose
22	  different composition behavior. A wrapper-level merge could therefore be
23	  surprising even if it works for simple settings objects.
24	- Three-way sync could preserve child edits better than re-copying, but needs a
25	  durable base snapshot and precise treatment of arrays, renames, deletes,
26	  executable modes, and conflicts.
27	
28	## Options to compare
29	
30	| Option | Benefit | Cost/risk |
31	|---|---|---|
32	| Keep copy + digest acknowledgement | Explicit, portable, easy to debug | Repeated manual updates |
33	| Declarative `extends` materialised at apply | Compact child definitions | Merge semantics become a public API |
34	| Three-way sync command | Preserves independent child edits | Complex conflict/base storage and recovery |
35	
36	## Open questions
37	
38	- How often do parent changes need to propagate, and how many files are
39	  repeatedly copied in practice?
40	- Are conflicts mostly structured settings, or arbitrary prompts, skills, and
41	  executable assets?
42	- Should inheritance be engine-neutral or defer to each harness's native
43	  mechanisms?
44	- Can every effective combo still be inspected, exported, and reproduced
45	  without running an opaque merge?
46	
47	## Exit criteria
48	
49	- At least three meaningful derived combos and two parent-update events have
50	  been maintained with the copy workflow.
51	- The maintenance cost and conflict types are recorded with concrete examples.
52	- A decision note specifies merge/delete/array/mode/conflict behavior for any
53	  proposed alternative and includes migration/rollback steps.
54	- If complexity is justified, a throwaway prototype proves deterministic
55	  materialisation and conflict reporting before changing the public schema.
56	
57	## Decision
58	
59	2026-08-30: use complete copies and digest acknowledgements now. Do not add
60	declarative inheritance or three-way sync until the exit criteria show a real
61	maintenance problem.

12:## Project Trust
14:On interactive startup, pi asks before trusting a project folder that contains project-local settings, resources, or project `.agents/skills` and has no saved decision for the folder or a parent folder in `~/.pi/agent/trust.json`. Trusting a project allows pi to load `.pi/settings.json` and `.pi` resources, install missing project packages, and execute project extensions.
16:Non-interactive modes (`-p`, `--mode json`, and `--mode rpc`) do not show a trust prompt. Without an applicable saved trust decision, they use `defaultProjectTrust` from global settings: `ask` (default) and `never` ignore those project resources, while `always` trusts them. Pass `--approve`/`-a` or `--no-approve`/`-na` to override project trust for one run.
18:If no extension or saved decision applies, `defaultProjectTrust` controls the fallback behavior. Set it to `"ask"`, `"always"`, or `"never"` in `~/.pi/agent/settings.json`, or change it with `/settings`.
22:Use `/trust` in interactive mode to save a project trust decision for future sessions, including trust for the immediate parent folder. It writes `~/.pi/agent/trust.json` only; the current session is not reloaded, so restart pi for changes to take effect.
24:## All Settings
26:### Model & Thinking
51:### UI & Display

```text
1	# Settings
2	
3	Pi uses JSON settings files with project settings overriding global settings.
4	
5	| Location | Scope |
6	|----------|-------|
7	| `~/.pi/agent/settings.json` | Global (all projects) |
8	| `.pi/settings.json` | Project (current directory) |
9	
10	Edit directly or use `/settings` for common options. To save startup model defaults interactively, use `/model` and press Ctrl+S on the desired model. To save the startup thinking level, use `/thinking` and press Ctrl+S.
11	
12	## Project Trust
13	
14	On interactive startup, pi asks before trusting a project folder that contains project-local settings, resources, or project `.agents/skills` and has no saved decision for the folder or a parent folder in `~/.pi/agent/trust.json`. Trusting a project allows pi to load `.pi/settings.json` and `.pi` resources, install missing project packages, and execute project extensions.
15	
16	Non-interactive modes (`-p`, `--mode json`, and `--mode rpc`) do not show a trust prompt. Without an applicable saved trust decision, they use `defaultProjectTrust` from global settings: `ask` (default) and `never` ignore those project resources, while `always` trusts them. Pass `--approve`/`-a` or `--no-approve`/`-na` to override project trust for one run.
17	
18	If no extension or saved decision applies, `defaultProjectTrust` controls the fallback behavior. Set it to `"ask"`, `"always"`, or `"never"` in `~/.pi/agent/settings.json`, or change it with `/settings`.
19	
20	`pi config` and package commands use the same project trust flow, except `pi update` never prompts. Pass `--approve` to trust project-local settings for one command or `--no-approve` to ignore them.
21	
22	Use `/trust` in interactive mode to save a project trust decision for future sessions, including trust for the immediate parent folder. It writes `~/.pi/agent/trust.json` only; the current session is not reloaded, so restart pi for changes to take effect.
23	
24	## All Settings
25	
26	### Model & Thinking
27	
28	| Setting | Type | Default | Description |
29	|---------|------|---------|-------------|
30	| `defaultProvider` | string | - | Startup provider (e.g., `"anthropic"`, `"openai"`; saved with Ctrl+S in `/model`, or edited manually) |
31	| `defaultModel` | string | - | Startup model ID (saved with Ctrl+S in `/model`, or edited manually) |
32	| `defaultThinkingLevel` | string | - | Startup thinking level (saved with Ctrl+S in `/thinking`, or edited manually): `"off"`, `"minimal"`, `"low"`, `"medium"`, `"high"`, `"xhigh"`, `"max"` |
33	| `modelThinkingLevels` | object | - | Per-model startup thinking levels keyed by `"provider/modelId"`; configure from `/settings` → Default thinking level per model or edit manually |
34	| `hideThinkingBlock` | boolean | `false` | Hide thinking blocks in output |
35	| `showCacheMissNotices` | boolean | `false` | Show transcript notices for significant prompt-cache misses and compaction or branch-summary usage |
36	| `thinkingBudgets` | object | - | Custom token budgets per thinking level. Anthropic, Google, and Bedrock use these natively. OpenAI-compatible models use them when `compat.thinkingTokenBudgetField` (or `supportsThinkingTokenBudget`) is set. |

<summary>Tool use: **Read**</summary>
 `/Users/david/.local/lib/node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/docs/session-format.md`

```text
1	# Session File Format
2	
3	Sessions are stored as JSONL (JSON Lines) files. Each line is a JSON object with a `type` field. Session entries form a tree structure via `id`/`parentId` fields, enabling in-place branching without creating new files.
4	
5	## File Location
6	
7	```
8	~/.pi/agent/sessions/--<path>--/<timestamp>_<uuid>.jsonl
9	```
10	
11	Where `<path>` is the working directory with `/` replaced by `-`.
12	
13	## Deleting Sessions
14	
15	Sessions can be removed by deleting their `.jsonl` files under `~/.pi/agent/sessions/`.
16	
17	Pi also supports deleting sessions interactively from `/resume` (select a session and press `Ctrl+D`, then confirm). When available, pi uses the `trash` CLI to avoid permanent deletion.
18	
19	## Session Version
20	
21	Sessions have a version field in the header:
22	
23	- **Version 1**: Linear entry sequence (legacy, auto-migrated on load)
24	- **Version 2**: Tree structure with `id`/`parentId` linking
25	- **Version 3**: Renamed `hookMessage` role to `custom` (extensions unification)
26	
27	Existing sessions are automatically migrated to the current version (v3) when loaded.
28	
29	## Source Files
30	
31	Source on GitHub ([pi-mono](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi-mono)):
32	- [`packages/coding-agent/src/core/session-manager.ts`](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi-mono/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/core/session-manager.ts) - Session entry types and SessionManager
33	- [`packages/coding-agent/src/core/messages.ts`](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi-mono/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/core/messages.ts) - Extended message types (BashExecutionMessage, CustomMessage, etc.)
34	- [`packages/ai/src/types.ts`](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi-mono/blob/main/packages/ai/src/types.ts) - Base message types (UserMessage, AssistantMessage, ToolResultMessage)
35	- [`packages/agent/src/types.ts`](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi-mono/blob/main/packages/agent/src/types.ts) - AgentMessage union type
36	
37	For TypeScript definitions in your project, inspect `node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/dist/` and `node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-ai/dist/`.
38	
39	## Message Types
40	
41	Session entries contain `AgentMessage` objects. Understanding these types is essential for parsing sessions and writing extensions.
42	
43	### Content Blocks
44	
45	Messages contain arrays of typed content blocks:
46	
47	```typescript
48	interface TextContent {
49	  type: "text";
50	  text: string;
51	}
52	
53	interface ImageContent {
54	  type: "image";
55	  data: string;      // base64 encoded
56	  mimeType: string;  // e.g., "image/jpeg", "image/png"
57	}
58	
59	interface ThinkingContent {
60	  type: "thinking";
61	  thinking: string;
62	}
63	
64	interface ToolCall {
65	  type: "toolCall";
66	  id: string;
67	  name: string;
68	  arguments: Record<string, any>;
69	}
70	```
71	
72	### Base Message Types (from pi-ai)
73	
74	```typescript
75	interface UserMessage {
76	  role: "user";
77	  content: string | (TextContent | ImageContent)[];
78	  timestamp: number;  // Unix ms
79	}
80	
81	interface AssistantMessage {
82	  role: "assistant";
83	  content: (TextContent | ThinkingContent | ToolCall)[];
84	  api: string;
85	  provider: string;
86	  model: string;
87	  usage: Usage;
88	  stopReason: "stop" | "length" | "toolUse" | "error" | "aborted";
89	  errorMessage?: string;
90	  timestamp: number;
91	}
92	
93	interface ToolResultMessage {
94	  role: "toolResult";
95	  toolCallId: string;
96	  toolName: string;
97	  content: (TextContent | ImageContent)[];
98	  details?: any;      // Tool-specific metadata
99	  usage?: Usage;      // Nested LLM work performed by the tool
100	  isError: boolean;
101	  timestamp: number;
102	}
103	
104	interface Usage {
105	  input: number;
106	  output: number;
107	  cacheRead: number;
108	  cacheWrite: number;
109	  totalTokens: number;
110	  cost: {
111	    input: number;
112	    output: number;
113	    cacheRead: number;
114	    cacheWrite: number;
115	    total: number;
116	  };
117	}
118	```
119	
120	The exported pi-ai `StopReason` type also includes `"pending"`, but that value is reserved for partial messages in streaming events. Terminal `done`/`error` messages replace it with a completion reason before pi persists the assistant message, so `"pending"` should never appear in session JSONL.
121	
122	### Extended Message Types (from pi-coding-agent)
123	
124	```typescript
125	interface BashExecutionMessage {
126	  role: "bashExecution";
127	  command: string;
128	  output: string;
129	  exitCode: number | undefined;
130	  cancelled: boolean;
131	  truncated: boolean;
132	  fullOutputPath?: string;
133	  excludeFromContext?: boolean;  // true for !! prefix commands
134	  timestamp: number;
135	}
136	
137	interface CustomMessage {
138	  role: "custom";
139	  customType: string;            // Extension identifier
140	  content: string | (TextContent | ImageContent)[];
141	  display: boolean;              // Show in TUI
142	  details?: any;                 // Extension-specific metadata
143	  timestamp: number;
144	}
145	
146	interface BranchSummaryMessage {
147	  role: "branchSummary";
148	  summary: string;
149	  fromId: string;                // Entry we branched from
150	  timestamp: number;
151	}
152	
153	interface CompactionSummaryMessage {
154	  role: "compactionSummary";
155	  summary: string;
156	  tokensBefore: number;
157	  timestamp: number;
158	}
159	```
160	
161	### AgentMessage Union
162	
163	```typescript
164	type AgentMessage =
165	  | UserMessage
166	  | AssistantMessage
167	  | ToolResultMessage
168	  | BashExecutionMessage
169	  | CustomMessage
170	  | BranchSummaryMessage
171	  | CompactionSummaryMessage;
172	```
173	
174	## Entry Base
175	
176	All entries (except `SessionHeader`) extend `SessionEntryBase`:
177	
178	```typescript
179	interface SessionEntryBase {
180	  type: string;
181	  id: string;           // 8-char hex ID
182	  parentId: string | null;  // Parent entry ID (null for first entry)
183	  timestamp: string;    // ISO timestamp
184	}
185	```
186	
187	## Entry Types
188	
189	### SessionHeader
190	
191	First line of the file. Metadata only, not part of the tree (no `id`/`parentId`).
192	
193	```json
194	{"type":"session","version":3,"id":"uuid","timestamp":"2024-12-03T14:00:00.000Z","cwd":"/path/to/project"}
195	```
196	
197	For sessions with a parent (created via `/fork`, `/clone`, or `newSession({ parentSession })`):
198	
199	```json
200	{"type":"session","version":3,"id":"uuid","timestamp":"2024-12-03T14:00:00.000Z","cwd":"/path/to/project","parentSession":"/path/to/original/session.jsonl"}
201	```
202	
203	### SessionMessageEntry
204	
205	A message in the conversation. The `message` field contains an `AgentMessage`.
206	
207	```json
208	{"type":"message","id":"a1b2c3d4","parentId":"prev1234","timestamp":"2024-12-03T14:00:01.000Z","message":{"role":"user","content":"Hello"}}
209	{"type":"message","id":"b2c3d4e5","parentId":"a1b2c3d4","timestamp":"2024-12-03T14:00:02.000Z","message":{"role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Hi!"}],"provider":"anthropic","model":"claude-sonnet-4-5","usage":{...},"stopReason":"stop"}}
210	{"type":"message","id":"c3d4e5f6","parentId":"b2c3d4e5","timestamp":"2024-12-03T14:00:03.000Z","message":{"role":"toolResult","toolCallId":"call_123","toolName":"bash","content":[{"type":"text","text":"output"}],"isError":false}}
211	```
212	
213	### ModelChangeEntry
214	
215	Emitted when the user switches models mid-session.
216	
217	```json
218	{"type":"model_change","id":"d4e5f6g7","parentId":"c3d4e5f6","timestamp":"2024-12-03T14:05:00.000Z","provider":"openai","modelId":"gpt-4o"}
219	```
220	
221	### ThinkingLevelChangeEntry
222	
223	Emitted when the user changes the thinking/reasoning level.
224	
225	```json
226	{"type":"thinking_level_change","id":"e5f6g7h8","parentId":"d4e5f6g7","timestamp":"2024-12-03T14:06:00.000Z","thinkingLevel":"high"}
227	```
228	
229	### CompactionEntry
230	
231	Created when context is compacted. Stores a summary of earlier messages.
232	
233	```json
234	{"type":"compaction","id":"f6g7h8i9","parentId":"e5f6g7h8","timestamp":"2024-12-03T14:10:00.000Z","summary":"User discussed X, Y, Z...","firstKeptEntryId":"c3d4e5f6","tokensBefore":50000}
235	```
236	
237	Newer harness-generated compactions embed the retained post-compaction context directly on the entry, instead of `firstKeptEntryId`:
238	
239	```json
240	{"type":"compaction","id":"f6g7h8i9","parentId":"e5f6g7h8","timestamp":"2024-12-03T14:10:00.000Z","summary":"User discussed X, Y, Z...","tokensBefore":50000,"retainedTail":[{"role":"user","content":"latest request"},{"role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"latest reply"}],"provider":"anthropic","model":"claude-sonnet-4-5","usage":{...},"stopReason":"stop"}]}
```
</details></tool-use>

220	`npmCommand` is used for all npm package-manager operations, including installs, uninstalls, and dependency installs inside git packages. User-scoped npm packages install under `~/.pi/agent/npm/`; project-scoped npm packages install under `.pi/npm/`. Use argv-style entries exactly as the process should be launched. When `npmCommand` is configured, git package dependency installs use plain `install` to avoid npm-specific flags in wrappers or alternate package managers.
221	
222	### Tools
223	
224	| Setting | Type | Default | Description |
225	|---------|------|---------|-------------|
226	| `defaultTools` | string[] | - | Built-in tools enabled initially. When omitted, Pi uses its standard defaults |
227	
228	`defaultTools` selects the built-in tools enabled at startup. Extension and SDK custom tools remain enabled. Available built-ins are `read`, `bash`, `powershell`, `edit`, `write`, `grep`, `find`, and `ls`:
229	
230	```json
231	{
232	  "defaultTools": ["bash", "edit", "write"]
233	}
234	```
235	
236	On Windows, select `powershell` instead of `bash`, or include both:
237	
238	```json
239	{
240	  "defaultTools": ["read", "powershell", "edit", "write"]
241	}
242	```
243	
244	An empty array starts with no built-in tools while preserving extension and SDK custom tools. `--tools` replaces this behavior with a strict allowlist for all tools, `--no-tools` disables all tools, and `--no-builtin-tools` disables the built-in defaults. `--exclude-tools` filters the resulting list. A project `defaultTools` array replaces the global array.
245	
246	### Sessions
247	
248	| Setting | Type | Default | Description |
249	|---------|------|---------|-------------|
250	| `sessionDir` | string | - | Directory where session files are stored. Accepts absolute or relative paths, plus `~`. |
251	
252	```json
253	{ "sessionDir": ".pi/sessions" }
254	```
255	
256	When multiple sources specify a session directory, precedence is `--session-dir`, `PI_CODING_AGENT_SESSION_DIR`, then `sessionDir` in settings.json.
257	
258	### Model Cycling
259	
260	| Setting | Type | Default | Description |
261	|---------|------|---------|-------------|
262	| `enabledModels` | string[] | - | Model patterns for Ctrl+P cycling (same format as `--models` CLI flag) |
263	
264	```json
265	{
266	  "enabledModels": ["claude-*", "gpt-4o", "gemini-2*"]
267	}
268	```
269	
270	### Markdown
271	
272	| Setting | Type | Default | Description |
273	|---------|------|---------|-------------|
274	| `markdown.codeBlockIndent` | string | `"  "` | Indentation for code blocks |
275	| `markdown.mermaid` | string | `"streaming"` | Mermaid rendering mode: `"off"`, `"final"`, or `"streaming"` |
276	
277	### Resources
278	
279	These settings define where to load extensions, skills, prompts, and themes from.
280	
281	Paths in `~/.pi/agent/settings.json` resolve relative to `~/.pi/agent`. Paths in `.pi/settings.json` resolve relative to `.pi`. Absolute paths and `~` are supported.
282	
283	| Setting | Type | Default | Description |
284	|---------|------|---------|-------------|
285	| `packages` | array | `[]` | npm/git packages to load resources from |
286	| `extensions` | string[] | `[]` | Local extension file paths or directories |
287	| `skills` | string[] | `[]` | Local skill file paths or directories |
288	| `prompts` | string[] | `[]` | Local prompt template paths or directories |
289	| `themes` | string[] | `[]` | Local theme file paths or directories |
290	| `enableSkillCommands` | boolean | `true` | Register skills as `/skill:name` commands |
291	
292	Arrays support glob patterns and exclusions. Use `!pattern` to exclude. Use `+path` to force-include an exact path and `-path` to force-exclude an exact path.
293	
294	#### packages
295	
296	String form loads all resources from a package:
297	
298	```json
299	{
300	  "packages": ["pi-skills", "@org/my-extension"]
301	}
302	```
303	
304	Object form filters which resources to load:
305	
306	```json
307	{
308	  "packages": [
309	    {
310	      "source": "pi-skills",
311	      "skills": ["brave-search", "transcribe"],
312	      "extensions": []
313	    }
314	  ]
315	}
316	```
317	
318	See [packages.md](packages.md) for package management details.
319	
320	## Example
321	
322	```json
323	{
324	  "defaultProvider": "anthropic",
325	  "defaultModel": "claude-sonnet-4-20250514",
326	  "defaultThinkingLevel": "medium",
327	  "modelThinkingLevels": {
328	    "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-20250514": "high"
329	  },
330	  "theme": "dark",
331	  "compaction": {
332	    "enabled": true,
333	    "reserveTokens": 16384,
334	    "keepRecentTokens": 20000
335	  },
336	  "retry": {
337	    "enabled": true,
338	    "maxRetries": 3
339	  },
340	  "enabledModels": ["claude-*", "gpt-4o"],
341	  "warnings": {
342	    "anthropicExtraUsage": true
343	  },
344	  "packages": ["pi-skills"]
345	}
346	```
347	
348	## Project Overrides
349	
350	Project settings (`.pi/settings.json`) override global settings. Nested objects are merged:
351	
352	```json
353	// ~/.pi/agent/settings.json (global)
354	{
355	  "theme": "dark",
356	  "compaction": { "enabled": true, "reserveTokens": 16384 }
357	}
358	
359	// .pi/settings.json (project)
360	{
361	  "compaction": { "reserveTokens": 8192 }
362	}
363	
364	// Result
365	{
366	  "theme": "dark",
367	  "compaction": { "enabled": true, "reserveTokens": 8192 }
368	}
369	```
```

<summary>Tool use: **Read**</summary>
 `/Users/david/.local/lib/node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/docs/session-format.md`

```text
306	## Tree Structure
307	
308	Entries form a tree:
309	- First entry has `parentId: null`
310	- Each subsequent entry points to its parent via `parentId`
311	- Branching creates new children from an earlier entry
312	- The "leaf" is the current position in the tree
313	
314	```
315	[user msg] ─── [assistant] ─── [user msg] ─── [assistant] ─┬─ [user msg] ← current leaf
316	                                                            │
317	                                                            └─ [branch_summary] ─── [user msg] ← alternate branch
318	```
319	
320	## Context Building
321	
322	`buildContextEntries()` walks from the current leaf to the root, producing the active entry list while honoring compaction:
323	
324	1. Collects all entries on the path
325	2. If a `CompactionEntry` is on the path:
326	   - Includes the compaction entry first
327	   - If `retainedTail` is present, it acts as a self-contained checkpoint and entries after the compaction are included
328	   - Otherwise entries from `firstKeptEntryId` to the compaction are included
329	   - Then entries after compaction are included
330	3. Preserves non-message entries in the selected range so interactive mode can render them
331	
332	`buildSessionContext()` builds on that entry list to produce the message list for the LLM:
333	
334	1. Extracts current model and thinking level settings from the full path
335	2. Converts selected entries to messages:
336	   - `message` -> stored `AgentMessage`
337	   - `compaction` -> `compactionSummary` plus `retainedTail` when present
338	   - `branch_summary` -> `branchSummary`
339	   - `custom_message` -> `CustomMessage`
340	   - `custom` -> no context message
341	
342	This makes newer compactions act like self-contained checkpoints. `retainedTail` is optional only so older sessions that only store `firstKeptEntryId` continue to load correctly.
343	
344	## Parsing Example
345	
346	```typescript
347	import { readFileSync } from "fs";
348	
349	const lines = readFileSync("session.jsonl", "utf8").trim().split("\n");
350	
351	for (const line of lines) {
352	  const entry = JSON.parse(line);
353	
354	  switch (entry.type) {
355	    case "session":
356	      console.log(`Session v${entry.version ?? 1}: ${entry.id}`);
357	      break;
358	    case "message":
359	      console.log(`[${entry.id}] ${entry.message.role}: ${JSON.stringify(entry.message.content)}`);
360	      break;
361	    case "compaction":
362	      console.log(`[${entry.id}] Compaction: ${entry.tokensBefore} tokens summarized`);
363	      break;
364	    case "branch_summary":
365	      console.log(`[${entry.id}] Branch from ${entry.fromId}`);
366	      break;
367	    case "custom":
368	      console.log(`[${entry.id}] Custom (${entry.customType}): ${JSON.stringify(entry.data)}`);
369	      break;
370	    case "custom_message":
371	      console.log(`[${entry.id}] Extension message (${entry.customType}): ${entry.content}`);
372	      break;
373	    case "label":
374	      console.log(`[${entry.id}] Label "${entry.label}" on ${entry.targetId}`);
375	      break;
376	    case "model_change":
377	      console.log(`[${entry.id}] Model: ${entry.provider}/${entry.modelId}`);
378	      break;
379	    case "thinking_level_change":
380	      console.log(`[${entry.id}] Thinking: ${entry.thinkingLevel}`);
381	      break;
382	  }
383	}
384	```
385	
386	## SessionManager API
387	
388	Key methods for working with sessions programmatically.
389	
390	### Static Creation Methods
391	- `SessionManager.create(cwd, sessionDir?)` - New session
392	- `SessionManager.open(path, sessionDir?)` - Open existing session file
393	- `SessionManager.continueRecent(cwd, sessionDir?)` - Continue most recent or create new
394	- `SessionManager.inMemory(cwd?)` - No file persistence
395	- `SessionManager.forkFrom(sourcePath, targetCwd, sessionDir?)` - Fork session from another project
396	
397	### Static Listing Methods
398	- `SessionManager.list(cwd, sessionDir?, onProgress?)` - List sessions for a directory
399	- `SessionManager.listAll(onProgress?)` - List all sessions across all projects
400	
401	### Instance Methods - Session Management
402	- `newSession(options?)` - Start a new session (options: `{ parentSession?: string }`)
403	- `setSessionFile(path)` - Switch to a different session file
404	- `createBranchedSession(leafId)` - Extract branch to new session file
405	
406	### Instance Methods - Appending (all return entry ID)
407	- `appendMessage(message)` - Add message
408	- `appendThinkingLevelChange(level)` - Record thinking change
409	- `appendModelChange(provider, modelId)` - Record model change
410	- `appendCompaction(summary, firstKeptEntryId, tokensBefore, details?, fromHook?)` - Add compaction
411	- `appendCustomEntry(customType, data?)` - Extension state (not in context)
412	- `appendSessionInfo(name)` - Set session display name
413	- `appendCustomMessageEntry(customType, content, display, details?)` - Extension message (in context)
414	- `appendLabelChange(targetId, label)` - Set/clear label
415	
416	### Instance Methods - Tree Navigation
417	- `getLeafId()` - Current position
418	- `getLeafEntry()` - Get current leaf entry
419	- `getEntry(id)` - Get entry by ID
420	- `getBranch(fromId?)` - Walk from entry to root
421	- `getTree()` - Get full tree structure
422	- `getChildren(parentId)` - Get direct children
423	- `getLabel(id)` - Get label for entry
424	- `branch(entryId)` - Move leaf to earlier entry
425	- `resetLeaf()` - Reset leaf to null (before any entries)
426	- `branchWithSummary(entryId, summary, details?, fromHook?)` - Branch with context summary
427	
428	### Instance Methods - Context & Info
429	- `buildContextEntries()` - Get active branch entries with compaction applied
430	- `buildSessionContext()` - Get messages, thinkingLevel, and model for LLM
431	- `getEntries()` - All entries (excluding header)
432	- `getHeader()` - Session header metadata
433	- `getSessionName()` - Get display name from latest session_info entry
434	- `getCwd()` - Working directory
435	- `getSessionDir()` - Session storage directory
436	- `getSessionId()` - Session UUID
437	- `getSessionFile()` - Session file path (undefined for in-memory)
438	- `isPersisted()` - Whether session is saved to disk
```
</details></tool-use>

1	/**
2	 * RPC mode: Headless operation with JSON stdin/stdout protocol.
3	 *
4	 * Used for embedding the agent in other applications.
5	 * Receives commands as JSON on stdin, outputs events and responses as JSON on stdout.
6	 *
7	 * Protocol:
8	 * - Commands: JSON objects with `type` field, optional `id` for correlation
9	 * - Responses: JSON objects with `type: "response"`, `command`, `success`, and optional `data`/`error`
10	 * - Events: AgentSessionEvent objects streamed as they occur
11	 * - Extension UI: Extension UI requests are emitted, client responds with extension_ui_response

The extension contract is broad but mode-sensitive: extension commands and hooks still run headlessly; RPC can round-trip standard dialogs and notifications; JSON/print modes cannot prompt; custom TUI components, renderers, editor replacement, and terminal input remain terminal-only. Permission gates are extension patterns rather than a built-in universal policy, and default sibling tool calls run concurrently after sequential preflight—important because a remote approval bridge must not assume one tool at a time.

330	Use for project instructions (`AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md`), conventions, common commands. All matching files are concatenated.
331	
332	Disable context file loading with `--no-context-files` (or `-nc`).
333	
334	### System Prompt
335	
336	Replace the default system prompt with `.pi/SYSTEM.md` (project) or `~/.pi/agent/SYSTEM.md` (global). Append without replacing via `APPEND_SYSTEM.md`.
337	
338	---
339	
340	## Customization
341	
342	### Prompt Templates
343	
344	Reusable prompts as Markdown files. Type `/name` to expand.
345	
346	```markdown
347	<!-- ~/.pi/agent/prompts/review.md -->
348	Review this code for bugs, security issues, and performance problems.
349	Focus on: {{focus}}
350	```
351	
352	Place in `~/.pi/agent/prompts/`, `.pi/prompts/`, or a [pi package](#pi-packages) to share with others. See [docs/prompt-templates.md](docs/prompt-templates.md).
353	
354	### Skills
355	
356	On-demand capability packages following the [Agent Skills standard](https://agentskills.io). Invoke via `/skill:name` or let the agent load them automatically.
357	
358	```markdown
359	<!-- ~/.pi/agent/skills/my-skill/SKILL.md -->
360	# My Skill
361	Use this skill when the user asks about X.
362	
363	## Steps
364	1. Do this
365	2. Then that
366	```
367	
368	Place in `~/.pi/agent/skills/`, `~/.agents/skills/`, `.pi/skills/`, or `.agents/skills/` (from `cwd` up through parent directories) or a [pi package](#pi-packages) to share with others. See [docs/skills.md](docs/skills.md).
369	
370	### Extensions
371	
372	<p align="center"><img src="docs/images/doom-extension.png" alt="Doom Extension" width="600"></p>
373	
374	TypeScript modules that extend pi with custom tools, commands, keyboard shortcuts, event handlers, and UI components.
375	
376	```typescript
377	export default function (pi: ExtensionAPI) {
378	  pi.registerTool({ name: "deploy", ... });
379	  pi.registerCommand("stats", { ... });
380	  pi.on("tool_call", async (event, ctx) => { ... });
381	}
382	```
383	
384	The default export can also be `async`. pi waits for async extension factories before startup continues, which is useful for one-time initialization such as fetching remote model lists before calling `pi.registerProvider()`.
385	
386	**What's possible:**
387	- Custom tools (or replace built-in tools entirely)
388	- Sub-agents and plan mode
389	- Custom compaction and summarization
390	- Permission gates and path protection
391	- Custom editors and UI components
392	- Status lines, headers, footers
393	- Git checkpointing and auto-commit
394	- SSH and sandbox execution
395	- MCP server integration
396	- Make pi look like Claude Code
397	- Games while waiting (yes, Doom runs)
398	- ...anything you can dream up
399	
400	Place in `~/.pi/agent/extensions/`, `.pi/extensions/`, or a [pi package](#pi-packages) to share with others. See [docs/extensions.md](docs/extensions.md) and [examples/extensions/](examples/extensions/).
401	
402	### Themes
403	
404	Built-in: `dark`, `light`. Themes hot-reload: modify the active theme file and pi immediately applies changes.
405	
406	Place in `~/.pi/agent/themes/`, `.pi/themes/`, or a [pi package](#pi-packages) to share with others. See [docs/themes.md](docs/themes.md).
407	
408	### Pi Packages
409	
410	Bundle and share extensions, skills, prompts, and themes via npm or git. Find packages on [npmjs.com](https://www.npmjs.com/search?q=keywords%3Api-package) or [Discord](https://discord.com/channels/1456806362351669492/1457744485428629628).
411	
412	> **Security:** Pi packages run with full system access. Extensions execute arbitrary code, and skills can instruct the model to perform any action including running executables. Review source code before installing third-party packages.
413	
414	```bash
415	pi install npm:@foo/pi-tools
416	pi install npm:@foo/pi-tools@1.2.3      # pinned version
417	pi install git:github.com/user/repo
418	pi install git:github.com/user/repo@v1  # tag or commit
419	pi install git:git@github.com:user/repo
420	pi install git:git@github.com:user/repo@v1  # tag or commit
421	pi install https://github.com/user/repo
422	pi install https://github.com/user/repo@v1      # tag or commit
423	pi install ssh://git@github.com/user/repo
424	pi install ssh://git@github.com/user/repo@v1    # tag or commit
425	pi remove npm:@foo/pi-tools
426	pi uninstall npm:@foo/pi-tools          # alias for remove
427	pi list
428	pi update                               # update pi only
429	pi update --all                         # update pi and packages
430	pi update --extensions                  # update packages only
431	pi update --models                      # refresh model catalogs only
432	pi update --self                        # update pi only
433	pi update --self --force                # reinstall pi even if current
434	pi update npm:@foo/pi-tools             # update one package
435	pi config                               # enable/disable extensions, skills, prompts, themes
436	```
437	
438	Packages install to `~/.pi/agent/git/` (git) or `~/.pi/agent/npm/` (npm). Use `-l` for project-local installs (`.pi/git/`, `.pi/npm/`). Git `@ref` values are pinned tags or commits; pinned packages are skipped by `pi update --extensions` and `pi update --all`, so use `pi install git:host/user/repo@new-ref` to move an existing package to a new ref. Git packages install dependencies with `npm install --omit=dev` by default, so runtime deps must be listed under `dependencies`; when `npmCommand` is configured, git packages use plain `install` for compatibility with wrappers. If you use a Node version manager and want package installs to reuse a stable npm context, set `npmCommand` in `settings.json`, for example `["mise", "exec", "node@20", "--", "npm"]`.
439	
440	Create a package by adding a `pi` key to `package.json`:
441	
442	```json
443	{
444	  "name": "my-pi-package",
445	  "keywords": ["pi-package"],
446	  "pi": {
447	    "extensions": ["./extensions"],
448	    "skills": ["./skills"],
449	    "prompts": ["./prompts"],
450	    "themes": ["./themes"]
451	  }
452	}
453	```
454	
455	Without a `pi` manifest, pi auto-discovers from conventional directories (`extensions/`, `skills/`, `prompts/`, `themes/`).
456	
457	See [docs/packages.md](docs/packages.md).
458	
459	---
460	
461	## Programmatic Usage
462	
463	### SDK
464	
465	```typescript
466	import { createAgentSession, ModelRuntime, SessionManager } from "@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent";
467	
468	const modelRuntime = await ModelRuntime.create();
469	const { session } = await createAgentSession({
470	  sessionManager: SessionManager.inMemory(),
471	  modelRuntime,
472	});
473	
474	await session.prompt("What files are in the current directory?");
475	```
476	
477	For advanced multi-session runtime replacement, use `createAgentSessionRuntime()` and `AgentSessionRuntime`.
478	
479	See [docs/sdk.md](docs/sdk.md) and [examples/sdk/](examples/sdk/).
```
</details></tool-use>

## Package metadata
- **Name:** `pi-discord-bridge`
- **Version:** `1.0.1`
- **Published:** July 3, 2026
- **Type:** Pi extension
- **License:** MIT
- **Author:** `notdezzi`
- **Size:** 81.8 KB
- **Dependencies:** 1 dependency and 3 peer dependencies
- **Official status:** Not labeled official; based on the listed author, it should be treated as a community/third-party package.
- **Source repository:** No package-specific repository is identified. The page’s GitHub link points to the broader Pi `coding-agent` path.

## Description and features
The extension connects Pi coding sessions with Discord. It can:
- Create or reuse a Discord channel for each project.
- Create a separate thread for each Pi session.
- Stream assistant output, tool calls, and tool results.
- Forward Discord messages into Pi.
- Abort turns through commands or a stop reaction.
- Register Discord slash commands.
- Support muting, reconnection, testing, compaction, and starting new sessions.

## Installation
Recommended Pi command:

```text
/pi-install npm:pi-discord-bridge
```

Alternatively, add `npm:pi-discord-bridge` to Pi’s package settings.

## Architecture and API use
The package declares `./index.ts` as its extension entry point. It integrates with Pi’s extension/package system and communicates with Discord through a bot. Its documented interface includes Discord slash commands such as `/session`, `/abort`, `/compact`, `/new`, `/mute`, and status/reconnection commands, plus Pi-side commands for Discord status, testing, muting, reconnection, arming session replacement, and launcher status.

## Authentication and security
Configuration is read from `~/.pi/.env`, including:
- Discord bot token.
- Allowed Discord user IDs.
- Guild and channel identifiers.
- Enablement and rendering controls.

The Discord bot requires permissions including message sending/history access, thread creation/management, reactions, and possibly channel management. The package page warns that Pi packages can execute code and affect agent behavior, so the source should be reviewed before installation.

## Sessions, concurrency, and lifecycle
The documented model is one project channel per working directory and one thread per Pi session. Channels may be created or reused, while session threads receive short generated names. The extension supports session creation, aborting, compaction, muting, reconnection, and Discord-driven input. No explicit limits or guarantees about concurrent sessions, process isolation, persistence, or failure recovery are stated.
```

## Package metadata

- **Name:** `pi-slack-bridge`
- **Version:** `0.3.0`
- **Type:** Pi extension
- **Author:** thanhtientc
- **License:** MIT
- **Published:** August 18, 2026
- **Size:** 313 KB
- **Dependencies:** 1 runtime dependency and 3 peer dependencies
- **npm:** `pi-slack-bridge`
- **Source repository:** https://github.com/comsysto/pi-slack-bridge
- **Package home:** The repository README
- **Status:** Presented as a community package, not an official Pi-maintained package.

## Description and installation

This extension lets users control a Pi coding-agent session through Slack, using Slack Socket Mode. It is derived from `pi-messenger-bridge` but focuses exclusively on Slack.

Install with:

```text
pi install npm:pi-slack-bridge
```

The manifest loads `./dist/bridge/index.js`.

## Main features

- Two-way Slack messaging with Pi
- Slack file transfer in both directions
- Slack Block Kit-based Markdown formatting
- Remote stop requests
- Slack status details such as working directory, model, and context information
- Slack-thread association for separate Pi sessions
- Session history replay when resuming or handing over
- Creation, listing, resumption, and switching of Pi sessions
- Terminal-to-Slack handover
- Local opt-in or opt-out of automatic bridging
- Deterministic terminal commands and Slack dot commands that do not invoke the model
- Support for Pi skills and prompt templates through Slack commands

## Architecture and API use

- Implemented as a Pi extension loaded by the Pi harness.
- Uses Slack Socket Mode for real-time communication.
- Relies on Slack messaging, file, reaction, user, and direct-message capabilities.
- Uses Slack Block Kit Markdown blocks for formatted output.
- Uses `tmux` to host and switch between Pi terminal sessions.
- Uses local configuration, lock, download, and handoff files under `~/.pi`.
- Provides terminal commands under `/slk-bridge` and Slack commands beginning with `.bridge`.
- Includes a test suite covering configuration, locking, block splitting, history extraction, and formatting.

## Slack setup and authentication

Required Slack credentials:

- Bot token beginning with `xoxb-`
- App-level token beginning with `xapp-`
- Socket Mode enabled
- App Home Messages tab enabled
- App-level `connections:write` permission

The README lists bot permissions for messaging, file access, direct-message history and metadata, reactions, and user identification.

A first-time Slack user receives a six-digit challenge that appears in the Pi terminal. The user enters it in Slack; successful verification makes that user trusted for the bridge.

## Security and warnings

- Configuration is stored at `~/.pi/slk-bridge.json`.
- The page states that configuration and its parent directory receive restrictive permissions.
- Downloads go under `~/.pi/slk-bridge-downloads/slack/`.
- Handoff data goes under `~/.pi/slk-bridge-handoffs/`.
- Environment variables override file-based settings.
- Challenge verification allows three attempts and expires after two minutes.
- User identifiers are namespaced by transport.
- Only one Slack user can be trusted until claiming is reopened with:

```text
/slk-bridge releaseclaim
```

The package can execute code and affect agent behavior, so the page advises reviewing third-party source before installation.

## Session, concurrency, and lifecycle claims

- Only one terminal session can own the Slack bridge at a time.
- A newly connected session takes ownership from the previous one.
- Switching sessions creates a separate Slack thread.
- Handover requires an already authenticated Slack target.
- Session switching and handoff depend on `tmux` and having `pi` available on `PATH`.
- A single-instance guard prevents duplicate Slack connections.
- Automatic connection can occur after configuration or on later Pi startup when enabled in the local configuration.
```

## Package metadata

- **Name:** `pi-web-ui`
- **Version:** `0.58.0`
- **Published:** August 30, 2026
- **Type:** Pi extension
- **License:** MIT
- **Author:** `xingshuyin`
- **Source repository:** https://github.com/xing-shuyin/pi-web-ui
- **Size:** 2.3 MB
- **Dependencies:** 15; peers: 0
- **Pi manifest:** loads `./extensions`

## Description and installation

A browser-based chat and development interface for the Pi coding agent, supporting conversations, tool inspection, files, terminals, Git, models, plugins, themes, and settings.

```bash
npm i -g pi-web-ui
# or
npx pi-web-ui
```

It requires Node.js 22.19 or newer and a configured Pi installation.

## Main features

- Streaming chat, thinking blocks, tool-call status, slash commands, steering, and edit/re-ask branching.
- Multiple conversations per project with background activity.
- File uploads, image handling, previews, line selection, media downloads, and file-tree watching.
- Embedded terminal using xterm.js and node-pty.
- Git status, diffs, branches, commits, push, and pull.
- Model configuration, API-key management, thinking levels, presets, themes, and vision-model bridging.
- Goal-oriented review loops and background-task monitoring.
- Optional UI/agent-tool plugins, including mail, database, editor, and terminal-related integrations.
- Foreground execution plus Docker, systemd, launchd, Windows Task Scheduler, and desktop-shortcut deployment.

## Architecture and API use

The Pi SDK runs inside the server process. Browser communication uses WebSocket streaming, with updates throttled to approximately 60 ms. The application also serves HTTP endpoints for files, health checks, media, and static assets. Terminal sessions use per-client PTYs, and the server watches workspace files with `fs.watch`.

## Authentication and security

- The default bind address is loopback-only.
- Provider credentials and custom headers remain server-side and are not sent to browsers.
- WebSocket connections enforce matching origin and host authority; reverse proxies may use an allowlist.
- No user-login or authentication system is described.
- LAN exposure requires explicitly binding to a non-loopback host and applying appropriate network protection.
- A local control socket supports service status and quiesce operations.

## Sessions, concurrency, and lifecycle

- Session data is stored under `<cwd>/.pi-web` or the configured data directory and survives upgrades and uninstall.
- Each project conversation has its own agent runtime and can continue running while another conversation is selected.
- Follow-up messages can be queued while a response is active.
- Quiesce mode blocks new chats, prompts, forks, and resumes while allowing active runs to finish.
- Services can be installed, started, stopped, restarted, updated, and removed.
- Tool calls exceeding 20 minutes are automatically aborted; bash commands can be stopped independently.

## Warnings

- The page warns that Pi packages can execute code and affect agent behavior, so the source should be reviewed before installation.
- Native `node-pty` installation may require allowing npm install scripts, especially with npm 12 or newer.
- Plugins can install dependencies automatically and may contain local configuration or state that is not always preserved during forced upgrades.
- The page does not identify the package as an official Pi/Earendil package; it is presented as a separately authored package with its own repository.
```

# pi-telegram

![pi-telegram screenshot](screenshot.png)

**A Telegram companion hub for live Pi sessions.**

`pi-telegram` turns a private Telegram DM into a mobile operator surface for Pi. It accepts prompts, queues work, streams readable previews, delivers final replies and files, exposes safe controls, and lets companion extensions add Telegram-native capabilities without owning a second bot loop.

It is a **runtime adapter**, not a remote terminal. Start or supervise work in the Pi TUI, then continue from Telegram while away from the keyboard. Each Telegram destination follows a running Pi instance and sends prompts into that instance's currently active session; it is not permanently bound to one session file or session identity. The bridge preserves Pi session semantics instead of pretending Telegram is a PTY, shell, process launcher, or session browser. That boundary is the product: Telegram gets safe runtime handles, not raw terminal power.

Every completed intermediate commentary block from a Telegram-originated turn is delivered once as its own message before the existing final reply. Proactive push is enabled by default for local, autonomous, and unclassified extension follow-up work: `assistant.proactivePush` projects visible checkpoints and the final answer to the authorized Telegram target once and in order, preserving assistant-authored `telegram_button` comments as interactive prompt buttons; set it explicitly to `false` to disable only that local/autonomous projection. Neither path mirrors local prompts, thinking, tool traffic, token deltas, or stale-generation work. The separate `Activity` setting defaults to `verbose` so new installations discover collapsed provider-exposed thinking and tool evidence immediately; operators can narrow it to one class or choose `quiet`. See [Outbound](docs/outbound.md#public-assistant-output) and the [configuration reference](docs/public-api.md#configuration-api).

## Project status and purpose

- `badlogic/pi-telegram` is a public MIT-licensed GitHub project that bridges Telegram direct messages into a Pi coding session.
- The visible repository shows 7 commits, 5 issues, 10 pull requests, 286 stars, and 93 forks. No release or package metadata is shown.
- Neither the README nor the visible page labels it official or experimental.
- It supports text, images, albums, files, streamed replies, stopping active runs, and returning generated files.

## Installation and operation

Install from Git:

```text
pi install git:github.com/badlogic/pi-telegram
```

Run for one invocation:

```text
pi -e git:github.com/badlogic/pi-telegram
```

Telegram setup requires a BotFather-created bot and its token. After starting Pi, run:

```text
/telegram-setup
```

Configuration is stored at:

```text
~/.pi/agent/telegram.json
```

The bridge is attached to the currently active Pi session with:

```text
/telegram-connect
```

Other lifecycle commands are:

```text
/telegram-disconnect
/telegram-status
```

## Authentication and admission control

- The bot token is entered during `/telegram-setup`.
- After connecting, the operator opens the bot DM and sends `/start`.
- The first Telegram user to do this becomes the sole permitted user.
- The README does not explain how that pairing is stored, changed, reset, or protected across sessions.
- Group, channel, multi-user, and role-based access behavior is not documented.

## Pi integration and tools

Documented Pi-facing behavior includes:

- Incoming text is forwarded with a `[telegram]` prefix.
- Downloaded media is placed under `~/.pi/agent/tmp/telegram`.
- Images are passed to Pi as image inputs.
- Pi can return files through the `telegram_attach` tool; those files are sent with the next Telegram response.

The README does not expose Pi event-handler names, tool schemas, approval prompts, permission scopes, sandboxing, or confirmation behavior. It also does not state whether attachment requests require user approval.

## Sessions and persistence

- The bridge is explicitly tied to one Pi session at a time.
- Only the connected session should own the bot.
- Disconnecting stops polling for the current session.
- The configuration file persists on disk, but the README does not specify which values it contains or whether the Telegram-user pairing and session association persist there.
- No session database, cross-session routing, or multi-process coordination is described.

## Streaming and message behavior

- Assistant text is previewed in Telegram while Pi generates a response.
- The extension first attempts Telegram’s `sendMessageDraft`.
- If that is unavailable for the bot, it uses `sendMessage` followed by `editMessageText`.
- Replies exceeding Telegram’s 4096-character limit are divided into multiple messages.
- Responses are ordinary bot messages rather than replies attached to the triggering message.
- No detailed Pi event model, cancellation event, stream buffering policy, or error-reporting behavior is given.

## Concurrency and stopping

- A Telegram message received while Pi is working is queued.
- Queued messages are processed in arrival order.
- Sending either of these commands aborts the active Pi turn:

```text
stop
/stop
```

The README does not describe parallel turns, queue size limits, persistence across restarts, or behavior when a queued request fails.

## Process lifecycle and limitations

- Connecting starts Telegram polling; disconnecting stops it.
- The Pi process must be running for the session-local bridge to operate.
- Reconnection, retry/backoff, crash recovery, daemonization, shutdown handling, and duplicate polling protection are not documented.
- Media is downloaded onto the local filesystem, and outbound artifacts are explicitly sent through Pi’s attachment tool.
- The documented interface assumes Telegram DMs and a running Pi session; no web UI or other Telegram conversation types are covered.

## Scope

This is a **Pi extension/package**, not a separately documented daemon. Installation is through Pi’s package command, and the bridge uses Pi’s in-process APIs. The supplied page does not include source contents, so module boundaries and implementation details cannot be verified.

## Supported transports

- **Telegram:** bot token; configured through BotFather.
- **WhatsApp:** QR-based linked-device login; persistent authentication directory. After linking, the owner must message their own number to activate it.
- **Slack:** bot token plus app token, using Socket Mode.
- **Discord:** bot token, with privileged message-content access enabled and appropriate server permissions.
- **Matrix:** homeserver URL plus access token; invited rooms are joined automatically. Encryption is enabled by default.

Configuration can come from the Pi menu, environment variables, or `~/.pi/msg-bridge.json`. Environment variables take precedence over the file.

## Pi integration and message direction

The README identifies two Pi-native mechanisms:

- `sendUserMessage()` brings remote input into the Pi conversation.
- `turn_end` events are used to send completed Pi-side activity back to remote users.

Therefore the intended flow is bidirectional:

1. An admitted messenger user sends input.
2. The bridge injects it into Pi.
3. Pi’s response and optionally tool-call activity are sent back.

Multi-turn conversations are claimed as supported. The documentation does not specify whether each transport shares one Pi session, whether chats get separate session identifiers, or whether conversations survive Pi restarts.

There is no documented token-by-token streaming protocol, partial-message editing, typing indicator behavior, attachment handling, or cross-messenger message relay. Tool visibility is a configurable feature, but its exact formatting is unspecified.

## Admission and authentication

New users receive a six-digit challenge. The code is displayed in the Pi terminal, and the user submits it in the bot conversation. Successful users become trusted.

The configuration stores:

- Trusted identities
- One administrator identity
- Transport-specific user IDs

IDs are prefixed with their transport, such as `telegram:...` or `whatsapp:...`, to prevent collisions or impersonation across services.

Trusted users may use direct-message administration commands to:

- List or revoke trusted users
- Inspect enabled channels
- Enable channels with `all`, `mentions`, or `trusted-only` access
- Disable channels
- Toggle tool visibility

The README does not explain challenge expiration, retry limits, brute-force protection, administrator bootstrap rules, or whether authentication is tied to a specific Pi project.

## Sessions and persistence

Persistent state is described at two levels:

- Main bridge configuration: `~/.pi/msg-bridge.json`
- WhatsApp authentication: `~/.pi/msg-bridge-whatsapp-auth/`, unless overridden

The configuration includes transport credentials, authentication state, connection preference, widget preference, debugging, and Matrix encryption settings.

The page does **not** document:

- A conversation-to-Pi-session mapping format

## Commands and UI

The Pi-side menu is opened with `/msg-bridge`. Its documented functions cover:

- Transport configuration

The menu’s command form accepts transport-specific credentials. Direct-message administration uses `/help`, `/trusted`, `/revoke`, `/channels`, `/enable`, `/disable`, and `/toggletools`.

## Files and project layout

The repository index lists:

- `src/` — implementation, but individual responsibilities are not shown

The documented development scripts provide build, type-check, test, lint, and lint-fix operations. No test results or coverage information are provided.

## Permissions and security

The README specifies:

- `~/.pi/` directory: mode `700`
- Main configuration: mode `600`
- WhatsApp authentication directory: mode `700`

Credentials may be stored in the configuration file or environment, so host filesystem protection is important. Environment values override file values.

Important warnings include:

- Matrix encryption requires verifying the bot device from another Matrix client.
- Disabling Matrix encryption exposes plaintext to the homeserver.
- With encryption disabled, encrypted rooms cannot be used.

The challenge mechanism and transport-qualified identities provide admission and namespace separation, but the page does not discuss rate limiting, secret rotation, audit logs, message redaction, prompt injection, or protection against malicious content sent by trusted users.

## Concurrency, ownership, and lifecycle

To prevent duplicate polling when Pi sub-agents are created, the bridge uses:

- A process-global guard
- A PID lock at `~/.pi/msg-bridge.lock`

This indicates that one owning Pi process is expected to maintain transport connections. The documentation does not describe stale-lock recovery, PID validation, lock races, multiple independent Pi instances, or handoff behavior.

No standalone service manager, background daemon mode, restart policy, shutdown hook, reconnection strategy, or crash recovery behavior is documented.

<tool-use data-tool-type="read" data-tool-name="WebFetch"><details>
<summary>Tool use: **WebFetch**</summary>
 `https://github.com/ni3do/pi-remote-agent`

```text
## Architecture

- **Flow:** Discord or Slack messages enter an Express-based bridge with bot adapters, which calls the Pi SDK’s `AgentSession`; the agent operates on the mounted workspace.
- **Interfaces:** Web UI, HTTP API on port 3000, Discord, and Slack all use the same running Pi agent process.
- **Web UI:** Provides chat, multiple web sessions, WebSocket-delivered responses, cross-interface activity monitoring, tool-call details, and an activity log.
- **HTTP endpoints:**
  - `POST /api/chat` submits a message for a specified `threadId`.
  - `POST /api/session/new` resets or creates a session for that identifier.
  - `GET /health` provides a health check.
- **Discord:** Requires a bot token and Message Content Intent. It supports mentions, direct messages, automatic replies within tagged threads, and `!new`/`!status`.
- **Slack:** Uses Socket Mode, bot/app tokens, a signing secret, event subscriptions, mentions, direct messages, and `!new`.

## Pi integration and authentication

- Pi is integrated directly through its SDK and `AgentSession`; no A2A layer is included.
- LLM access can use provider API keys, with Anthropic and OpenAI variables documented. The configuration says an API key is required, though it also permits another provider.
- Claude Pro/Max authentication can be transferred through Pi’s `auth.json`, mounted into the container. Pi is expected to refresh that credential.
- The HTTP and web interfaces have no documented authentication or admission control. The README explicitly recommends adding Express authentication before public exposure.
- Bot access is described as limited to configured channels or users, but the supplied material does not explain where or how that allowlist is configured.

## Sessions and persistence

- Discord and Slack threads receive separate sessions with retained conversational history.
- The web UI supports independent sessions, while activity visibility spans all sources.
- Pi sessions are stored in a named Docker volume and survive container restarts and Dokploy redeployments.
- Workspace files persist through a bind mount. Dokploy’s layout also supports persistent SSH material.
- The material does not specify session eviction, recovery semantics, cross-interface session sharing, or exact storage formats.

## Streaming, concurrency, and queueing

- Web chat responses are streamed through WebSockets; the documented WebSocket path is `/ws`.
- The activity view receives real-time events, including tool execution and results.
- The repository description says one Pi agent process serves every interface, but it does not document whether requests are serialized, queued, interrupted, or executed concurrently.
- `MAX_SESSIONS` is shown as configurable, with an example value of eight, but its enforcement behavior is not explained.
- No rate limits, backpressure policy, timeout rules, cancellation controls, or per-user quotas are stated.
- The API example does not establish whether HTTP responses stream or wait for completion.

## Permissions and sandboxing

- The agent can read and modify the mounted project and execute arbitrary commands.
- The recommended boundary is a dedicated workspace rather than the host filesystem.
- Running with reduced container privileges is suggested, but no concrete sandbox, user mapping, seccomp profile, network restriction, resource limit, or command policy is supplied.
- SSH keys may be mounted read-only into the container, and GitHub credentials plus Git identity variables support repository operations. These capabilities increase the impact of a compromised or misused agent.

## Container and process lifecycle

- Docker Compose builds and runs the service; a local-development override uses the local `workspace` directory.
- Dokploy can build, start, redeploy, and optionally auto-deploy from Git pushes.
- Workspace data and Pi sessions are designed to survive rebuilds and restarts.
- Discord and Slack startup is conditional on their environment variables; the web/API service is presented as always available.
- The supplied README does not describe health-based restarts, graceful shutdown, worker supervision, log retention, database migrations, or behavior after an agent crash.

## Configuration and stated limitations

- Main settings include provider credentials, `WORKSPACE_DIR`, `PORT`, bot credentials, Slack Socket Mode credentials, GitHub access, and `MAX_SESSIONS`.
- Optional mounts can provide SSH keys and project-specific `AGENTS.md` instructions.
- The deployment guidance supports domains and HTTPS through Dokploy, but does not itself secure the application.
- The central stated limitation is trust: the agent has broad workspace and command execution authority, while public HTTP exposure lacks built-in authentication.
- A2A is intentionally absent because the project targets human-to-agent interaction; adding it would require an agent-card endpoint and task-lifecycle wrapper.
- No license, formal threat model, authorization model, audit retention policy, or detailed operational limits are provided in the supplied content.
```

## Architecture boundaries

- `index.ts` is the composition root: it connects Pi APIs, Telegram adapters, stores, lifecycle hooks, and domain runtimes. Reusable policy belongs in focused `/lib` domains, not in the composition layer.
- Local modules follow a “Flat Domain DAG”: imports remain acyclic, cohesive domains are preferred, and `Zones:` headers expose cross-cutting responsibility.
- Major boundaries include:
  - **Transport:** Bot API access, polling, ownership locks, and the Threaded Mode bus.
  - **Authority:** journals, queue receipts, ownership, handoff, and recovery.
  - **Interaction:** updates, routing, media, prompts, controls, menus, and rendering.
  - **Pi integration:** lifecycle, commands, tools, prompt guidance, and session fencing.
  - **Delivery:** previews, final replies, activity output, attachments, voice, and generated applications.
- The bridge uses Pi’s public extension surface. It does not mutate private TUI state or emulate terminal input.

## Runtime and session ownership

- Telegram is assigned to a **Pi instance**, identified by process/runtime identity and working directory, rather than permanently to a session file.
- Prompts enter the session currently active in that instance at dispatch time. Local session replacement, resume, fork, or reload can change the session while retaining the instance’s Telegram assignment.
- Session-local state includes queues, active turns, previews, menus, lifecycle hooks, and runtime controllers.
- Profile-scoped durable state includes the bot identity, journal cursor, transport owner slot, logs, state snapshots, thread bindings, and IPC endpoint.
- Transport ownership and semantic queue ownership are separate. Losing the Telegram lock prevents new transport work but does not automatically erase locally accepted queue work.
- A session generation fences delayed callbacks, lifecycle events, previews, controls, compaction, and shutdown effects. Stale generations must fail closed before touching Pi or Telegram.
- Pi remains the supported host: “Pi is the primary and only officially supported host.” Alternate hosts need to reproduce required lifecycle semantics, especially the `agent_settled` boundary.

## Telegram polling and leadership

- Each bot profile has one `getUpdates` loop. Only the exact owner recorded in the private ownership store may poll.
- The owner slot is acquired during connect, preserved as restart intent during graceful quit, and released by disconnect after confirmation.
- Ownership checks are frequent and heartbeat publication is less frequent; every mutation is serialized through an ownership transaction and atomically published.
- Poll requests are bounded by Telegram’s long-poll timeout plus transport grace. Late responses are fenced after cancellation.
- Polling health is distinct from inbound execution. Diagnostics expose phases such as startup, long-polling, journal persistence, retrying, and stopped.
- Read-only menu operations perform required local mutation first, then render or synchronize asynchronously so Telegram offset progress is not held up.
- Passive Pi `print` and `json` modes never become hidden polling owners.

## Queue durability and journal authority

- The journal is the admission authority. A complete Telegram response batch is durably recorded before its offset advances.
- Journal publication and offset publication are separate atomic steps:
  1. Record admitted updates and the new cursor.
  2. Advance the Telegram offset once.
  3. Wake the worker without waiting for semantic processing.
- Every queued prompt or control carries exact source receipts. A receipt records the relevant update identities plus acquiring process, birth identity, session generation, acquisition, and timing data.
- Queue ownership has no time-based expiry. Resolution requires exact settlement, authenticated handoff, or transaction-verified proof that the former process is dead.
- A dispatched prompt remains queued until Pi accepts it. Receipt settlement occurs immediately before normal Pi message submission, favoring no replay over duplicate execution in the narrow crash window afterward.
- Queue lanes rank as control, priority prompt, then default prompt. Keep/Skip and priority changes mutate one queue object rather than creating shadow entries.
- Retryable failures become durable retry records with exponential delay capped at one minute. Independent later entries continue to drain.
- Live handoff transfers one exact receipt to one authenticated recipient. The recipient stages and accepts it atomically; the donor cannot settle or cancel during the transfer.

## Journal storage and recovery

- The durable format combines a compact snapshot with immutable revisioned transaction segments. Readers reject gaps, conflicting revisions, malformed data, identity mismatches, and filename/revision disagreement.
- Compaction runs under the journal lock after segment-count or byte thresholds, publishes a complete private snapshot, then removes obsolete segments on a best-effort basis.
- Journal and segment sizes are bounded. Capacity failures pause polling; valid authority is not silently deleted or reset.
- Startup resumes legacy failed entries as retryable work rather than discarding inbound authority.
- Corruption recovery is conservative: only classifier-approved disposable artifacts may be moved into a timestamped recovery directory, and only after ownership and polling safety checks. Uncertain files remain evidence.
- The process-crash guarantee stops at successful atomic rename visibility; filesystem, host, or power failure can still lose recent writes.

## Threaded Mode and multi-instance behavior

- Private-chat forum threads provide the multi-instance surface. A leader owns polling, direct Bot API calls, the local IPC endpoint, follower liveness, and thread provisioning.
- Other manually launched Pi processes register as followers. They retain their own sessions, queues, active work, previews, and menus, while routing permitted Telegram operations through the leader.
- Followers heartbeat frequently; the leader prunes stale registrations, but heartbeat loss alone does not delete a durable thread binding.
- Leadership can move after stale-owner detection. Election and cleanup are fenced by leader epoch and authenticated registration generation.
- Each live instance has at most one active bound thread. Reconciliation protects pending creations, prevents collisions, and deletes only with current proof.
- Thread names are generated when provisioned and represent instance identity; roles such as leader or follower are operational state, not the user-facing thread name.
- Unbound-thread messages are handled explicitly: the leader may reclaim an available thread, or the system presents a forward/restore choice. Threadless ordinary prompts cannot silently enter an arbitrary instance.
- Profiles are isolated parallel bot runtimes, including journals, locks, logs, state, bindings, and IPC paths.

## Lifecycle

- Session start restores work asynchronously when ownership and identity checks permit; it does not wait for election or reconciliation.
- Session replacement suspends polling and watchers without surrendering restart ownership, then allows the new generation to resume.
- Shutdown clears session-local controllers, fences old callbacks, and settles or discards remaining local queue receipts according to exact ownership rules.
- Telegram-owned activity controls previews, typing, abort history, and final delivery. Local or autonomous Pi work can still produce typing and optionally proactive output when configured.
- Pi’s semantic settlement event, rather than a lower-level agent-end event alone, determines when unrecovered failures may be finalized and queue dispatch can continue.

## Deployment model

- Install the extension in the Pi agent environment; configuration is stored under `~/.pi/agent/telegram.json`.
- Connect a selected profile to acquire its owner slot. Named profiles are parallel bot configurations, while shared assistant and voice settings remain global.
- In Threaded Mode, launch each additional Pi process independently and run connect there to register it as a follower.
- Runtime files under `~/.pi/agent/tmp/telegram/` include ownership, journals, state snapshots, logs, and profile-specific IPC artifacts. They must not be treated as interchangeable or removed wholesale during repair.
- Deployment assumes cooperating Pi processes and atomic local file operations; it does not create a hidden daemon.

## Explicit non-goals

- Remote terminal control or a generic Telegram shell.
- A Telegram session browser, full session navigator, or hidden headless Pi runtime.
- PTY injection, ANSI manipulation, private TUI mutation, or terminal forwarding.
- Automatic spawning of arbitrary follower processes or unbound Telegram threads.
- A complete Telegram topic/thread read model; the API does not provide sufficient listing support.
- A thread-renaming feature or agent-directed naming workflow.
- Mirroring arbitrary TUI `confirm`, `input`, `select`, or `custom` prompts into Telegram.
- Competing polling loops opened by companion extensions.
- Automatic replay of ambiguous non-idempotent sends.
- Power-loss durability, filesystem-level durability, or unrestricted cleanup of authority files.
```
