<tool-use data-tool-type="read" data-tool-name="WebFetch"><details>
<summary>Tool use: **WebFetch**</summary>
 `https://docs.slack.dev/reference/objects/conversation-object`

```text
### Stable canonical identity

Use the conversation ID, scoped by its workspace:

```text
slack:{context_team_id}:{conversation_id}
```

If consumers need an explicit type distinction:

```text
slack:{context_team_id}:{conversation_kind}:{conversation_id}
```

Derive `conversation_kind` from the flags:

- `channel`: `is_channel`
- `group`: `is_group` — legacy private channel, typically with an ID beginning with `G`
- `im`: `is_im` — one-to-one DM; `user` identifies the other participant
- `mpim`: `is_mpim` — private conversation among multiple users

Treat `is_private` as the privacy classification, not as the conversation kind. Do not use `name` or `name_normalized` as identity because names can change.

### Shared and connected conversations

For shared conversations, retain these attributes alongside the canonical key:

- `is_shared`: shared across workspaces in some manner
- `is_ext_shared`: shared with an external organization
- `is_org_shared`: shared among workspaces in one Enterprise organization
- `is_pending_ext_shared`: awaiting external-sharing approval
- `conversation_host_id`: hosting workspace or Enterprise organization
- `enterprise_id`: Enterprise organization
- `shared_team_ids`, `connected_team_ids`, and `internal_team_ids`: associated workspaces
- `pending_shared` and `pending_connected_team_ids`: pending associations

Use `context_team_id` plus the conversation ID for the primary route scope. Add host or Enterprise metadata when routing must distinguish shared-network context; do not substitute workspace lists or mutable names for the conversation ID.
```
</details></tool-use>

<tool-use data-tool-type="read" data-tool-name="WebFetch"><details>
<summary>Tool use: **WebFetch**</summary>
 `https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels/channel-routing`

```text
- Replies return to the originating channel; the model cannot choose another channel.
- Reply metadata includes `ReplyToId`, `ReplyToBody`, and `ReplyToSender`; quoted material is also added to the message body.
- Slack and Discord threads receive a `:thread:<id>` session suffix. Telegram forum topics use `:topic:<id>`. These preserve conversation separation.
- By default, group and channel sessions remain isolated. Sharing them into the main session changes context only, not reply destination or mention rules.
- For shared main-session DMs, an owner is inferred only when `allowFrom` contains one concrete, non-wildcard sender. Messages from other senders update metadata but cannot replace the main session’s `lastRoute`, preventing replies from following the last sender.
- Explicit outbound channel prefixes must match the selected channel; cross-channel targets fail. Account selection should be explicit in multi-account setups, otherwise fallback may choose the first normalized account.

<summary>Tool use: **WebFetch**</summary>
 `https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/session`

```text
## Reset and expiry

- Sessions persist indefinitely unless manually reset or a reset policy is configured.
- Daily resets use the session’s start time and gateway-local hour—not later metadata updates.
- Idle resets use the last real user/channel interaction. Heartbeats, cron, exec, and other system events do not prolong them.
- If daily and idle policies both apply, the earlier expiry wins.
- Provider-owned CLI sessions also remain persistent by default; use `/reset` or configure expiry.
- Resetting discards queued system notices associated with the previous session.

## Identity and DM security

- The default `dmScope: main` combines every DM into one context. This is unsafe when multiple people can contact the agent.
- Prefer `per-channel-peer`; use `per-peer` when the same sender should share context across channels.
- `per-account-channel-peer` adds account-level separation.
- `identityLinks` can merge one person’s channel identities under a canonical peer ID. Configure this carefully: incorrect linking can expose private context.
- Verify isolation with `openclaw security audit`.

## Route ownership and overrides

- The gateway owns session state; clients only query it.
- Groups, rooms, and channels are separate by default. A binding can route a specific room into the main session.
- Such a binding changes only session-key selection. It does not alter DM handling, mention rules, delivery context, or reply destination.
- The binding’s route-specific setting takes precedence over the global group setting.

## Incognito and retention caveats

- Incognito is available only when creating a thread in the Control UI.
- Its session data stays in memory and vanishes after gateway restart; it skips automatic memory flushing and transcript archiving.
- Incognito does not prevent tool-driven file writes or explicit saving elsewhere. Provider processing and diagnostic logging still apply.
- Admin-scope connections and the gateway operator can still observe incognito activity.
- Maintenance may prune ordinary sessions, but archived and pinned sessions are protected from automatic cleanup.
- Retention limits can be exceeded when protected, active, or durable external sessions consume the available capacity.

## Restart recovery

- After an interrupted turn, the gateway attempts recovery up to three failed backend starts.
- The allowance refreshes only after a genuine backend turn begins. For some CLI backends, observed assistant output or tool activity is required.
- Merely accepting, queueing, or preparing a resume does not refresh the allowance.
- Once recovery is exhausted, use WebChat’s new-session resume option or `/new`/`/reset`; the old transcript remains available.
```
</details></tool-use>

161:The bearer token grants effective shell access. The bridge exposes a `/api/bash` endpoint by design — it's part of pi's RPC protocol — so anyone with the token can run arbitrary commands as the bridge process's user. Treat the token like an SSH key:
174:- **Bearer-token auth** with constant-time compare (`crypto.timingSafeEqual`) on REST and WS handshake.
175:- **No cookie-based auth.** CSRF via `Authorization: Bearer ...` is impossible because browsers don't auto-attach `Authorization` headers cross-origin.
176:- **Optional `Origin` allowlist** (`PI_RPC_BRIDGE_ALLOWED_ORIGINS`) for defense-in-depth against browser-based CSRF. When set, browser clients must present a matching `Origin` header. Non-browser clients (iOS, curl, our `ws-client`) don't send `Origin` and are unaffected. Exact-match only — subdomain wildcards (`https://*.example.com`) are not supported; list each origin explicitly.
183:- **TLS termination** — operator's responsibility (Caddy/nginx/Tailscale upstream). The bridge speaks plain HTTP/WS so it can run behind any TLS terminator without double-encryption overhead.
184:- **Filesystem path sandboxing** — moot under the threat model. Anyone with the token has shell access via `/api/bash`; restricting `sessionPath` or `outputPath` doesn't add real defense.
185:- **Rate limiting** — single-trusted-user assumption; brute-forcing a 256-bit token is computationally infeasible. If you deploy in a hostile multi-user environment, add rate limiting at the transport layer (proxy / firewall).
186:- **Audit log shipping** — server logs are local. Ship them yourself if needed (`journalctl`, `log stream`, etc.).
190:- **Tier 3+ for any non-trusted-network deployment.** Tailscale-internal traffic is encrypted, but a stolen token from a compromised device is full-access. mTLS in front (Tier 3) raises the bar.
192:- **Don't run multiple bridges sharing a token.** Per-bridge tokens give you a clean rotation story per device/workspace.
197:All endpoints carry no session id; they operate on pi's currently active session. JSON bodies/responses. Bearer token in `Authorization: Bearer ...` for everything except `/health`.

249:# Health (no auth)
253:REST returns 200 on **preflight ack** (pi confirms it accepted the command), not on completion. The body is pi's `data` field if any, else `{ ok: true }`. Async work — including model output, tool calls, and retries — is observed via the WebSocket event stream. `agent_end` is the completion signal.
257:### WebSocket
271:Bearer token at handshake via the `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` header as `bearer.<token>`. Server-side ping every 30s; clients that miss a pong are dropped.
273:Multi-client fan-out: every authenticated client receives every event. For interactive extension UI requests (`confirm` / `select` / `input` / `editor`), the bridge accepts the **first** `extension_ui_response` arriving from any client and drops subsequent ones for the same id. Fire-and-forget UI events (`notify`, `setStatus`, etc.) are pure broadcast — clients render them however they want without responding.
283:### Tier 1: Tailscale (~5 min, lowest friction)
285:Install Tailscale on your bridge host and on each client device. Set the bridge's `bindHost` to your tailnet IP. Done — Tailscale handles authenticated peer-to-peer connectivity, NAT traversal, encryption (WireGuard underneath), and ACLs.
287:**Trade-off:** Tailscale's coordination plane is hosted by Tailscale Inc. Identity goes through 3rd-party SSO. Data is end-to-end encrypted but metadata about your network is visible to Tailscale. Fine for personal homelab; less appealing if your threat model includes the Tailscale control plane.
291:[Headscale](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale) is an open-source reimplementation of Tailscale's coordination server. Self-host it on your homelab (or on a small VPS). Tailscale's iOS / macOS / Linux clients all support a custom login server URL — point them at your Headscale instance and the rest of the experience is identical to Tier 1.
293:**Trade-off:** Same iOS NetworkExtension limitation as Tailscale (only one VPN active at a time). No 3rd-party metadata leak.
303:    client_auth {
316:### Tier 4: Self-hosted WireGuard + router-level upstream VPN (~half day, most sovereign)
318:A fully sovereign setup with no 3rd-party network overlay. Run a WireGuard server on your homelab router (GL.iNet / OpenWrt / Asus-Merlin / pfSense). Phone connects via WireGuard to your home network. The router optionally runs a privacy VPN (ProtonVPN, Mullvad, etc.) for upstream egress so all phone traffic gets that protection automatically when at home.
324:### Tier 5: Behind an authenticating reverse proxy (SMB / team)
326:For SMB or team deployments where you want SSO integration, audit, and centralized access policy. Deploy Authelia / oauth2-proxy / Pomerium / Cloudflare Access in front of the bridge. The reverse proxy handles auth, then forwards a pre-authenticated request.
328:**Note:** v0 only supports bearer-token auth. To use Tier 5 you currently configure the proxy to inject the same bearer token after its own auth succeeds. A native "trusted-proxy" mode (where the bridge accepts pre-auth via `X-Forwarded-User` from a configured upstream IP) is on the roadmap.
334:The bridge is meant to run continuously. The supervisor inside `index.ts` will auto-restart pi if it exits unexpectedly, but you'll want OS-level supervision for the bridge itself.

469:### `Bearer token must be at least 32 characters`
470:Your token is too short. Regenerate: `openssl rand -hex 32` produces 64 hex characters (256 bits).
473:The bridge refuses to load a config file readable by group or other (security: it contains your bearer token). Fix:
479:Set `PI_RPC_BRIDGE_CWD` to the directory pi should run in. The agent's tools (Read, Edit, Bash) operate relative to this path.
482:Pi crashed or is restarting. The bridge auto-restarts pi after `restartBackoffMs` (default 2s); retry after a few seconds. Check the bridge's stderr — it tees pi's stderr inline (`[pi] ...` prefix). Common causes: pi misconfigured (no provider/model set), provider unreachable (Ollama not running, etc.).
485:- Bind host: by default the bridge listens only on `127.0.0.1`. Set `PI_RPC_BRIDGE_BIND_HOST` to your overlay IP (e.g. Tailscale IP) for remote access.
489:- Token mismatch: confirm the value you're sending matches what the bridge has loaded. Tokens drift after a config rotation; restart the bridge after editing.
490:- WebSocket: the token goes in `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: bearer.<token>`, not `Authorization`. Most WebSocket libraries take an array of subprotocols at connect time.
491:- Origin: if you set `PI_RPC_BRIDGE_ALLOWED_ORIGINS`, browser clients must send a matching `Origin` header. Subdomain wildcards aren't supported.
493:### Bridge restarts pi every few seconds in a loop

=== k3-2o/pi-remote ===
3:> WebSocket-first server runtime for Pi Coding Agent. Start it once, talk to Pi from anywhere.
11:pi-remote is a thin server that turns Pi's RPC mode into a network service. It handles process management, session multiplexing, and transport. Pi does the thinking. The pipe is dumb.
17:- **WebSocket** — the real protocol. Connection = session. All Pi commands available. Extension UI flows bidirectionally.
18:- **HTTP** — sugar layer for curl, cron, webhooks. `/v1/chat` streams SSE.
19:- **Session management** — one Pi process per session. Auto-cleanup. Pool with eviction. Idle reset policies.
21:- **Daemon mode** — `--detach` for quick dev, `systemd` for production.
22:- **CLI** — `start`, `stop`, `status`, `health`, `sessions`, `logs`, `relay`.
23:- **SDKs** — JavaScript and Python clients. Import from npm or copy-paste.

226	export function buildActiveBranch(
227	  sessionOrEntries: readonly unknown[] | { entries: readonly unknown[] },
228	): ActiveSessionEntry[] {
229	  const entries = Array.isArray(sessionOrEntries) ? sessionOrEntries : sessionOrEntries?.entries;
230	  if (!Array.isArray(entries)) fail('PIA_INVALID_SESSION', 'Session entries must be an array');
231	
232	  const byId = new Map<string, ActiveSessionEntry>();
233	  let leaf: ActiveSessionEntry | undefined;
234	  for (const rawEntry of entries) {
235	    if (!isRecord(rawEntry) || typeof rawEntry.id !== 'string' || rawEntry.id === '') continue;
236	    const entry = rawEntry as ActiveSessionEntry;
237	    if (byId.has(entry.id)) {
238	      fail('PIA_INVALID_SESSION_TREE', `Duplicate session entry id: ${entry.id}`);
239	    }
240	    byId.set(entry.id, entry);
241	    leaf = entry;
242	  }
243	  if (!leaf) return [];
244	
245	  const reverse: ActiveSessionEntry[] = [];
246	  const visited = new Set<string>();
247	  let current: ActiveSessionEntry | undefined = leaf;
248	  while (current) {
249	    if (visited.has(current.id)) {
250	      fail('PIA_INVALID_SESSION_TREE', `Cycle in session entry parents at ${current.id}`);
251	    }
252	    visited.add(current.id);
253	    reverse.push(current);
254	    if (current.parentId === null || current.parentId === undefined) break;
255	    if (typeof current.parentId !== 'string' || current.parentId === '') {
256	      fail('PIA_INVALID_SESSION_TREE', `Invalid parentId on session entry ${current.id}`);
257	    }
258	    const parent = byId.get(current.parentId);
259	    if (!parent) {
260	      fail('PIA_INVALID_SESSION_TREE', `Missing parent ${current.parentId} for session entry ${current.id}`);
261	    }
262	    current = parent;
263	  }
264	  return reverse.reverse();
265	}

268	export function parseSessionContent(
269	  content: string,
270	  { engine, filePath = '<session>' }: ParseSessionOptions = {},
271	): ParsedSession {
272	  if (engine !== undefined) requireEngine(engine);
273	  if (typeof content !== 'string' || content === '') {
274	    fail('PIA_INVALID_SESSION', `Empty session file: ${filePath}`);
275	  }
276	
277	  const physicalLines = content.split('\n');
278	  if (physicalLines.at(-1) === '') physicalLines.pop();
279	  if (physicalLines.length === 0) fail('PIA_INVALID_SESSION', `Empty session file: ${filePath}`);
280	
281	  let logicalIndex = 0;
282	  let titleSlot: OmpTitleSlot | undefined;
283	  const first = parseLine(physicalLines[0], 1, filePath);
284	  if (first.type === 'title') {
285	    if (engine === 'pi') {
286	      fail('PIA_FOREIGN_SESSION', `OMP title slot found while parsing a Pi session: ${filePath}`);
287	    }
288	    if (!isTitleSlot(first)) {
289	      fail('PIA_INVALID_SESSION', `Malformed OMP title slot in ${filePath}`);
290	    }
291	    if (Buffer.byteLength(`${physicalLines[0]}\n`, 'utf8') !== OMP_TITLE_SLOT_BYTES) {
292	      fail('PIA_INVALID_SESSION', `OMP title slot is not ${OMP_TITLE_SLOT_BYTES} bytes in ${filePath}`);
293	    }
294	    titleSlot = first;
295	    logicalIndex = 1;
296	  }
297	
298	  if (logicalIndex >= physicalLines.length) {
299	    fail('PIA_INVALID_SESSION', `Session header is missing from ${filePath}`);
300	  }
301	  const headerRecord = parseLine(physicalLines[logicalIndex], logicalIndex + 1, filePath);
302	  if (
303	    headerRecord.type !== 'session' ||
304	    typeof headerRecord.id !== 'string' ||
305	    headerRecord.id === '' ||
306	    typeof headerRecord.cwd !== 'string'
307	  ) {
308	    fail('PIA_INVALID_SESSION', `First logical record is not a valid session header in ${filePath}`);
309	  }
310	  const header = headerRecord as SessionHeader;
311	
312	  const entries: SessionEntry[] = [];
313	  for (let index = logicalIndex + 1; index < physicalLines.length; index += 1) {
314	    entries.push(parseLine(physicalLines[index], index + 1, filePath));
315	  }
316	  // Validate the tree while parsing so callers never receive a subtly corrupt active branch.
317	  const branch = buildActiveBranch(entries);
318	  const inferredEngine = engine || (titleSlot ? 'omp' : undefined);
319	  const branchTitle = latestEntryTitle(branch);
320	  const headerTitle = typeof header.title === 'string' ? header.title.trim() : '';
321	  const title = titleSlot?.title.trim() || branchTitle || headerTitle || undefined;
322	
323	  return {
324	    engine: inferredEngine,
325	    title,
326	    titleSlot,
327	    header,
328	    id: header.id,
329	    cwd: header.cwd,
330	    entries,
331	    activeBranch: branch,
332	  };
333	}

356	  }
357	  const [content, stat] = await Promise.all([fs.readFile(filePath, 'utf8'), fs.stat(filePath)]);
358	  if (!stat.isFile()) fail('PIA_INVALID_SESSION_PATH', `Session path is not a file: ${filePath}`);
359	  const parsed = parseSessionContent(content, { engine: options.engine, filePath });
360	  return {
361	    ...parsed,
362	    path: filePath,
363	    filePath,
364	    mtime: stat.mtime,
365	    mtimeMs: stat.mtimeMs,
366	    size: stat.size,
367	  };

370	/** List direct JSONL children newest-first. A missing leaf is an empty history. */
371	export async function listSessions({
372	  sessionDir,
373	  engine,
374	}: ListSessionsOptions = {}): Promise<ParsedSessionFile[]> {
375	  if (typeof sessionDir !== 'string' || sessionDir.trim() === '') {
376	    fail('PIA_INVALID_SESSION_PATH', 'sessionDir must be a non-empty path');
377	  }
378	  const directory = path.resolve(sessionDir);
379	  let children: Dirent<string>[];
380	  try {
381	    children = await fs.readdir(directory, { withFileTypes: true, encoding: 'utf8' });
382	  } catch (error) {
383	    if (hasErrorCode(error, 'ENOENT')) return [];
384	    throw error;
385	  }
386	
387	  const files = children
388	    .filter((entry) => entry.isFile() && entry.name.endsWith('.jsonl'))
389	    .map((entry) => path.join(directory, entry.name))
390	    .sort();
391	  const sessions = await Promise.all(files.map((filePath) => parseSessionFile(filePath, { engine })));
392	  sessions.sort((left, right) => right.mtimeMs - left.mtimeMs || left.path.localeCompare(right.path));
393	  return sessions;
394	}

396	/** Resolve only an explicit absolute path, an unambiguous ID prefix, or explicit latest. */
397	export async function resolveSession({
398	  sessionDir,
399	  selector,
400	  latest = false,
401	  engine,
402	}: ResolveSessionOptions = {}): Promise<ParsedSessionFile> {
403	  if (selector !== undefined && (typeof selector !== 'string' || selector.trim() === '')) {
404	    fail('PIA_INVALID_SESSION_SELECTOR', 'Session selector must be a non-empty string');
405	  }
406	  if (latest && selector !== undefined && selector !== 'latest') {
407	    fail('PIA_INVALID_SESSION_SELECTOR', 'Choose either a selector or latest, not both');
408	  }
409	  if (selector && path.isAbsolute(selector)) {
410	    return await parseSessionFile(selector, { engine });
411	  }
412	
413	  const wantsLatest = latest || selector === 'latest';
414	  if (!wantsLatest && selector === undefined) {
415	    fail('PIA_SESSION_SELECTOR_REQUIRED', 'Specify an absolute session path, ID prefix, or latest');
416	  }
417	  const sessions = await listSessions({ sessionDir, engine });
418	  if (sessions.length === 0) {
419	    fail('PIA_SESSION_NOT_FOUND', `No sessions found under ${path.resolve(sessionDir || '')}`);
420	  }
421	  if (wantsLatest) return sessions[0];

423	  const prefix = selector!.toLowerCase();
424	  const matches = sessions.filter((session) => session.id.toLowerCase().startsWith(prefix));
425	  if (matches.length === 0) fail('PIA_SESSION_NOT_FOUND', `No session ID starts with ${selector}`);
426	  if (matches.length > 1) {
427	    fail('PIA_AMBIGUOUS_SESSION', `Session ID prefix ${selector} matches ${matches.length} sessions`, {
428	      matches: matches.map((session) => ({ id: session.id, path: session.path })),
429	    });
430	  }
431	  return matches[0];

440	): true {
441	  const objectOptions = typeof sourceOrOptions === 'object' ? sourceOrOptions : undefined;
442	  const sourceEngine = objectOptions
443	    ? objectOptions.sourceEngine || objectOptions.source?.engine
444	    : sourceOrOptions;
445	  const targetEngine = objectOptions ? objectOptions.targetEngine : maybeTargetEngine;

368	function renderSelection(
369	  header: string,
370	  blocks: readonly ConversationBlock[],
371	  included: ReadonlySet<number>,
372	  truncated: ReadonlyMap<ConversationBlock, ConversationBlock>,
373	  maxBytes: number,
374	): SelectionResult {

376	  const omittedBlocks = blocks.length - selected.length;
377	  const notes: string[] = [];
378	  if (omittedBlocks > 0) notes.push(`${omittedBlocks} earlier conversation block(s) omitted`);
379	  if (truncated.size > 0) notes.push(`${truncated.size} retained block(s) truncated`);
380	  const omission = notes.length > 0
381	    ? `\n\n> ${notes.join('; ')} to stay within the ${maxBytes}-byte handoff limit.`
382	    : '';
383	  const renderedBlocks = selected.map((block) => renderBlock(truncated.get(block) || block));
384	  const content = `${header}${omission}${renderedBlocks.length ? `\n\n${renderedBlocks.join('\n\n')}` : ''}\n`;
385	  return { content, omittedBlocks, retainedBlocks: selected.length, truncatedBlocks: truncated.size };
386	}

388	function truncateBlock(block: ConversationBlock, targetBytes: number): ConversationBlock | undefined {
389	  const prefix = `${block.heading}\n\n`;
390	  const marker = '\n[… retained block truncated …]';

392	  if (bodyBudget <= utf8Bytes(marker)) return undefined;
393	  return { ...block, body: truncateUtf8Head(block.body, bodyBudget, marker) };

396	function fitBlocks(
397	  header: string,
398	  blocks: readonly ConversationBlock[],
399	  maxBytes: number,
400	): FittedResult {
401	  const headerOnly = `${header}\n`;
402	  if (utf8Bytes(headerOnly) > maxBytes) {
403	    fail('PIA_HANDOFF_LIMIT_TOO_SMALL', 'Handoff limit cannot preserve the required goal and provenance');
404	  }
405	  const full = `${header}${blocks.length ? `\n\n${blocks.map(renderBlock).join('\n\n')}` : ''}\n`;
406	  if (utf8Bytes(full) <= maxBytes) {
407	    return {
408	      content: full,
409	      omittedBlocks: 0,
410	      retainedBlocks: blocks.length,
411	      truncatedBlocks: 0,
412	      totalBlocks: blocks.length,
413	    };
414	  }
415	
416	  const included = new Set<number>();
417	  const truncated = new Map<ConversationBlock, ConversationBlock>();
418	  for (let index = 0; index < blocks.length; index += 1) {
419	    if (blocks[index].required) included.add(index);
420	  }
421	  const firstUser = blocks.findIndex((block) => block.kind === 'user');
422	  if (firstUser >= 0) included.add(firstUser);
423	  if (blocks.length > 0) included.add(blocks.length - 1);
424	
425	  let result = renderSelection(header, blocks, included, truncated, maxBytes);
426	  while (utf8Bytes(result.content) > maxBytes) {
427	    const candidates = [...included]
428	      .map((index) => ({ index, block: truncated.get(blocks[index]) || blocks[index] }))
429	      .sort((left, right) => utf8Bytes(renderBlock(right.block)) - utf8Bytes(renderBlock(left.block)));
430	    const candidate = candidates[0];
431	    if (!candidate) {
432	      fail('PIA_HANDOFF_LIMIT_TOO_SMALL', 'Handoff limit cannot preserve required conversation context');
433	    }
434	    const overflow = utf8Bytes(result.content) - maxBytes;
435	    const currentBytes = utf8Bytes(renderBlock(candidate.block));
436	    const next = truncateBlock(candidate.block, Math.max(96, currentBytes - overflow - 64));
437	    if (!next || utf8Bytes(renderBlock(next)) >= currentBytes) {
438	      fail('PIA_HANDOFF_LIMIT_TOO_SMALL', 'Handoff limit cannot preserve required conversation context');
439	    }
440	    truncated.set(blocks[candidate.index], next);
441	    result = renderSelection(header, blocks, included, truncated, maxBytes);
442	  }
443	
444	  for (let index = blocks.length - 1; index >= 0; index -= 1) {
445	    if (included.has(index)) continue;
446	    const tentative = new Set(included);
447	    tentative.add(index);
448	    const next = renderSelection(header, blocks, tentative, truncated, maxBytes);
449	    if (utf8Bytes(next.content) <= maxBytes) included.add(index);
450	  }
451	
452	  result = renderSelection(header, blocks, included, truncated, maxBytes);
453	  return { ...result, totalBlocks: blocks.length };
454	}

```text
## Gateway reference: inbound media handling

### Staging and provenance
- Record each inbound attachment in arrival order with its local path, URL, MIME type, and media category.
- Preserve the original media for the downstream model, even when preprocessing is disabled or fails.
- For text-only Gateway/WebChat models, retain images as `media://inbound/*` references so later tools or vision models can inspect them.
- CLI runs may receive attachment path, URL, MIME type, directory, index, and per-run output-path variables.

### Selection and count limits
- Select attachments independently for image, audio, and video processing.
- The default is the first matching attachment only.
- Each capability can choose first or all matching items, impose `maxAttachments`, and prefer the first, last, path-based, or URL-based candidate.
- When processing all items, output labels include their position and total count.

### Size and execution controls
- Each capability has an input ceiling, with defaults of 10 MB for images, 20 MB for audio, and 50 MB for video.
- Individual model entries can override size, timeout, prompt, and output-length limits.
- An oversized attachment is skipped for that model and passed to the next eligible fallback.
- Default timeouts are 60 seconds for image/audio and 120 seconds for video.
- Audio smaller than 1024 bytes is treated as invalid and receives a deterministic placeholder transcript.

### Cleanup and retention
- CLI processing receives a scratch output directory and scratch base filename for the current run.
- The page does not define scratch-directory deletion, media retention duration, or lifecycle guarantees for staged files.
- It also does not specify deletion behavior for inbound originals or generated artifacts.

### Trust boundaries
- Extracted document text is marked as externally supplied content with an identifier and source metadata before entering media prompts.
- Host-local paths supplied for unsupported files are treated as untrusted metadata; self-service extraction guidance is only exposed when host-path access is proven.
- Operator allowlist or MIME-policy rejections do not reveal local paths or instructions that could bypass the policy.
- URL-based file sources can be disabled, producing a bounded rejection marker.

### Failures and bounded output
- Understanding is non-blocking: errors, timeouts, unavailable models, disabled capabilities, scope restrictions, and selection misses do not stop reply processing.
- Provider or CLI failures trigger the next configured or auto-detected fallback.
- File outcomes include unreadable, unsupported, empty, URL-disabled, and policy-rejected cases.
- Skipped or unhandled media is represented by model-visible markers.
- At most five skip markers are emitted per message; additional skips collapse into one count summary.
- Every candidate receives one disposition, such as handled, native-vision handoff, not selected, disabled, unavailable, scope-denied, or failed.

### Result provenance
- Successful understanding adds a capability-specific summary block while retaining captions as user-provided text.
- Audio success additionally supplies a transcript variable; command parsing uses the caption when available, otherwise the transcript.
- Audio transcripts may optionally be echoed before agent processing, using the configured format.
- Native-vision handoffs do not add an image-summary marker.
- PDF page-image fallback preserves a file-block placeholder while forwarding rendered pages to a vision-capable model.
```

```text
### Binding

- Treat each Pi extension confirmation as a plugin approval request tied to one operation.
- The Gateway creates a pending request with a `plugin:` identifier and pauses execution.
- The approval should describe the action, target, and risk; optional typed scope can expose recipients, amounts, or visibility.
- If parameters are modified while requesting approval, OpenClaw preserves the approved snapshot and applies overrides only after approval.
- Approval is per call. `allow-always` is not automatically persistent unless the extension implements its own trust storage.

### IM transport and authorization

- Forwarding is separately configured under `approvals.plugin`; exec-approval settings do not apply.
- Routing can target specific IM destinations and restrict eligible agents, for example through `agentFilter` and channel/recipient targets.
- A connected approval-capable client, supported same-chat command flow, or configured forwarding route must be available; otherwise the request fails closed.
- Resolve using the request ID and an offered decision: `allow-once`, `allow-always`, or `deny`.
- Decisions not advertised by the request, malformed responses, timeouts, cancellation, and missing routes block execution.
- Channel-specific approver authorization applies, but its detailed rules are outside the supplied content.
```

1: <p align="center">
2:   <img src="branding/logo-full.svg" width="140" alt="Remote Pi logo" />

4: 
5: <h1 align="center">Remote Pi</h1>
6: 
7: <p align="center">
8:   Control your <a href="https://github.com/earendil-works/pi">Pi coding agent</a> from your phone.
9:   Pair with a one-time QR code and chat with your local agent — even when you're away from your computer.
10: </p>
11: 
12: ---
13: 
14: ## Links
15: 
16: - **Official site** — <https://remote-pi.jacobmoura.work>
17: - **Package documentation** — <https://pi.dev/packages/remote-pi?name=remote-pi>
18: - **GitHub** — <https://github.com/jacobaraujo7/remote_pi>
19: 
20: ### Downloads
21: 
22: | Platform | Status |
23: |---|---|
24: | Google Play (Android) | [Get it on Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=work.jacobmoura.remotepi) |
25: | App Store (iOS) | [Download on the App Store](https://apps.apple.com/app/remote-pi-coding-agent/id6773499691) |
26: | APK (sideload, Android) | [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/jacobaraujo7/remote_pi/releases) |
27: 
28: ## What's in this repo
29: 
30: | Package | Stack | Role |
31: |---|---|---|
32: | [`app/`](./app) | Flutter (iOS / Android) | Mobile client |
33: | [`pi-extension/`](./pi-extension) | Node + TypeScript | Pi extension exposing `/remote-pi` |
34: | [`relay/`](./relay) | Rust + Tokio | WebSocket routing + signed mesh membership storage |
35: | [`site/`](./site) | NextJS | Landing page + legal pages |
36: 
37: ## Architecture
38: 
39: ```
40: Flutter app ──wss──► Relay (Rust) ◄──wss── Pi extension (Node)
41:                                                   │
42:                                            Local Pi process
43:                                                   │
44:                                            UDS broker (local mesh)
45:                                                   │
46:                                            Other agents on the same machine
47: ```
48: 
49: - **Pairing** via short-lived QR code; peers persisted in Keychain (mobile) and `~/.pi/remote/` (desktop)
50: - **Ed25519 authentication** — the Relay handshake proves possession of the connection key; App↔Pi pairing is enforced by the endpoints. For Pi↔Pi routing, the current Relay permits a route when a correctly signed Owner blob lists both Pi keys; that check does not prove the Owner paired with or controls either Pi
51: - **TLS protects traffic in transit**, but current payloads are not E2E; see [`relay/README.md`](./relay/README.md) for the exact trust boundary
52: 
53: ## Local agent mesh
54: 
55: When multiple Pi agents run on the same machine, they discover each other through
56: a **Unix Domain Socket broker** managed by the extension. One agent wins the
57: leader election and binds the socket; the others connect as clients. For targets
58: on that same machine, agents use the opaque addresses returned by `list_peers` —
59: no relay, no network, no extra config.
60: 
61: Three LLM-facing tools are exposed in the Pi chat:
62: 
63: - `list_peers` — lists local and cross-PC addresses available to the agent
64: - `agent_send` — sends a unicast message and waits for a delivery ACK. Compatible ACK values are `received`, `busy`, `denied`, and `timeout`; current brokers return `received`, `denied`, or `timeout`, while `busy` only indicates a dropped message from an old broker leader that must be restarted before resending. Broadcast is `sent` with no ACK. Asynchronous content replies use `re`
65: - `agent_request` — request/response with timeout, available only as deprecated legacy behavior
66: 
67: This lets you set up local multi-agent workflows (e.g. a `backend` agent asks a
68: `frontend` agent for help) entirely on your machine, in parallel with the remote
69: mobile pairing.
70: 
71: ## Relay
72: 
73: A free community relay is available at:
74: 
75: ```
76: wss://relay-rp1.jacobmoura.work
77: ```
78: 
79: It's enough to get started, but the relay operator can see the content of your
80: messages and is a single point of trust for routing. **For sensitive work, we
81: strongly recommend running your own relay** — it's a single Docker command and
82: the only thing your traffic ever touches is your own infrastructure.
83: 
84: Full security trade-offs and the self-hosting guide live in
85: **[`relay/README.md`](./relay/README.md)**.
86: 
87: ## Getting started
88: 
89: Install the Pi extension in any project where Pi runs:
90: 
91: ```bash
92: pi install npm:remote-pi
93: ```
94: 
95: Then in the Pi chat, run:
96: 
97: ```
98: /remote-pi
99: ```
100: 
101: The setup wizard walks you through agent name, session name, and relay choice,
102: then prints a QR code. Scan it with the Remote Pi mobile app and you're paired.
103: 
104: ### Recommended companion: `@eko24ive/pi-ask`
105: 
106: ```bash
107: pi install npm:@eko24ive/pi-ask
108: ```
109: 
110: With pi-ask installed, the agent's `ask_user` clarification prompts (structured
111: questions with options, multi-select, and previews) render natively in the
112: mobile app — answer from your phone and the flow resolves on the desktop.
113: Without it, the agent simply asks in plain chat text (also answerable from the
114: phone, just unstructured). Remote Pi works either way; pi-ask is optional.
115: 
116: ## Status
117: 
118: The MVP is functional. Planning notes and roadmap live in [`plan/`](./plan).
119: 
120: ## License
121: 
122: License is per-package — see each subproject's `LICENSE` file (the `pi-extension`
123: is MIT). A repository-wide license decision is pending.
```

=== relay/README.md ===
# Remote Pi — Relay

A lightweight WebSocket relay server that connects the **Remote Pi** mobile app to
`pi-extension` processes running on your operating system. It handles peer routing,
presence, authorized Pi-to-Pi forwarding, and signed membership metadata.

For a full overview of the project, see the
[root README](../README.md).

---

## Protocol & Security

For wire format, identity model, ACK protocol, cross-PC routing, mesh
membership, trust model, and failure modes, see
[PROTOCOL.md](../PROTOCOL.md) at the repo root. It is the canonical reference
for everything the relay enforces on the wire.

---

## How it works

Every device authenticates with an Ed25519 keypair during the WebSocket handshake
(challenge-response). The Relay then applies these content boundaries:

- For App↔Pi traffic, the outer `ct` remains opaque and is never decoded.
- Pi→Pi `pi_envelope` frames and signed membership blobs are parsed in memory only
  as needed for routing and authorization.
- No envelope body, key material, or signature is logged or persisted as a message
  payload. SQLite persistence is limited to Owner-signed membership authorization
  metadata, not message traffic.
- A route is eligible when any correctly signed Owner blob directly lists both
  canonical Pi keys. This does not prove that the Owner paired with or controls
  either Pi, and is not a stronger trust guarantee. Membership is not transitive
  across overlapping Owner blobs.
- The positive authorization cache can retain a revoked permission for at most
  60 seconds. Negative sender misses are cached for 1 second, and the cache is
  bounded.

---

## Public relay

A shared relay is available at:

```
https://relay-rp1.jacobmoura.work
```

You can use it to get started without any setup. However, be aware of the security
trade-offs below.

### Security considerations

Messages are protected in two ways on the public relay:

- **TLS (SSL)** — the WebSocket connection is encrypted in transit.
- **Ed25519 connection key** — challenge-response authenticates possession of the
  announced connection key. It does not itself prove App pairing or authorize every
  route.

App↔Pi pairing and room addressing are client protocol responsibilities. Pi→Pi
forwarding has separate Relay route eligibility: any correctly signed Owner blob
must directly list both Pi keys. This does not prove that the Owner paired with
or controls either Pi, and is not a stronger trust guarantee.

The shipped Relay never decodes the outer `ct` and does not log or persist message
traffic. That implementation behavior is not an end-to-end trust boundary: the
relay operator controls the TLS endpoint, executable, and host, and a compromised
or malicious operator could replace or instrument the service to inspect or retain
traffic. Pi→Pi envelope content is also parsed transiently in the Relay process for
routing and authorization.

**If you handle sensitive work — private code, credentials, proprietary data — we
strongly recommend running your own relay.**

---

## Self-hosted relay (recommended for privacy)

Running your own relay removes the shared Relay operator from the trust path and
places the TLS endpoint, executable, and storage under infrastructure you control.

### Docker (quickest)

```bash
docker run -d \
  --name remote-pi-relay \
  -p 3000:3000 \
  -v remote-pi-data:/data \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  jacobmoura7/remote-pi-relay
```

The relay listens on a **single port** (`3000` by default) and serves three
surfaces at once:

- `GET /` — WebSocket upgrade (the peer protocol)
- `GET /health` — health check (returns `200 OK`)
- `GET / POST /mesh/<owner_pk_hash>` — signed membership versions

Point your app and `pi-extension` to `ws://<your-server-ip>:3000` (or `wss://`
if you put it behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy such as Caddy or nginx).

**`/data` volume**: the relay stores its SQLite database (signed membership
versions) at `/data/mesh.db` inside the container. Mount a named volume (as in
the example above) or a host directory (`-v /srv/remote-pi:/data`) so the state
survives `docker rm` and image upgrades. Without a mount, the database is
recreated empty each time the container starts and clients re-publish their
state at the next mutation.

### Environment variables

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `REMOTEPI_RELAY_PORT` | `3000` | TCP port that serves the WebSocket upgrade, `/health`, and `/mesh/*` (all on the same port) |
| `REMOTEPI_MESH_DB_PATH` | `/data/mesh.db` in Docker · `data/mesh.db` (cwd-relative) for bare-metal builds | Path to the SQLite database that stores signed membership versions. The parent directory is created automatically on first boot. The Docker image presets this to `/data/mesh.db` and declares `/data` as a volume — see the volume note above |
| `RUST_LOG` | _(none)_ | Log level filter — e.g. `info`, `debug`, `warn` |

Example with a custom port and logging (volume mount is the same):

```bash
docker run -d \
  --name remote-pi-relay \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  -v remote-pi-data:/data \
  -e REMOTEPI_RELAY_PORT=8080 \
  -e RUST_LOG=info \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  jacobmoura7/remote-pi-relay
```

### Mesh membership endpoint

The `/mesh/<owner_pk_hash>` endpoint stores **Owner-signed** lists of Pi keys,
keyed by `sha256(owner_pk)` in lowercase hex. It enables an app on a new device
(same Apple ID / Google account) to recover its peer list automatically after
restoring the Owner Ed25519 key from iCloud Keychain / Block Store.

The relay verifies every `POST` against the embedded `owner_pk` using Ed25519
and only accepts versions strictly greater than the current one (monotonic).
Bodies are capped at 500 KB. The relay does not create membership: it stores the
Owner-signed authorization metadata and treats Pi A↔B as route-eligible when any
correctly signed Owner blob directly lists both keys, without transitive
authorization across blobs. This does not prove that the Owner paired with or
controls either Pi, and is not a stronger trust guarantee. The shipped POST
endpoint prevents an unprivileged caller from modifying a particular Owner slot
without that Owner private key. This is not protection against Relay/operator
compromise: an operator controls the executable and SQLite authorization state.
A positive authorization cache entry can delay a revocation for at most 60
seconds; negative sender misses are cached for 1 second, and the cache is bounded.

**Self-hosting note**: the SQLite database at `REMOTEPI_MESH_DB_PATH`
(`/data/mesh.db` inside the official Docker image) is your operational
responsibility — make sure `/data` is on a persistent volume and back it up
alongside any other server state. If you lose it, clients re-publish their
current view at their next mutation.

**Storage layout**: SQLite runs in the default rollback-journal mode (NOT
WAL), so only `mesh.db` persists. During a write transaction a transient
`mesh.db-journal` may appear in the same directory and is deleted on commit.
Both files live under `REMOTEPI_MESH_DB_PATH`'s parent directory — typically
`/data/` in Docker or `data/` next to the binary on bare metal. The directory
is created automatically on first boot. This database contains membership
authorization metadata only, never message traffic.

For upgrades, deploy Relay 0.3 first: old Extensions can consume its UUID
errors. Then coordinate the Extension 0.6 rollout and minimize mixed old/new
Extensions because mixed wire-label interoperability is deferred. Extension
0.6's old-Relay error shim is for an old Relay or Relay rollback, not the reason
Relay-first is safe. The centralized rollout gates are in
[Plan 51](../plan/51-cross-pc-mesh-routing-hardening.md).

### Behind a reverse proxy (HTTPS/WSS)

For production use, put the relay behind a TLS-terminating proxy. Example Caddy config:

```
relay.yourdomain.com {
    reverse_proxy localhost:3000
}
```

Then set your app and `pi-extension` relay URL to `wss://relay.yourdomain.com`.

---

## Building from source

```bash
cargo build --release
./target/release/relay
```

```bash
REMOTEPI_RELAY_PORT=8080 RUST_LOG=info ./target/release/relay
```

## Running tests

```bash
cargo test
cargo clippy -- -D warnings
```

- **3-second acknowledgement:** Not specified in this content. It only requires a successful HTTP 200 response to the verification challenge.
- **Retries:** A dashboard Retry button is available when URL verification times out or fails. Event-delivery retry behavior is not described.
- **Queue recommendation:** Separate event intake from processing and reactions, particularly for high-volume workspaces or subscriptions.
- **App rate limiting:** The page directs readers to the Events API rate-limiting section for maximum event-volume guidance but gives no limits here.
- **Event ordering:** No event-ordering guarantees or guidance are stated.
```

92:`re` correlating it to the original message id.

95:`~/.pi/remote/sessions/<session-name>/broker.sock`. When sibling PCs are paired,
96:a leader-capable Extension or MCP participant bridges the opaque cross-PC
97-addresses over the relay; local-only use stays on UDS when relay access is off.

101:The first agent to enter a session becomes the *leader* (hosts the broker);
102:the rest are *followers*. If the leader exits, a follower automatically takes

254-## The relay
255-
256-The relay is the network boundary. TLS protects transit, but the Relay can see
257:routed plaintext protocol content and metadata; use a relay you trust or
258-self-host. There is no systemwide or PC-mesh E2E guarantee. For Pi-to-Pi
259-forwarding, the Relay currently permits a route when any correctly signed Owner
260:blob lists both canonical Pi keys. That does not prove the Owner paired with or
261-controls either Pi.
262-
263-### Upgrade order (Relay 0.3 first, then Extension 0.6)
--
266-Relay's UUID errors. Extension 0.6 carries a one-release legacy wire-label
267-shim, so mixed new/old Extensions interoperate when both select the same unique
268-colon-free signed nickname label, or when neither has one and both use the
269:canonical standard-padded key prefix. Delimiter or collision cases, like
270-divergent nickname views, are unsupported and may be silently dropped by the
271-old receiver. Upgrade all Extension/MCP participants in one maintenance window.
272-The shim does not replace the receiver-local aliases returned by `list_peers`;
273-addresses remain opaque.
274-
275:Extension 0.6 accepts an old Relay's lowercase 32-hex trusted error ID only as
276-a narrow shim for an old Relay or Relay rollback; that shim is not why
277-Relay-first is safe.
278-

296-[Tailscale](https://tailscale.com), [WireGuard](https://www.wireguard.com),
297-or your own VPC. Because the relay's network-level protection is just TLS +
298:keypair authentication, layering a VPN on top means **only your devices** can
299-even reach the WebSocket port — defense in depth.
300-

350-## Agent network: deeper look
351-
352:Each session is one Unix-domain-socket broker plus N peers. The broker
353:multiplexes messages by opaque `to` address and broadcasts system events
354-(`peer_joined`, `peer_left`).
355-
356-Inside the LLM, the agent skill uses `list_peers` for discovery and
--
362-agent_send({
363-  to: "/repo/api@backend", // exact opaque address returned by list_peers
364-  body: { task: "add /healthz endpoint" },
365:  re: "<id>" // set to the received message id when replying
366-})
367-```
368-
369:A unicast `agent_send` waits for the broker delivery ACK and returns the public
370-status `received`, `denied`, or `timeout`; broadcast is fire-and-forget. A
371:trusted Relay's closed transport reason is returned in `details` without
372-changing those statuses: `offline` maps to `timeout`, while `not_authorized`
373-and `bad_envelope` map to `denied`. Genuine silence is a reasonless `timeout`.
374-Do not blindly retry authorization or envelope failures. Trusted Relay errors
--
378-Mesh addresses are opaque routing values: echo them verbatim, including
379-receiver-local PC aliases with percent-encoded bytes (such as `%3A` or `%25`)
380-or collision suffixes containing `~`. Never parse, build, decode, or normalize
381:an address for routing or security. A PC alias is receiver-local presentation
382-and routing only, so different PCs may list the same sibling under different
383:aliases. The canonical 32-byte Ed25519 Pi public key is the PC's technical
384-identity; never use an alias as proof of identity.
385-
386-`agent_request` remains available only as a deprecated legacy Pi tool. Prefer
387-`agent_send`, then handle any later inbox/turn reply whose `re` matches the
388:original message id.
389-
390-The wire format is a 5-field envelope `{ from, to, id, re, body }` serialized
391:as one JSON line per message. The leader's broker writes an `audit.jsonl`
392:log at `~/.pi/remote/sessions/<name>/audit.jsonl` for postmortem inspection.
393-
394-Useful commands:
395-
--
397-|---|---|
398-| `/remote-pi` | Join the local mesh (and start the relay, if enabled) |
399-| `/remote-pi peers` | List local + cross-PC mesh peers, grouped by PC |
400:| `/remote-pi rename <new>` | Rename this agent in the current session |
401-| `/remote-pi stop` | Leave the local mesh and disconnect the relay |
402-
403:Name collisions inside a session get a numeric suffix automatically
404:(`backend`, `backend#2`, `backend#3`). The broker assigns it and returns the
405-real name to the peer.

410-
411:### Local session (one Pi, one terminal)
412-
413-| Command | Description |
414-|---|---|
--
416-| `/remote-pi setup` | Run the setup wizard and update local config |
417-| `/remote-pi status` | Show local mesh + relay status |
418-| `/remote-pi stop` | Stop everything for **this** terminal (mesh + relay) |
419:| `/remote-pi pair` | Show QR code + copy-paste pairing URI for a new mobile device |
420:| `/remote-pi devices` | List paired mobile devices (online/offline per device) |
421:| `/remote-pi revoke <shortid>` | Revoke a paired device by its shortid |
422-| `/remote-pi set-relay <url>` | Persist a new relay URL (http:// or https://) |
423-| `/remote-pi relay [start\|stop\|status]` | Relay-only control — leaves local mesh membership untouched (no verb = toggle) |
424-| `/remote-pi relay url <url>` | Same as `set-relay` |

427:### Daemon fleet (one supervisor, N background Pis — see [Daemon mode](#daemon-mode))
428-
429-| Command | Description |
430-|---|---|
431:| `/remote-pi create <cwd> [--name X]` | Register a folder as a daemon |
432:| `/remote-pi remove <id>` | Unregister a daemon (local config preserved) |
433:| `/remote-pi daemons` | List registered daemons + state |
434:| `/remote-pi daemon start` | Start every registered daemon |

437:| `/remote-pi daemon status` | Detailed runtime status (pid, uptime, restart count) |

439:| `/remote-pi cron add <id> "<expr>" "<prompt>"` | Schedule a recurring prompt (`--tz`, `--wake`, `--no-skip-busy`, `--catchup`) |

443-| `/remote-pi cron remove <jobId>` | Delete a job |

--
451-
452-### Scheduled prompts (`cron`)
453-
454:`remote-pi cron` schedules **recurring prompts** to daemons through the
455:supervisor — e.g. a daily "summarise new PRs". Output flows fire-and-forget to
456:the mesh/app like any prompt; the cron layer only audits the dispatch.
457-
458-- **Schedule** is a cron expression (croner syntax; an optional 6th *seconds*
459-  field is supported), with an optional IANA timezone via `--tz`:
--
463-  ```
464-
465-- **Minimum interval is 60s** — more frequent schedules are rejected (guards
466:  token cost + pileup). A fire is **skipped when the daemon is mid-turn**
467:  (`--no-skip-busy` to override); `--wake` starts a stopped daemon first;
468:  `--catchup` runs once on supervisor start if the previous run was missed.
469:- **Prerequisite**: the supervisor must run as a service (`remote-pi install`).
470-  Without it there is no scheduler, and `cron` commands say so instead of
471-  silently pretending to schedule.
472-- **Audit**: every fire **and** every skip appends one line to
473-  `~/.pi/remote/cron.jsonl` with a `result` of `delivered`,
474:  `woke_and_delivered`, `deliver_failed`, `skipped_busy`, `skipped_down`, or
475-  `skipped_disabled` — read it with `remote-pi cron log`.
476-
477:Step-by-step walkthrough: the [daemon tutorial](https://remote-pi.jacobmoura.work/tutorials/daemon).
478-
479-### Footer + title
480-
481:- `📡 local (N)` — current agent session and peer count (local mesh)
482:- `🟢 relay` — relay connected, at least one device paired (globally)
483:- `🟡 relay waiting for pairing` — relay connected, no device paired yet
484-- `📱 <shortid>` — a mobile device is actively connected right now
485-
486-Window title: `<agent-name> · On` when relay is up, `<agent-name> · Off`

493-
494-When you want a Pi to keep running in the background (responding to
495-mobile prompts at 3am, processing cron jobs, monitoring a folder while
496:you're not at the keyboard), promote it to a **daemon** managed by a
497:single OS-level supervisor.
498-
499:See [`docs/daemon.md`](./docs/daemon.md) for troubleshooting.

501-### One-time setup
502-
503-```bash
504:# Install the package globally so `remote-pi` and `pi-supervisord`
505-# are on your PATH (`pi install npm:remote-pi` alone makes the Pi
506-# extension available but does NOT expose the CLI binaries — see
507-# https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/configuring-npm/package-json#bin).
508-npm install -g remote-pi
509-
510:# Install the supervisor as a user-level system service. Linux uses
511-# systemd --user; macOS uses launchd LaunchAgent. Both auto-start at
512-# login and survive reboots.
513-remote-pi install
514-```
515-
516-The `install` command:
517:- Writes `~/.config/systemd/user/remote-pi-supervisord.service` (Linux)
518:  or `~/Library/LaunchAgents/dev.remotepi.supervisord.plist` (macOS)
519-- Activates it via `systemctl --user enable --now` or `launchctl bootstrap`
520:- The supervisor starts immediately and re-starts on every login
521-
522-### Per-folder workflow
523-
--
526-```bash
527-# 1. Configure the agent interactively first (one time).
528-cd ~/Movies
529:pi                                 # /remote-pi → setup wizard, /remote-pi pair, etc
530-
531:# 2. Promote to a daemon. The id is derived from the cwd
532-#    (sha256(realpath)[:8]), stable across machines.
533-remote-pi create ~/Movies --name "Video Editor"
534-# → Daemon registered: id=4e39152d name="Video Editor" cwd=/Users/x/Movies
535-
536:# 3. Start it (supervisor spawns `pi --mode rpc` for this folder).
537:remote-pi daemon start

--
555-### Removing or uninstalling
556-
557-```bash
558:remote-pi remove <id>              # unregister one daemon (config preserved)
559:remote-pi uninstall                # remove the supervisor service (registry kept)
560-```
561-
562-`uninstall` is reversible — re-running `install` later brings every
563:registered daemon back. To wipe the registry entirely, `rm
564:~/.pi/remote/daemons.json`.
565-
566-### Where to find logs
567-
568-| Platform | Command |
569-|---|---|
570:| Linux | `journalctl --user -u remote-pi-supervisord -f` |
571:| macOS | `tail -f ~/.pi/remote/supervisord.log` |
572-
573:Each spawned daemon's stderr is forwarded into the supervisor's log
574-with a `[<cwd>]` prefix, so a single log stream shows every agent.
575-
576-### Caveats (plan/26 trade-offs)
577-
578:- **Tool approval is not gated.** Daemons inherit the same Pi config
579-  the interactive run uses — Bash, Edit, Write etc. all execute without
580:  prompting. Configure Pi's tool permissions to taste before promoting
581:  a folder to daemon.
582-- **Pairing still happens interactively.** Daemons don't show a QR
583:  themselves; the keypair + paired devices come from the prior `pi`
584:  session in the same folder.
585:- **Single supervisor.** If `pi-supervisord` crashes all daemons go
586:  down with it. systemd/launchd restarts it within seconds; daemons
587-  come back automatically.
588:- **One daemon per cwd.** The `roomIdForCwd` derivation makes daemons
589:  by-path; two daemons in the same folder is rejected at `create` time.

_**Agent - sidechain (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-08-30 18:13:46Z)**_

The remaining design tension is crash consistency: Pi’s own session entries are append-only, but its internal follow-up queue is not a durable gateway inbox, and its session writer has no documented multi-writer contract. The safe model is therefore one gateway-owned durable FIFO/lease per Pi session, submit only when that session is idle, and treat cross-store “accepted but outcome unknown” states explicitly rather than claiming exactly-once execution.

5	  - Explaining /queue modes or message steering behavior
9	OpenClaw serializes inbound auto-reply runs (all channels) through a tiny in-process queue to prevent multiple agent runs from colliding, while still allowing safe parallelism across sessions.
18	- A lane-aware FIFO queue drains each lane with a configurable concurrency cap (default 1 for unconfigured lanes; `main` uses `min(16, max(8, available CPU parallelism))`, and `subagent` defaults to 8).
19	- `runEmbeddedAgent` enqueues by **session key** (lane `session:<key>`) to guarantee only one active run per session.
20	- Each session run is then queued into a **global lane** (`main` by default) so overall parallelism is capped by `agents.defaults.maxConcurrent`.
28	- `mode: "steer"`
29	- a built-in 500ms debounce for steer, followup, and collect batching
30	- `cap: 20`
31	- `drop: "summarize"`
33	Same-turn steering is the default. A prompt that arrives mid-run is injected into the active runtime when the run can accept steering, so no second session run is started. If the active run cannot accept steering, OpenClaw waits for the active run to finish before starting the prompt.
39	- `steer`: inject messages into the active runtime. OpenClaw lets an already-running tool finish, skips sequential calls that have not started, and makes the steer visible before the next tool launch or model decision. Parallel calls continue once their batch has crossed its launch checkpoint. Codex app-server receives one batched `turn/steer` and applies it at the next model boundary. If the run is not actively streaming or steering is unavailable, OpenClaw waits until the active run ends before starting the prompt.
40	- `followup`: do not steer. Enqueue each message for a later agent turn after the current run ends.
41	- `collect`: do not steer. Coalesce queued messages into a **single** followup turn after the quiet window. If messages target different channels/threads, they drain individually to preserve routing.
44	For runtime-specific timing and dependency behavior, see [Steering queue](/concepts/queue-steering). For the explicit `/steer <message>` command, see [Steer](/tools/steer).

64	Per-session `/queue` options apply to queued delivery. The `debounce` option also sets the Codex steering quiet window in `steer` mode:
66	- `debounce`: quiet window before draining queued followups or collect batches; in Codex `steer` mode, quiet window before sending batched `turn/steer`. Bare numbers are milliseconds; units `ms`, `s`, `m`, `h`, and `d` are accepted.
67	- `cap`: max queued messages per session. Values below `1` are ignored.
68	- `drop: "summarize"` (default): drop the oldest queued entries as needed, keep compact summaries, and inject them as a synthetic followup prompt.
69	- `drop: "old"`: drop the oldest queued entries as needed, without preserving summaries.
70	- `drop: "new"`: reject the newest message when the queue is already full.
72	The queue uses a built-in 500ms debounce. `cap` defaults to `20`, and `drop` defaults to `summarize`.

76	When channel streaming is `partial` or `block`, steering can look like several short visible replies while the active run reaches runtime boundaries:
78	- `partial`: the preview may finalize early, then a new preview starts after steering is accepted.
80	- Without streaming, steering falls back to a followup after the active run when the runtime cannot accept same-turn steering.
82	`steer` does not abort in-flight tools. Skipped OpenClaw tool calls receive synthetic paired error results so the transcript remains valid. Use `/queue interrupt` when the newest message should abort the current run.

```text
9	OpenClaw ships with conservative defaults. On a regular host install the Gateway binds to loopback; most chat channels answer an unknown DM sender with a pairing code instead of processing the message; and group access is allowlisted, usually behind a mention gate. The exceptions are deliberate and documented: container images default to an exposed bind (pair that with auth - see the [exposure runbook](/gateway/security/exposure-runbook)), and a few workspace channels such as ClickClack trust workspace membership by default - each channel page states its exact defaults. Run on those defaults and you are in good shape, and one command tells you if you have drifted:
18	  **One trust boundary per gateway.** This guidance assumes one trusted
20	  each other. Group chats and [multi-user](/concepts/multi-user) operation
28	## Scope: one trust boundary per gateway
30	- Supported: one trust boundary per gateway - a single operator or a mutually trusting team (prefer one OS user/host/VPS per boundary).
31	- Not supported: one shared gateway/agent used by mutually untrusted or adversarial users.
53	`--fix` is intentionally narrow: it flips open group policies to allowlists, tightens state/config/include-file permissions (`600` files, `700` dirs), and on Windows uses ACL resets instead of POSIX `chmod`.
57	- **Inbound access** - DM/group policies, allowlists: can strangers trigger the bot?
58	- **Tool blast radius** - elevated tools + open rooms: could prompt injection become shell/file/network actions?
60	- **Exec approval drift** - `security="full"`, `autoAllowSkills`, interpreter allowlists without `strictInlineEval`. `security="full"` alone is a broad posture warning, not proof of a bug - it is the chosen default for trusted-operator setups; tighten it only when your threat model needs approval or allowlist guardrails.
64	- **Plugins** - loading without an explicit allowlist.
73	1. Anything "open" + tools enabled: lock down DMs/groups first (pairing/allowlists), then tighten tool policy/sandboxing.
111	`tools.toolsBySender`, sender ownership, and owner-only tool inventories are evaluated against the current turn's originating requester. They do not authenticate or sanitize other content in that model prompt, including quoted text, prior shared-room history, forwarded content, fetched content, attachments, tool results, or other prompt inputs. Content from another person can therefore influence an owner-triggered turn when it is included in that turn's context.
113	Treat these controls as defense in depth that reduces direct capability for a requester, not as hostile multi-user isolation. Use `contextVisibility` to filter supported channel-supplied context, restrict tools and sandbox the agent, and use separate gateways and ideally separate OS users or hosts when participants are mutually adversarial.
115	## Trust boundary matrix
123	| Prompt/content guardrails                                 | Reduce model abuse risk                           | "Prompt injection alone proves auth bypass"                                   |
126	| Node pairing and node commands                            | Operator-level remote execution on paired devices | "Remote device control should be treated as untrusted user access by default" |
127	| `gateway.nodes.pairing.autoApproveCidrs`                  | Opt-in trusted-network node enrollment policy     | "A disabled-by-default allowlist is an automatic pairing vulnerability"       |
135	- Claims that assume hostile multi-tenant operation on one shared host or config.
136	- Normal operator read-path access (for example `sessions.list` / `sessions.preview` / `chat.history`) classified as IDOR in a shared-gateway setup.
153	- Direct loopback backend clients authenticated with the shared gateway token/password can make internal control-plane RPCs without presenting a user device identity. This is not a remote or browser pairing bypass - network clients, node clients, device-token clients, and explicit device identities still go through pairing and scope-upgrade enforcement.
154	- Exec approvals (allowlist + ask) are guardrails for operator intent, not hostile multi-tenant isolation. They bind exact request context and best-effort direct local file operands; they do not semantically model every runtime/interpreter loader path. Use sandboxing and host isolation for strong boundaries.
165	1. **Identity first** - decide who can talk to the bot (DM pairing / allowlists / explicit "open").
166	2. **Scope next** - decide where the bot can act (group allowlists + mention gating, tools, sandboxing, device permissions).
169	## DM access: pairing, allowlist, open, disabled
176	| `allowlist` | Unknown senders blocked, no pairing handshake.                                                                                                                                                                       |
177	| `open`      | Anyone can DM (public). Requires the channel allowlist to include `"*"` (explicit opt-in).                                                                                                                           |
187	Prefer pairing + allowlists for DMs. For groups, decide by membership, not by channel type: a private room whose members you trust - your team, family, or friends - is a normal deployment for `groupPolicy: "open"` (any member can trigger the bot). Keep sender allowlists or mention gating on rooms where strangers can join or post, and treat `dmPolicy="open"` as a deliberate opt-in.
189	### Allowlists (two layers)
191	- **DM allowlist** (`allowFrom` / `channels.discord.allowFrom` / `channels.slack.allowFrom`; legacy: `channels.discord.dm.allowFrom`, `channels.slack.dm.allowFrom`): who can DM the bot. When `dmPolicy="pairing"`, approvals write to `~/.openclaw/credentials/<channel>-allowFrom.json` (default account) or `<channel>-<accountId>-allowFrom.json` (non-default accounts), merged with config allowlists.
192	- **Group allowlist** (channel-specific): which groups/channels/guilds the bot accepts at all.
193	  - `channels.whatsapp.groups`, `channels.telegram.groups`, `channels.imessage.groups`: per-group defaults like `requireMention`; when set, also acts as a group allowlist (include `"*"` to keep allow-all behavior). Customize mention triggers with `agents.entries.*.groupChat.mentionPatterns` (for example `["@openclaw", "@mybot"]`) so `requireMention` gates on your own bot names.
194	  - `groupPolicy="allowlist"` + `groupAllowFrom`: restrict who can trigger the bot inside a group session (WhatsApp/Telegram/Signal/iMessage/Microsoft Teams).
195	  - `channels.discord.guilds` / `channels.slack.channels`: per-surface allowlists + mention defaults.
196	  - Check order: `groupPolicy`/group allowlists first, then mention/reply activation. Replying to a bot message (implicit mention) does **not** bypass `groupAllowFrom`.
200	### DM session isolation (multi-user mode)
202	By default, OpenClaw routes all DMs into the main session for cross-device continuity. If multiple people can DM the bot (open DMs or a multi-person allowlist), isolate DM sessions:
217	Local CLI onboarding preserves an explicit `session.dmScope` and otherwise leaves it unset, so the `"main"` default applies: all direct messages across channels share the agent's rolling main session (the personal-agent default). For shared or multi-user inboxes, set `session.dmScope: "per-channel-peer"`; `openclaw security audit` recommends isolation when it detects multi-user DM traffic.
219	This is a messaging-context boundary, not a host-admin boundary. If users are mutually adversarial and share the same Gateway host/config, run separate gateways per trust boundary instead.
227	- **Trigger authorization**: who can trigger the agent (`dmPolicy`, `groupPolicy`, allowlists, mention gates).
233	- `"allowlist"`: supplemental context filtered to senders allowed by active allowlist checks.
234	- `"allowlist_quote"`: like `allowlist`, but still keeps one explicit quoted reply.
236	Set per channel or per room/conversation - see [Groups](/channels/groups#context-visibility-and-allowlists). Reports that only show "model can see quoted/historical text from non-allowlisted senders" are hardening findings addressable with `contextVisibility`, not auth or sandbox bypasses by themselves; a security-impacting report still needs a demonstrated trust-boundary bypass.
238	## Prompt injection
244	Two caveats keep this from being a solved problem. Adaptive human attackers still break models that score well on static benchmarks, with published success rates above 80% against state-of-the-art defenses once the attacker adapts. And smaller or older models remain markedly easier to steer. So treat model choice as your first and cheapest layer, then keep hard enforcement - tool policy, exec approvals, sandboxing, and channel allowlists - for anything whose blast radius you would not accept on a bad day.
246	Prompt injection does not require public DMs: even if only you can message the bot, any **untrusted content** it reads (web search/fetch results, browser pages, emails, docs, attachments, pasted logs/code) can carry adversarial instructions. The content itself is a threat surface, not just the sender.
248	Red flags to treat as untrusted:
257	- Keep inbound DMs locked down (pairing/allowlists). Groups are a supported deployment, not a last resort: use mention gating and `contextVisibility` so the agent reads what it needs and no more. Reserve extra caution for genuinely public rooms, where anyone can post untrusted content.
260	- Limit high-risk tools (`exec`, `browser`, `web_fetch`, `web_search`) to trusted agents or explicit allowlists.
261	- If you allowlist interpreters (`python`, `node`, `ruby`, `perl`, `php`, `lua`, `osascript`), enable `tools.exec.strictInlineEval` so inline eval forms (`-c`, `-e`, and similar) still need explicit approval. In allowlist mode, any heredoc segment (`<<`) always requires reviewer or explicit approval, regardless of quoting - an allowlisted command cannot use a heredoc body to bypass allowlist review.
262	- Reduce blast radius by using a read-only or tool-disabled **reader agent** to summarize untrusted content, then pass the summary to your main agent.
263	- For Gmail hooks, the built-in per-message session isolates conversation context but does not remove the target agent's tool or workspace permissions. Route untrusted mail to a dedicated reader agent, apply [per-agent sandbox and tool restrictions](/tools/multi-agent-sandbox-tools), and constrain any handoff to the main agent with [`tools.agentToAgent`](/gateway/config-tools#tools-agenttoagent). See [Gmail integration](/gateway/configuration-reference#gmail-integration).
265	- For OpenResponses URL inputs (`input_file` / `input_image`), set a tight `gateway.http.endpoints.responses.files.urlAllowlist` / `images.urlAllowlist` and keep `maxUrlParts` low (empty allowlists count as unset). Use `files.allowUrl: false` / `images.allowUrl: false` to disable URL fetching entirely.
271	For tool-enabled agents or agents that read untrusted content, prompt-injection risk with older/smaller models is often too high. Do not run those workloads on weak model tiers.
275	- Do not use older/weaker/smaller tiers for tool-enabled agents or untrusted inboxes.
276	- If you must use a smaller model, reduce blast radius: read-only tools, strong sandboxing, minimal filesystem access, strict allowlists. Enable sandboxing for all sessions and disable `web_search`/`web_fetch`/`browser` unless inputs are tightly controlled.
277	- For chat-only personal assistants with trusted input and no tools, smaller models are usually fine.
279	### External content and untrusted-input wrapping
281	OpenResponses `input_file` text is still injected as untrusted external content even though the Gateway decodes it locally - the block carries `<<<EXTERNAL_UNTRUSTED_CONTENT ...>>>` boundary markers plus `Source: External` metadata (this path omits the longer `SECURITY NOTICE:` banner used elsewhere). The same marker-based wrapping applies when media-understanding extracts text from attached documents before appending it to the media prompt.
283	OpenClaw also strips common self-hosted LLM chat-template special-token literals (Qwen/ChatML, Llama, Gemma, Mistral, Phi, GPT-OSS role/turn tokens) from wrapped external content and metadata before they reach the model. Self-hosted OpenAI-compatible backends (vLLM, SGLang, TGI, LM Studio, custom Hugging Face tokenizer stacks) sometimes tokenize literal strings like `<|im_start|>` or `<|start_header_id|>` as structural chat-template tokens inside user content; without this sanitization, untrusted text in a fetched page, email body, or file-contents tool output could forge a synthetic `assistant`/`system` role boundary. Sanitization happens at the external-content wrapping layer, so it applies uniformly across fetch/read tools and inbound channel content. Hosted providers (OpenAI, Anthropic) already apply their own request-side sanitization; keep external-content wrapping enabled and prefer backend settings that split/escape special tokens when available.
287	This does not replace `dmPolicy`, allowlists, exec approvals, sandboxing, or `contextVisibility` - it closes one specific tokenizer-layer bypass.
297	Hook payloads are untrusted content even when delivery comes from systems you control (mail/docs/web content can carry prompt injection). Weak model tiers increase this risk - for hook-driven automation, prefer strong modern model tiers and keep tool policy tight (`tools.profile: "messaging"` or stricter), plus sandboxing where possible.
305	Slash commands and directives are honored only for authorized senders. Access-group entries referenced by channel allowlists are resolved automatically; there is no opt-in toggle. 372	To prevent cross-agent access, keep `agents.defaults.sandbox.scope` at `"agent"` (default) or use `"session"` for stricter per-session isolation. `scope: "shared"` uses a single container or workspace.

35-This is intentional. Pi is designed to operate on local source trees, invoke project toolchains, and integrate with the user's existing development environment. Real isolation needs to come from the operating system or a virtualization/container boundary.

Self-hosted relay\n (official Docker image, digest 65b35f75…) - relay transport itself works fine.\n\n Problem - interactive confirmation dialogs never reach the mobile app; the session silently hangs.\n\n Our Pi runs a permission-gate extension: mutating tool calls (e.g. any non-allowlisted bash command) pause on a confirm\n dialog in the TUI before executing. When a turn is driven from the phone:\n\n 1. From the app, ask the agent to run something gated (our probe: touch /tmp/remote-pi-gate-test).\n 2. {"body":"## Problem\n\nMesh membership anti-rollback floors are currently held only in process memory. After the process restarts, the floor is lost, so a membership from before a self-revocation can be replayed and accepted again.\n\nMemberships do not currently expire, and `issued_at` is informational rather than an enforced freshness boundary. This makes restart-persistent anti-rollback part of the mesh threat model rather than merely an availability improvement.\n\nThis limitation is documented in PR #67; that PR restores the in-process anti-rollback regression but intentionally does not claim restart persistence.\n\n## Required design work\n\nDesign and implement durable monotonic membership-version floors with explicit treatment of:\n\n- single-writer and multi-process locking semantics;\n- atomic storage with restrictive `0600` permissions;\n- write ordering, flush/fsync, and rename durability;\n- corruption, partial-write, deletion, and missing-state policy;\n- fail-closed behavior and its availability consequences;\n- concurrent monotonic updates without floor regression;\n- safe initialization and upgrade behavior for existing installations.\n\nA small best-effort JSON file is not sufficient if it can silently reset or regress the security floor.\n\n## Acceptance criteria\n\n- A pre-revocation membership cannot be accepted after a normal process restart.\n- Concurrent updates cannot lower or lose the highest accepted floor.\n- Corrupt, missing, deleted, and partially written state have documented and tested behavior.\n- Persistence and recovery behavior is covered by automated restart/concurrency tests.\n- Operator documentation states the durability and failure semantics accurately.\n\nRelated: #67","comments":[{"id":"IC_kwDOSklv6c8AAAABOMKS7w","author":{"login":"jacobaraujo7"},"authorAssociation":"OWNER","body":"Agreed on the framing: with memberships that don't expire and `issued_at` treated as informational, a floor that lives only in process memory means a restart re-opens the replay window. That makes restart persistence part of the threat model, not an availability nicety, and the acceptance criteria you listed are the right ones.\n\nRecording the constraint that makes this more than a JSON write, since it's the part that gets underestimated: the failure policy has to be decided before the storage format. A floor file that can silently reset or regress is worse than none — it reads as protection while providing none. So corrupt/missing/partial state has to fail closed, and fail-closed here means an agent that refuses to accept memberships, i.e. a real availability cost on a corrupted file. Whichever way that goes, the behavior needs to be documented for operators rather than discovered.\n\nConcretely the pieces I'd want covered, mostly restating yours with the ordering that matters: single-writer discipline (multiple Pi processes per machine share `~/.pi/remote`, so this needs actual locking, not last-write-wins), write-temp + fsync + rename for atomicity at 0600, monotonic compare-and-set so a concurrent update can never lower the floor, and tests that exercise restart and concurrency rather than just the happy path.\n\nNo timeline on this one — it's design work, not a patch, and #67's in-process fix holds the line in the meantime.
