8	---
9	
10	OpenClaw routes every inbound message to a **session** based on where it came
11	from: DMs, group chats, cron jobs, etc. All session state is owned by the
12	**gateway**; UI clients query the gateway for session data.
13	
14	To continue the same Gateway-owned session in the Control UI, terminal, or a
15	coding harness, see [Session synchronization and attachment](/concepts/session-attachment).
16	
17	For the personal-agent default — one rolling conversation shared by all your
18	DM channels, with group activity and background work flowing into it — see
19	[The main session](/concepts/main-session).
20	
21	## How messages are routed
22	
23	| Source          | Behavior                      |
24	| --------------- | ----------------------------- |
25	| Direct messages | Shared session by default     |
26	| Group chats     | Isolated per group by default |
27	| Rooms/channels  | Isolated per room by default  |
28	| Cron jobs       | Fresh session per run         |
29	| Webhooks        | Isolated per hook             |
30	
31	## DM isolation
32	
33	By default, all DMs share one session for continuity, which is fine for
34	single-user setups.
35	
36	<Warning>
37	If multiple people can message your agent, enable DM isolation. Without it, all
38	users share the same conversation context, so Alice's private messages would be
39	visible to Bob.
40	</Warning>
41	
42	```json5
43	{
44	  session: {
45	    dmScope: "per-channel-peer", // isolate by channel + sender
46	  },
47	}
48	```
49	
50	`session.dmScope` options:
51	
52	| Value                      | Behavior                                                 |
53	| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
54	| `main` (default)           | All DMs share the [main session](/concepts/main-session) |
55	| `per-peer`                 | Isolate by sender, across channels                       |
56	| `per-channel-peer`         | Isolate by channel + sender (recommended)                |
57	| `per-account-channel-peer` | Isolate by account + channel + sender                    |
58	
59	<Tip>
60	If the same person contacts you from multiple channels, use
61	`session.identityLinks` to map their identities to one canonical peer id so
62	they share a session.
63	</Tip>
64	
65	Verify your setup with `openclaw security audit`.
66	
67	## Group and room routing
68	
69	`session.groupScope` controls where non-direct peers store conversation
70	context:

31	## Session key shapes (examples)
32	
33	Direct messages collapse to the agent's **main** session by default:
34	
35	- `agent:<agentId>:<mainKey>` (default: `agent:main:main`)
36	
37	`session.dmScope` controls DM collapsing: `main` (default) shares one main
38	session, while `per-peer`, `per-channel-peer`, and `per-account-channel-peer`
39	keep DMs in separate sessions. A route binding can override the scope for its
40	matched peers via `bindings[].session.dmScope`.
41	
42	Even when direct-message conversation history is shared with main, sandbox and
43	tool policy use a derived per-account direct-chat runtime key for external DMs
44	so channel-originated messages are not treated like local main-session runs.
45	
46	With the default `session.groupScope: "per-group"`, groups and channels remain
47	isolated per channel:
48	
49	- Groups: `agent:<agentId>:<channel>:group:<id>`
50	- Channels/rooms: `agent:<agentId>:<channel>:channel:<id>`
51	
52	Set `session.groupScope: "main"` to route all non-direct peers into the agent's
53	main session, or use `bindings[].session.groupScope` for selected rooms. The
54	binding override wins over the global value. This changes shared context only;
55	mention gating and replies still use the originating group or channel.
56	
57	Threads:
58	
59	- Slack/Discord threads append `:thread:<threadId>` to the base key.
60	- Telegram forum topics embed `:topic:<topicId>` in the group key.
61	
62	Examples:
63	
64	- `agent:main:telegram:group:-1001234567890:topic:42`
65	- `agent:main:discord:channel:123456:thread:987654`
66	
67	## Main DM route pinning
68	
69	When `session.dmScope` is `main`, direct messages may share one main session.
70	To prevent the session's `lastRoute` from being overwritten by non-owner DMs,
71	OpenClaw infers a pinned owner from `allowFrom` when all of these are true:
72	
73	- `allowFrom` has exactly one non-wildcard entry.
179	
180	## Reply context
181	
182	Inbound replies include:
183	
184	- `ReplyToId`, `ReplyToBody`, and `ReplyToSender` when available.
185	- Quoted context is appended to `Body` as a `[Replying to ...]` block.
186	
187	This is consistent across channels.

```text
8	
9	OpenClaw serializes inbound auto-reply runs (all channels) through a tiny in-process queue to prevent multiple agent runs from colliding, while still allowing safe parallelism across sessions.
10	
11	## Why
12	
13	- Auto-reply runs can be expensive (LLM calls) and can collide when multiple inbound messages arrive close together.
14	- Serializing avoids competing for shared resources (session state, logs, CLI stdin) and reduces the chance of upstream rate limits.
15	
16	## How it works
17	
18	- A lane-aware FIFO queue drains each lane with a configurable concurrency cap (default 1 for unconfigured lanes; `main` uses `min(16, max(8, available CPU parallelism))`, and `subagent` defaults to 8).
19	- `runEmbeddedAgent` enqueues by **session key** (lane `session:<key>`) to guarantee only one active run per session.
20	- Each session run is then queued into a **global lane** (`main` by default) so overall parallelism is capped by `agents.defaults.maxConcurrent`.
21	- When verbose logging is enabled, queued runs emit a short notice if they waited more than ~2s before starting.
22	- Typing indicators still fire immediately on enqueue (when supported by the channel) so user experience is unchanged while the run waits its turn.
23	
24	## Defaults
25	
26	When unset, all inbound channel surfaces use:
27	
28	- `mode: "steer"`
29	- a built-in 500ms debounce for steer, followup, and collect batching
30	- `cap: 20`
31	- `drop: "summarize"`
32	
33	Same-turn steering is the default. A prompt that arrives mid-run is injected into the active runtime when the run can accept steering, so no second session run is started. If the active run cannot accept steering, OpenClaw waits for the active run to finish before starting the prompt.
34	
35	## Queue modes
36	
37	`/queue` controls what normal inbound messages do while a session already has an active run:
38	
39	- `steer`: inject messages into the active runtime. OpenClaw lets an already-running tool finish, skips sequential calls that have not started, and makes the steer visible before the next tool launch or model decision. Parallel calls continue once their batch has crossed its launch checkpoint. Codex app-server receives one batched `turn/steer` and applies it at the next model boundary. If the run is not actively streaming or steering is unavailable, OpenClaw waits until the active run ends before starting the prompt.
40	- `followup`: do not steer. Enqueue each message for a later agent turn after the current run ends.
41	- `collect`: do not steer. Coalesce queued messages into a **single** followup turn after the quiet window. If messages target different channels/threads, they drain individually to preserve routing.
42	- `interrupt`: abort the active run for that session, then run the newest message.
43	
102	
103	While a prompt sits in the followup/collect queue (for example a TUI or
104	webchat `chat.send` arriving while another turn is active), Gateway keeps a
105	**Gateway-owned cancel identity** for that client `runId` until the queued
106	content runs or is dropped. The identity follows content folded into an
107	overflow summary.
108	
109	- `chat.abort` with a specific `runId` cancels that turn while it is still
110	  queued, if the requester is authorized (same ownership rules as active runs).
111	- `chat.abort` for a session without `runId` cancels **authorized queued turns
112	  first**, then aborts authorized active runs. That order prevents queue drain
113	  from promoting work into a half-stopped session.
114	- Clearing the entire session queue without per-requester checks is not the
115	  stop path for multi-owner sessions.
116	- Queued waits are not projected as active agent runs for `sessions.list` and
130	## Scope and guarantees
131	
132	- Applies to auto-reply agent runs across all inbound channels that use the gateway reply pipeline (WhatsApp web, Telegram, Slack, Discord, Signal, iMessage, webchat, etc.).
133	- Default lane (`main`) is process-wide for inbound turns; set `agents.defaults.maxConcurrent` to allow multiple sessions in parallel.
134	- Heartbeat embedded runs use the bounded `cron-nested` lane for global admission so slow background work does not block inbound replies, while their configured heartbeat session lane still serializes work for that session.
135	- Additional lanes may exist (e.g. `cron`, `cron-nested`, `nested`, `subagent`) so background jobs can run in parallel without blocking inbound replies. Isolated cron agent turns hold a `cron` slot while their inner agent execution uses `cron-nested`. Shared non-cron `nested` flows keep their own lane behavior. These detached runs are tracked as [background tasks](/automation/tasks).
136	- Per-session lanes guarantee that only one agent run touches a given session at a time.
137	- No external dependencies or background worker threads; pure TypeScript + promises.
138	
139	## Troubleshooting
140	
141	- If commands seem stuck, enable verbose logs and look for "queued for ...ms" lines to confirm the queue is draining.
142	- Codex app-server runs that accept a turn and then stop emitting progress are interrupted by the Codex adapter so the active session lane can release instead of waiting for the outer run timeout.
143	- When diagnostics are enabled, sessions that remain in `processing` past the built-in warning threshold with no observed reply, tool, status, block, or ACP progress are classified by current activity:
144	  - Active work with recent progress logs as `session.long_running`. Owned silent model calls also stay `session.long_running` until the built-in abort threshold so slow or non-streaming providers are not reported as stalled too early.
145	  - Active work with no recent progress logs as `session.stalled`; owned model calls, blocked tool calls, and stalled embedded runs switch to `session.stalled` at or after the abort threshold. Ownerless stale model/tool activity is not hidden as long-running.
146	  - `session.stuck` is reserved for recoverable stale session bookkeeping, including idle queued sessions with stale ownerless model/tool activity.
```

17	<Note>
18	  **One trust boundary per gateway.** This guidance assumes one trusted
19	  boundary per gateway: a single operator, or a team whose members trust
20	  each other. Group chats and [multi-user](/concepts/multi-user) operation
21	  are supported deployments inside that boundary. OpenClaw is not a hostile
22	  multi-tenant security boundary for mutually adversarial users sharing one
23	  agent or gateway. For mixed-trust or adversarial-user operation, split
24	  trust boundaries: separate gateway + credentials, ideally separate OS
25	  users or hosts.
26	</Note>
27	
28	## Scope: one trust boundary per gateway
29	
30	- Supported: one trust boundary per gateway - a single operator or a mutually trusting team (prefer one OS user/host/VPS per boundary).
31	- Not supported: one shared gateway/agent used by mutually untrusted or adversarial users.
32	- Adversarial-user isolation needs separate gateways (and ideally separate OS users/hosts).
33	- Everyone who can message a tool-enabled agent shares that agent's delegated tool authority. That is fine for teammates who already trust each other; it is why adversarial users cannot share an agent.
34	- If someone can modify Gateway host state/config (`~/.openclaw`, including `openclaw.json`), treat them as a trusted operator.
35	- Inside one Gateway, authenticated operator access is a trusted control-plane role, not a per-user tenant role. [Named operator roles](/gateway/operator-scopes#named-operator-roles) bound what each teammate's connections can do; they are collaboration guardrails, not tenant isolation.
108	
109	### Requester-scoped controls and prompt context
110	
111	`tools.toolsBySender`, sender ownership, and owner-only tool inventories are evaluated against the current turn's originating requester. They do not authenticate or sanitize other content in that model prompt, including quoted text, prior shared-room history, forwarded content, fetched content, attachments, tool results, or other prompt inputs. Content from another person can therefore influence an owner-triggered turn when it is included in that turn's context.
112	
113	Treat these controls as defense in depth that reduces direct capability for a requester, not as hostile multi-user isolation. Use `contextVisibility` to filter supported channel-supplied context, restrict tools and sandbox the agent, and use separate gateways and ideally separate OS users or hosts when participants are mutually adversarial.
114	
115	## Trust boundary matrix
199	
200	### DM session isolation (multi-user mode)
201	
202	By default, OpenClaw routes all DMs into the main session for cross-device continuity. If multiple people can DM the bot (open DMs or a multi-person allowlist), isolate DM sessions:
203	
204	```json5
205	{ session: { dmScope: "per-channel-peer" } }
206	```
207	
208	`session.dmScope` values:
209	
210	| Value                      | Scope                                                                  |
211	| -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
212	| `main` (config default)    | All DMs share one session.                                             |
213	| `per-channel-peer`         | Each channel+sender pair gets an isolated DM context (secure DM mode). |
214	| `per-account-channel-peer` | Like above, split further by account (multi-account channels).         |
215	| `per-peer`                 | Each sender gets one session across all channels of the same type.     |
216	
217	Local CLI onboarding preserves an explicit `session.dmScope` and otherwise leaves it unset, so the `"main"` default applies: all direct messages across channels share the agent's rolling main session (the personal-agent default). For shared or multi-user inboxes, set `session.dmScope: "per-channel-peer"`; `openclaw security audit` recommends isolation when it detects multi-user DM traffic.
218	
219	This is a messaging-context boundary, not a host-admin boundary. If users are mutually adversarial and share the same Gateway host/config, run separate gateways per trust boundary instead.
220	
221	If the same person contacts you on multiple channels, use `session.identityLinks` to collapse those DM sessions into one canonical identity. See [Session Management](/concepts/session) and [Configuration](/gateway/configuration).
237	
238	## Prompt injection
239	
240	An attacker crafts a message that manipulates the model into unsafe action ("ignore your instructions", "dump your filesystem", "follow this link and run commands").
241	
242	Model choice now carries real weight here. Frontier models have become substantially more resistant: in a 2026 crowdsourced arena of 272K attacks across 41 agent scenarios - scored only when the agent both executed the harmful action **and** hid it from the user - success rates were 0.5% for Claude Opus 4.5, 1.0% for Sonnet 4.5, 1.3% for Haiku 4.5, and 8.5% for Gemini 2.5 Pro. Robustness tracked capability within a model family, so the models we recommend are a meaningful mitigation in their own right, not just a soft guardrail.
243	
244	Two caveats keep this from being a solved problem. Adaptive human attackers still break models that score well on static benchmarks, with published success rates above 80% against state-of-the-art defenses once the attacker adapts. And smaller or older models remain markedly easier to steer. So treat model choice as your first and cheapest layer, then keep hard enforcement - tool policy, exec approvals, sandboxing, and channel allowlists - for anything whose blast radius you would not accept on a bad day.
245	
246	Prompt injection does not require public DMs: even if only you can message the bot, any **untrusted content** it reads (web search/fetch results, browser pages, emails, docs, attachments, pasted logs/code) can carry adversarial instructions. The content itself is a threat surface, not just the sender.
247	
248	Red flags to treat as untrusted:
249	
250	- "Read this file/URL and do exactly what it says."
251	- "Ignore your system prompt or safety rules."
252	- "Reveal your hidden instructions or tool outputs."
253	- "Paste the full contents of ~/.openclaw or your logs."
254	
255	What helps in practice:
256	
257	- Keep inbound DMs locked down (pairing/allowlists). Groups are a supported deployment, not a last resort: use mention gating and `contextVisibility` so the agent reads what it needs and no more. Reserve extra caution for genuinely public rooms, where anyone can post untrusted content.
258	- Treat links, attachments, and pasted instructions as hostile by default.
259	- Run sensitive tool execution in a sandbox; keep secrets out of the agent's reachable filesystem. Sandboxing is opt-in: if sandbox mode is off, implicit `host=auto` resolves to the gateway host, while explicit `host=sandbox` still fails closed (no sandbox runtime available). Set `host=gateway` to make that behavior explicit in config.
260	- Limit high-risk tools (`exec`, `browser`, `web_fetch`, `web_search`) to trusted agents or explicit allowlists.
261	- If you allowlist interpreters (`python`, `node`, `ruby`, `perl`, `php`, `lua`, `osascript`), enable `tools.exec.strictInlineEval` so inline eval forms (`-c`, `-e`, and similar) still need explicit approval. In allowlist mode, any heredoc segment (`<<`) always requires reviewer or explicit approval, regardless of quoting - an allowlisted command cannot use a heredoc body to bypass allowlist review.
262	- Reduce blast radius by using a read-only or tool-disabled **reader agent** to summarize untrusted content, then pass the summary to your main agent.
263	- For Gmail hooks, the built-in per-message session isolates conversation context but does not remove the target agent's tool or workspace permissions. Route untrusted mail to a dedicated reader agent, apply [per-agent sandbox and tool restrictions](/tools/multi-agent-sandbox-tools), and constrain any handoff to the main agent with [`tools.agentToAgent`](/gateway/config-tools#tools-agenttoagent). See [Gmail integration](/gateway/configuration-reference#gmail-integration).
264	- Keep `web_search` / `web_fetch` / `browser` off for tool-enabled agents unless needed.
265	- For OpenResponses URL inputs (`input_file` / `input_image`), set a tight `gateway.http.endpoints.responses.files.urlAllowlist` / `images.urlAllowlist` and keep `maxUrlParts` low (empty allowlists count as unset). Use `files.allowUrl: false` / `images.allowUrl: false` to disable URL fetching entirely.

1: # Pi Agent Web
2: 
3: English | [Chinese](README.zh-CN.md)
4: 
5: Pi Agent Web is a local web workbench for Pi Coding Agent's RPC mode. It opens Pi's native JSONL
6: Sessions, keeps active Sessions independent, and lets background work continue while the Browser
7: moves between conversations.
8: 
9: Pi JSONL is the durable source of truth. Pi Agent Web does not copy Workspace or Session history
10: into another database.
11: 
12: > Pi Agent Web is a development preview. Interfaces can change and defects can interrupt work.
13: > Keep important work under version control and retain normal backups.
14: 
15: ## Product boundary
16: 
17: The Gateway is a single-user, same-origin control surface that listens only on loopback addresses.
18: It is not a hosted service, a LAN server, a multi-user collaboration system, or a security boundary
19: against a hostile local user. Do not expose `pi-web` through a public reverse proxy.
20: 
21: Provider credentials, extensions, settings, and Session history remain in the user's Pi
22: installation. Credential-free development and CI use deterministic fixtures.
23: 
24: ## What it provides
25: 
26: - Native Session discovery without a second history store.
27: - One independently supervised Pi process per active Session, with a bounded hot-process pool.
28: - One authenticated WebSocket carrying isolated Session channels.
29: - Streaming replies, reasoning, tool activity, Markdown, images, slash commands, and Extension UI.
30: - Session-scoped drafts, controls, projections, recovery, and background event ingestion.
31: - Fenced mutations, bounded payloads, explicit resync, and recoverable Session deletion.
32: 
33: Selecting a Session changes only the visible Browser view. It does not use Pi's global
34: `switch_session` or `new_session` commands, and it does not stop another Session.
35: 
36: ## Preview
37: 
38: <table>
39: <tr>
40: <td align="center"><img src="docs/assets/demo/overall.png" alt="Pi Agent Web conversation workbench" width="560" /><br /><sub>Conversation workbench</sub></td>
41: <td align="center"><img src="docs/assets/demo/tool-inspect.png" alt="Pi Agent Web tool inspector" width="560" /><br /><sub>Tool inspection</sub></td>
42: </tr>
43: <tr>
44: <td align="center"><img src="docs/assets/demo/dark-mode.png" alt="Pi Agent Web dark theme" width="560" /><br /><sub>Dark theme</sub></td>
45: <td align="center"><img src="docs/assets/demo/mobile.png" alt="Pi Agent Web narrow viewport" width="220" /><br /><sub>Narrow viewport</sub></td>
46: </tr>
47: </table>
48: 
49: The demo uses deterministic fixtures and contains no provider credentials, private paths, or user
50: Session history.
51: 
52: ## Architecture at a glance
53: 
54: ```text
55: Browser: selected view and Session-scoped stores
56:   -> one authenticated WebSocket with isolated Session channels
57:      -> Gateway: native catalog and bounded hot-process pool
58:         -> Pi RPC process per active Session
59:            -> native Pi JSONL
60: ```
61: 
62: A canonical JSONL file identifies a persisted Session. The canonical `cwd` in its header identifies
63: the Workspace. A dormant historical Session owns no process and starts on demand.
64: 
65: Mutations require the exact Session generation and current fencing token. Read-only observers do
66: not require a controller lease. Unknown identity or ordering fails closed and triggers explicit
67: recovery rather than silent cursor repair.
68: 
69: ## Quick start
70: 
71: Requirements: Node.js 22 or later, pnpm 11.21.0, and a compatible Pi Coding Agent runtime.
72: 
73: ```bash
74: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
75: pnpm dev
76: ```
77: 
78: Development mode starts the Gateway on port 3000 and Vite on port 5173 by default. Open the
79: loopback URL printed by Vite.
80: 
81: Build the SPA before starting the single-port CLI:
82: 
83: ```bash
84: pnpm build
85: pnpm start
86: 
87: # Forward CLI arguments through the root script.
88: pnpm start -- --pi-path /path/to/rpc-entry.js --port 3100 --no-open
89: ```
90: 
91: `pi-web` accepts only loopback hosts. It normally uses the exact Pi dependency installed with the
92: distribution. `--pi-path` and `PI_PATH` are expert overrides and must pass the same bounded version
93: and capability probe.
94: 
95: The names have different scopes: `pi-agent-web` is the repository and package namespace;
96: `pi-web` is the user-facing command.
97: 
98: ## Verification
99: 
100: ```bash
101: pnpm verify                 # lint, types, deterministic tests, and production build
102: pnpm test:smoke             # authenticated REST and WebSocket smoke test
103: pnpm test:browser           # packaged deterministic Browser suite
104: pnpm test:pack              # tarball install and CLI launch smoke test
105: pnpm test:compat            # exact-version Pi compatibility fixtures
106: pnpm bench:representative   # reproducible representative performance matrix
107: pnpm bench:stress           # explicit long-running stress matrix
108: PI_WEB_RUN_E2E=1 pnpm test:e2e:real  # explicit credential-bearing real-Pi acceptance
109: ```
110: 
111: The performance matrix is Issue #28 Phase 1 and remains incomplete. Structural correctness is
112: gated; host-sensitive latency, throughput, long-task, and heap results remain observational until a
113: reference-host baseline exists. See [Development](docs/development.md) for test boundaries.
114: 
115: ## Distribution status
116: 
117: The four `@pi-agent-web/*` packages are not published to npm. Clone the repository and use the
118: commands above. `pnpm test:pack` verifies local tarballs without implying a registry release.
119: 
120: The source is available under the [MIT License](LICENSE).
121: 
122: ## Repository map
123: 
124: ```text
125: packages/protocol  Browser-safe DTOs, guards, policy, and budgets
126: packages/server    Local Gateway, native discovery, and Session supervision
127: packages/ui        React workbench and Session-scoped Browser state
128: packages/cli       pi-web launcher and bounded shutdown
129: docs/              Current contracts and architecture decisions
130: ```
131: 
132: ## Documentation authority
133: 
134: - [Architecture](docs/architecture.md): identities, ownership, concurrency, and recovery
135: - [Protocol](docs/protocol.md): Pi RPC facts and the Browser/Gateway contract
136: - [UI and UX](docs/ui-ux.md): user-visible behavior and accessibility
137: - [Design](docs/design.md): visual language and acceptance criteria
138: - [Development](docs/development.md): test layers, CI, packaging, and release checks
139: - [Architecture decisions](docs/decisions/README.md): rationale, supersession, and rejected alternatives
140: - [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/leon-zym/pi-agent-web/issues): backlog and delivery status
141: 
142: Current contracts describe the product as it exists now. Historical reasoning belongs in ADRs.
143: Files under `docs/notes/` and `tmp/` are ignored working material, not product authority.
```
</details></tool-use>

1093	### ctx.getSystemPrompt()
1094	
1095	Returns Pi's current system prompt string.
1096	
1097	- During `before_agent_start`, this reflects chained system-prompt changes made so far for the current turn.
1098	- It does not include later `context` message mutations.
1099	- It does not include `before_provider_request` payload rewrites.
1100	- If later-loaded extensions run after yours, they can still change what is ultimately sent.
1101	
1102	```typescript
1103	pi.on("before_agent_start", (event, ctx) => {
1104	  const prompt = ctx.getSystemPrompt();
1105	  console.log(`System prompt length: ${prompt.length}`);
1106	});
1107	```
1108	
1109	## ExtensionCommandContext
1110	
1111	Command handlers receive `ExtensionCommandContext`, which extends `ExtensionContext` with session control methods. These are only available in commands because they can deadlock if called from event handlers.
1112	
1113	### ctx.getSystemPromptOptions()
1114	
1115	Returns the base inputs Pi currently uses to build the system prompt.
1116	
1117	```typescript
1118	const options = ctx.getSystemPromptOptions();
1119	const contextPaths = options.contextFiles?.map((file) => file.path) ?? [];
1120	```
1121	
1122	This has the same shape and mutability as `before_agent_start` `event.systemPromptOptions`: custom prompt, active tools, tool snippets, prompt guidelines, appended system prompt text, cwd, loaded context files, and loaded skills. It may include full context file contents, so treat it as sensitive extension-local data and avoid exposing it through command lists, logs, or autocomplete metadata.
1123	
1124	This reports the current base prompt inputs. It does not include per-turn `before_agent_start` chained system-prompt changes, later `context` event message mutations, or `before_provider_request` payload rewrites.
1125	
1126	### ctx.waitForIdle()
1127	
1128	Wait for the agent to fully settle, including automatic retries, auto-compaction retries, and queued continuations:
1129	
1130	```typescript
1131	pi.registerCommand("my-cmd", {
1132	  handler: async (args, ctx) => {
1133	    await ctx.waitForIdle();
1134	    // Agent is now idle, safe to modify session
1135	  },
1136	});
1137	```
1138	
1139	### ctx.newSession(options?)
1140	
1141	Create a new session:
1142	
1143	```typescript
1144	const parentSession = ctx.sessionManager.getSessionFile();
1145	const kickoff = "Continue in the replacement session";
1146	
1147	const result = await ctx.newSession({
1148	  parentSession,
1149	  setup: async (sm) => {
1150	    sm.appendMessage({
1151	      role: "user",
1152	      content: [{ type: "text", text: "Context from previous session..." }],
1153	      timestamp: Date.now(),
1154	    });
1155	  },
1156	  withSession: async (ctx) => {
1157	    // Use only the replacement-session ctx here.
1158	    await ctx.sendUserMessage(kickoff);
1159	  },
1160	});
1161	
1162	if (result.cancelled) {
1163	  // An extension cancelled the new session
1164	}
1165	```
1166	
1167	Options:
1168	- `parentSession`: parent session file to record in the new session header
1169	- `setup`: mutate the new session's `SessionManager` before `withSession` runs
1170	- `withSession`: run post-switch work against a fresh replacement-session context. Do not use captured old `pi` / command `ctx`; see [Session replacement lifecycle and footguns](#session-replacement-lifecycle-and-footguns).
1171	
1172	### ctx.fork(entryId, options?)
1173	
1174	Fork from a specific entry, creating a new session file:
1175	
1176	```typescript
1177	const result = await ctx.fork("entry-id-123", {
1178	  withSession: async (ctx) => {
1179	    // Use only the replacement-session ctx here.
1180	    ctx.ui.notify("Now in the forked session", "info");
1181	  },
1182	});
1183	if (result.cancelled) {
1184	  // An extension cancelled the fork
1185	}
1186	
1187	const cloneResult = await ctx.fork("entry-id-456", { position: "at" });
1188	if (cloneResult.cancelled) {
1189	  // An extension cancelled the clone
1190	}
1191	```
1192	
1193	Options:
1194	- `position`: `"before"` (default) forks before the selected user message, restoring that prompt into the editor
1195	- `position`: `"at"` duplicates the active path through the selected entry without restoring editor text
1196	- `withSession`: run post-switch work against a fresh replacement-session context. Do not use captured old `pi` / command `ctx`; see [Session replacement lifecycle and footguns](#session-replacement-lifecycle-and-footguns).
1197	
1198	### ctx.navigateTree(targetId, options?)
1199	
1200	Navigate to a different point in the session tree:
1201	
1202	```typescript

1204	  summarize: true,
1205	  customInstructions: "Focus on error handling changes",
1206	  replaceInstructions: false, // true = replace default prompt entirely
1207	  label: "review-checkpoint",

1210	
1211	Options:
1212	- `summarize`: Whether to generate a summary of the abandoned branch
1213	- `customInstructions`: Custom instructions for the summarizer
1214	- `replaceInstructions`: If true, `customInstructions` replaces the default prompt instead of being appended
1215	- `label`: Label to attach to the branch summary entry (or target entry if not summarizing)
1216	
1217	### ctx.switchSession(sessionPath, options?)
1218	
1219	Switch to a different session file:
1220	
1221	```typescript
1222	const result = await ctx.switchSession("/path/to/session.jsonl", {
1223	  withSession: async (ctx) => {
1224	    await ctx.sendUserMessage("Resume work in the replacement session");
1225	  },
1226	});
1227	if (result.cancelled) {
1228	  // An extension cancelled the switch via session_before_switch
1229	}
1230	```
1231	
1232	Options:
1233	- `withSession`: run post-switch work against a fresh replacement-session context. Do not use captured old `pi` / command `ctx`; see [Session replacement lifecycle and footguns](#session-replacement-lifecycle-and-footguns).
1234	
1235	To discover available sessions, use the static `SessionManager.list()` or `SessionManager.listAll()` methods:
1236	
1237	```typescript
1238	import { SessionManager } from "@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent";
1239	
1240	pi.registerCommand("switch", {
1241	  description: "Switch to another session",
1242	  handler: async (args, ctx) => {
1243	    const sessions = await SessionManager.list(ctx.cwd);
1244	    if (sessions.length === 0) return;
1245	    const choice = await ctx.ui.select(
1246	      "Pick session:",
1247	      sessions.map(s => s.file),
1248	    );
1249	    if (choice) {
1250	      await ctx.switchSession(choice, {
1251	        withSession: async (ctx) => {
1252	          ctx.ui.notify("Switched session", "info");
1253	        },
1254	      });
1255	    }
1256	  },
1257	});
1258	```
1259	
1260	### Session replacement lifecycle and footguns
1261	
1262	`withSession` receives a fresh `ReplacedSessionContext`, which extends `ExtensionCommandContext` with async `sendMessage()` and `sendUserMessage()` helpers bound to the replacement session.
1263	
1264	Lifecycle and footguns:
1265	- `withSession` runs only after the old session has emitted `session_shutdown`, the old runtime has been torn down, the replacement session has been rebound, and the new extension instance has already received `session_start`.
1266	- The callback still executes in the original closure, not inside the new extension instance. That means your old extension instance may already have run its shutdown cleanup before `withSession` starts.
1267	- Captured old `pi` / old command `ctx` session-bound objects are stale after replacement and will throw if used. Use only the `ctx` passed to `withSession` for session-bound work.
1268	- Previously extracted raw objects are still your responsibility. For example, if you capture `const sm = ctx.sessionManager` before replacement, `sm` is still the old `SessionManager` object. Do not reuse it after replacement.
1269	- Code in `withSession` should assume any state invalidated by your `session_shutdown` handler is already gone. Only capture plain data that survives shutdown cleanly, such as strings, ids, and serialized config.
1270	
1271	Safe pattern:
1272	
1273	```typescript
1274	pi.registerCommand("handoff", {
1275	  handler: async (_args, ctx) => {
1276	    const kickoff = "Continue from the replacement session";
1277	    await ctx.newSession({
1278	      withSession: async (ctx) => {
1279	        await ctx.sendUserMessage(kickoff);
1280	      },
1281	    });
1282	  },
1283	});
1284	```
1285	
1286	Unsafe pattern:
1287	
1288	```typescript
1289	pi.registerCommand("handoff", {
1290	  handler: async (_args, ctx) => {
1291	    const oldSessionManager = ctx.sessionManager;
1292	    await ctx.newSession({
1293	      withSession: async (_ctx) => {
1294	        // stale old objects: do not do this
1295	        oldSessionManager.getSessionFile();
1296	        pi.sendUserMessage("wrong");
1297	      },
1298	    });
1299	  },

```text
For a durable `getUpdates` cursor:

- Request the next batch with `offset = highest processed update_id + 1`; the offset must be `"greater by one than the highest"`.
- Recompute the cursor after every response: `"recalculate offset after each server response"`.
- Calling `getUpdates` with an offset higher than an update’s `update_id` confirms that update.
- Unacknowledged updates are retained for no more than `"not be kept longer than 24 hours"`.
```

<tool-use data-tool-type="read" data-tool-name="WebFetch"><details>
<summary>Tool use: **WebFetch**</summary>
 `https://zulip.com/api/get-events`

```text
- Send the greatest event number your client has already received as `last_event_id`; this acknowledges it. The documentation defines it as: **“The highest event ID in this queue that you've received and wish to acknowledge.”**
- The server returns only events after that number: **“An array of `event` objects (possibly zero-length if `dont_block` is set) with IDs newer than `last_event_id`.”**
- Missing numbers are normal: **“Event IDs are guaranteed to be increasing, but they are not guaranteed to be consecutive.”** Therefore, do not require contiguous IDs.
- For exactly-once handling, the page directs readers to the `call_on_each_event` implementation, describing it as an example of **“correctly processing each event exactly once.”** Persist or otherwise safely advance the acknowledged ID only after processing the corresponding event.
- The supplied page content does not include a `BAD_EVENT_QUEUE_ID` recovery procedure, so no recovery behavior for that error can be stated from this excerpt.
```

_**Agent - sidechain (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-08-30 18:15:15Z)**_

The remote comparators reinforce two design lessons. `remote-pi` has the strongest deployable broker/supervisor/identity substrate—real npm releases, mobile apps, Ed25519 pairing, UDS leader failover, keyring-backed identity, and daemon supervision—but its mobile queue is volatile, ordinary message IDs are not yet deduplicated, tool approvals are explicitly absent, and app completion still keys off `agent_end`. `pi-agent-web` has the cleanest concurrency model—canonical session identity, per-session processes, generation/fencing tokens, controller leases, barriers, bounded projections, explicit resync, and recoverable deletion—but it is loopback/single-user only, unreleased, and deliberately rejects unlisted Pi versions: 0.84.2 is current, 0.84.3 only candidate, and 0.84.4 is unsupported until added.

1:// PiClient — spawns `pi --mode rpc` as a child process, frames JSONL on its
2:// stdin/stdout, correlates request/response by id, broadcasts events to listeners,
3:// and supervises pi with crash-restart.
4-//
5:// This is a vendored, minimal subset of pi-mono's `rpc-client.ts`. We don't
6-// depend on @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent because that package pulls in the
7-// whole pi-mono ecosystem (pi-agent-core, pi-ai, pi-tui, photon-node WASM)
8-// which is wildly disproportionate to our needs.
9-//
10-// Lifecycle:
11://   1. start()                    spawns pi
12://   2. on pi exit (unexpected)    auto-restart after restartBackoffMs (unless stopping)
13://   3. stop()                     SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 1s; suppresses restart
14-//
15:// Listeners receive every line that is NOT a successfully-routed response.
16-// Responses with unmatched ids are logged and dropped (don't leak to clients).

**Analyzing Pi protocol compatibility**

I've noticed that the Pi 0.84 compatible protocol documentation mistakenly states the use of agent_end completion. The bridge operates as a dumb passthrough, so clients need to handle it. While it spawns Pi 0.84.4 correctly, I observe there’s no version pin or exact testing. I could say it's likely transport-compatible but not verified. It seems sessions won’t reconnect automatically, and a new Pi is started without the `--continue` flag unless configured. I need to inspect the default args in the configuration.

296	- Replaced the inherited pi-agent-core harness session model with the v4 lane-based `Session`, `SessionStorage`, and `SessionRepo` APIs, including durable operation records, global facts, shared sequence numbers, and tree-scoped lane views.

323	- Added inherited deferred provider request contracts, durable response handles, authenticated fetch/cancel dispatch, and faux-provider support for pending, ready, failed, and cancelled responses ([#7339](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/pull/7339) by [@davidbrai](https://github.com/davidbrai)).

 `https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/tree/v0.84.4/packages/client`

```text
- **Maturity:** Version 0.84.4 is documented as a public package, but the material gives no stability guarantee or maturity classification. No explicit experimental label appears.
- **Transport:** Runtime-neutral and based on a `ByteTransport` abstraction carrying length-prefixed CBOR. The factory must create a new transport per attempt, authenticate before resolving, preserve send order, and report data, closure, and errors. Unix sockets are provided separately through a Node/Bun-specific subpath with bounded pending output and backpressure handling.
- **Session lifecycle:** Connect, create or attach, acquire a lease, use it, then release it with `dispose()` or `detach()`. Creation grants exclusive ownership. Final lease release triggers protocol detachment. Failed explicit detachment restores the lease; failed cleanup disposal relinquishes local ownership and is reconciled later. Server removal or disconnection invalidates affected leases.
- **Concurrency and locking:** Leases are the ownership mechanism. Exclusive mode blocks all other leases; shared mode permits multiple shared consumers but not an exclusive owner. Released leases reject further commands, and acquisition conflicts produce an ownership error.
- **Reconnection:** There is no automatic reconnect. The caller must invoke `reconnect()` after disconnection. A fresh transport is required for each attempt, and disconnection invalidates existing leases.
- **Idempotency:** No general idempotency contract is described. Requests use correlation IDs. Detachment has limited retry behavior: explicit failure permits retry, while cleanup failure is locally relinquished and later reconciled.
- **Transcript cursor semantics:** Not documented in the supplied content. It describes authoritative snapshots, protocol events, cached session metadata, and non-mutating progress events, but specifies no transcript cursor, offset, replay, or resume rules.
```

### Maturity

- The package describes the protocol as experimental.
- Version 1 is binary, framed with a four-byte big-endian length followed by one definite-length CBOR item.
- It states that compatibility is not guaranteed.
- Transports must authenticate before exchanging protocol bytes.

### Sessions and IDs

- The initial client message is `hello`, carrying `PROTOCOL_VERSION`.
- Session listings expose normalized durable `SessionMetadata`.
- Required metadata: `id` and `createdAt`.
- Optional metadata: `updatedAt`, `parentSessionId`, `sessionName`, and `cwd`.
- Runtime details are provided only after acquiring a session through a `SessionSnapshot`.

### Attach and resume

- Session acquisition is mentioned, but no attach, resume, reconnect, or replay procedure is defined in the supplied content.
- Snapshots are authoritative; there is no documented client-side reconstruction protocol.

### Events and reconnect

- Messages include correlated request/response envelopes and server event envelopes.
- Progress events are temporary UI hints, not durable state.
- No event sequence numbers, acknowledgements, replay window, or reconnect behavior are specified.

### Locks and leases

- Locking appears as runtime information within an acquired `SessionSnapshot`.
- No lock acquisition, renewal, expiration, conflict, or lease protocol is described.

### Prompts and approvals

- The supplied README does not define prompt messages, approval requests, approval responses, or authorization state.

### Gateway assessment

This is a typed, framed transport protocol foundation, not a complete remote IM gateway contract. A gateway would still need documented semantics for session attachment/resumption, event ordering and replay, leases, prompts, and approvals.
```

1	# @earendil-works/pi-client
2	
3	Transport-neutral client for remote pi sessions. `PiClient` exchanges length-prefixed CBOR messages through a small `ByteTransport` interface. The package has no Node-specific imports.
4	
5	```ts
6	import { PiClient, type ByteTransportFactory } from "@earendil-works/pi-client";
7	
8	const transportFactory: ByteTransportFactory = async (handlers) => {
9	  // Connect using WebSocket, Unix socket, or another ordered byte transport.
10	  return {
11	    async send(chunk) {
12	      // Deliver chunks in invocation order and honor backpressure.
13	    },
14	    close() {},
15	  };
16	};
17	
18	const client = new PiClient({ transportFactory });
19	await client.connect();
20	const session = await client.createSession({ cwd: "/workspace" });
21	const unsubscribe = session.subscribe((snapshot) => render(snapshot));
22	await session.prompt("Inspect this project");
23	unsubscribe();
24	```
25	
26	Call `handlers.onData(chunk)` for inbound bytes, `handlers.onClose()` for an orderly terminal close, and `handlers.onError(error)` for transport failures. A factory must create a fresh transport for every connection attempt and complete any transport-specific authentication before resolving. For example, a WebSocket factory can provide credentials in its upgrade request.
27	
28	`PiClient` does not reconnect automatically. Call `reconnect()` after disconnection. One connection can attach several sessions. Requests are correlated by ID. Server snapshots and successful response snapshots are authoritative, while progress events do not mutate snapshot state optimistically. Read cached session metadata from `client.snapshot?.sessions`; call `listSessions()` to request refreshed durable metadata from the server. Runtime state is available after acquiring a session.
29	
30	`acquireSession()` returns an independent `SessionLease`; leases cannot be constructed directly. Use `{ mode: "exclusive" }` for a lifecycle or mutation coordinator and `{ mode: "shared" }` when multiple low-level consumers intentionally share the session. Exclusive acquisition fails with `PiSessionOwnershipError` while any lease exists, and shared acquisition fails while an exclusive lease exists. `attachSession()` is a shared-acquisition convenience method. `createSession()` returns an exclusive lease for the newly created session.
31	
32	Calling `dispose()` or `detach()` releases only that lease. A lease rejects commands as soon as release begins. The client sends the protocol detach request after the final lease is released. If explicit `detach()` fails, the lease becomes active again for retry. If cleanup-oriented `dispose()` fails, it reports the protocol error but relinquishes local ownership; `PiClient` reconciles the failed protocol cleanup before the next acquisition. A released lease becomes unavailable without affecting other shared leases. Server removal or disconnection invalidates every lease for the affected attachment, and disposing an invalidated lease is a no-op. Commands fail with `PiDisconnectedError` while the client is disconnected and `PiSessionDetachedError` when the client is connected but a lease is releasing, released, or invalidated. Leases implement `AsyncDisposable`.
33	
34	`subscribe()` observes authoritative snapshots. `onEvent()` observes protocol events. Both return an unsubscribe function. Structured errors returned by the server are exposed as `PiServerError`.
35	
36	## Limits and security
37	
38	`PiClientOptions.maxFrameLength` bounds inbound and outbound CBOR payloads. Configure matching limits on the client and server. Transports should separately bound queued outbound bytes and preserve send order.
39	
40	Treat peers as untrusted. Use a secure transport with appropriate access controls and authenticate during transport establishment.
41	
42	Subscriber exceptions are isolated from protocol state. Set `onListenerError` in `PiClientOptions` to report them to application logging or diagnostics.
43	
44	## Unix-domain sockets
45	
46	Node.js and Bun consumers can use the separately exported Unix-domain socket transport:
47	
48	```ts
49	import { PiClient } from "@earendil-works/pi-client";
50	import { createUnixTransportFactory } from "@earendil-works/pi-client/unix";
51	
52	const client = new PiClient({
53	  transportFactory: createUnixTransportFactory({
54	    path: "/tmp/pi.sock",
55	  }),
56	});
57	
58	await client.connect();
59	```
60	
61	`maxPendingBytes` bounds queued outbound data. It defaults to four times the protocol frame limit. The transport preserves send order and waits for socket backpressure before resolving each send.
62	
63	The `@earendil-works/pi-client` root remains transport- and runtime-neutral. Importing the Node-compatible transport requires the explicit `@earendil-works/pi-client/unix` subpath.
64
```

```text
1	# @earendil-works/pi-protocol
2	
3	Runtime-neutral schemas, types, CBOR encoding, and byte-stream framing for the experimental pi protocol.
4	
5	Protocol version `1` uses binary messages with this wire layout:
6	
7	1. A four-byte unsigned big-endian payload length.
8	2. One definite-length CBOR item containing the message.
9	
10	The first client message is always `hello`, containing `PROTOCOL_VERSION`. Subsequent messages use correlated request/response envelopes and server event envelopes. Session and server snapshots are authoritative. Progress events are transient UI hints and must not be reduced into authoritative state. Transports complete authentication before protocol bytes are exchanged.
11	
12	Session lists contain `SessionMetadata`, the normalized durable metadata available without acquiring a session runtime. Only `id` and `createdAt` are required; `updatedAt`, `parentSessionId`, `sessionName`, and `cwd` are included when supported by the backing store. Runtime state such as phase, model, thinking level, attachment, and locking appears only in an acquired `SessionSnapshot`.
13	
14	## Validated message API
15	
16	`encodeClientMessage()` and `encodeServerMessage()` validate a message and return a complete framed `Uint8Array`. The incremental decoders accept arbitrary fragmentation or coalescing, so they work with streams, sockets, and custom byte transports.
17	
18	```ts
19	import {
20	  PROTOCOL_VERSION,
21	  createServerMessageDecoder,
22	  encodeClientMessage,
23	  type ClientHello,
24	} from "@earendil-works/pi-protocol";
25	
26	const hello: ClientHello = {
27	  type: "hello",
28	  version: PROTOCOL_VERSION,
29	};
30	
31	transport.send(encodeClientMessage(hello));
32	
33	const decoder = createServerMessageDecoder({ maxFrameLength: 1024 * 1024 });
34	for (const message of decoder.push(incomingChunk)) {
35	  handleServerMessage(message);
36	}
37	decoder.end(); // Call when the byte stream closes to detect truncation.
38	```
39	
40	`ClientMessageDecoder` and `ServerMessageDecoder` are also available directly. Schema violations, malformed CBOR, and invalid framing throw `ProtocolValidationError`. Validation errors do not retain rejected payloads.
41	
42	`parseClientMessage()` and `parseServerMessage()` only validate already-decoded values. They do not parse JSON strings.
43	
44	## Transport support
45	
46	Every transport carries the same complete bytes: `[uint32-be CBOR length][CBOR payload]`. Transports may split or coalesce those bytes arbitrarily.
47	
48	This package does not bundle a transport. Consumers provide a byte-stream transport that preserves byte order and reports stream closure. Custom transports must handle arbitrary frame fragmentation and coalescing.
49	
50	All transports are untrusted. Configure matching frame limits and enforce access controls appropriate for the transport before exposing a connection to the protocol. Unix sockets can use filesystem permissions, while network transports can authenticate during connection establishment.
51	
52	## Encoding and framing
53	
54	`encodeCbor()` and `decodeCbor()` implement the protocol's strict RFC 8949 subset. `encodeFrame()` and `FrameDecoder` handle framing independently of schemas and CBOR.
55	
56	The CBOR subset supports:
57	
58	- `null` and booleans
59	- finite numbers, with integers restricted to JavaScript's safe range and non-integers encoded as float64
60	- UTF-8 strings
61	- `Uint8Array` byte strings
62	- definite-length arrays
63	- definite-length maps represented by objects with unique string keys
64	
65	Undefined object properties are omitted. JSON-valued protocol fields reject CBOR byte strings and non-plain objects. Top-level undefined, undefined array entries, sparse arrays, non-finite or unsafe numbers, tags, indefinite-length items, malformed UTF-8, trailing data, excessive nesting, and oversized values are rejected.
66	
67	Default limits are 16 MiB per CBOR payload/frame, 1,000,000 array elements or map entries, and 64 nested item levels. Options can configure these limits. A frame decoder validates the declared length before buffering payload bytes.
68	
69	All schemas reject unknown object properties. The protocol is experimental and has no compatibility guarantees.
70

Act as a software architect deciding the appropriate repository boundary, not as an implementation enthusiast. The target repository is /Users/david/Worktrees/pi-agents/feat-im-gateway. Established, evidence-backed facts from prior exploration:

- pia is a private, dependency-free Node TypeScript CLI that materializes Git-managed Pi/OMP combos, isolates runtime/session directories, launches native harnesses, parses offline JSONL sessions, and creates redacted handoffs. It is not a daemon, network service, SDK host, or transport. The branch has no committed gateway divergence.
- Combo trees can already carry Pi extensions/packages, but the combo schema has no service/transport config and the product supports both Pi and OMP.
- Stable Pi 0.84.4 surfaces are executable extensions, in-process AgentSession/AgentSessionRuntime SDK, and single-runtime JSONL RPC over stdio. pia run pi/base -- --mode rpc is mechanically possible. RPC provides detailed stream events and extension UI round-trips but no auth/network listener; one runtime has one active replaceable session.
- Pi extensions run with full process privilege, are session-scoped, and should start resources at session_start and close at session_shutdown. They can inject messages and observe/intercept events, but do not supply global process/session orchestration.
- Pi has no built-in sandbox or universal tool permission system. Project trust only gates project resources.
- The experimental CBOR pi-protocol/pi-client/pi-server stack supports multi-session attachment but promises no compatibility, supplies no turnkey coding-agent server/HTTP/WebSocket service, and needs an application-provided service.
- Current pia v3 JSONL session parsing is not the experimental v4/lane persistence model.
- Stable RPC has no multi-process lock around a shared JSONL session; a gateway must own sequencing, process lifecycle, authorization, durable mapping, retries/dedup, approval timeout, credential isolation, health/supervision, and platform payload rules.
- Kimaki's OpenCode reference adds all of those operational controls and explicitly treats chat identity as machine-access credentials.
- Pi upstream officially links earendil-works/pi-chat as a separate companion; it currently documents Discord/Telegram, per-conversation persistent workspaces, queued workers, and Gondolin VM isolation, but is not built into Pi core.

1	# pi-agents
2	
3	`pi-agents` keeps multiple [Pi](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi) and
4	[Oh My Pi](https://omp.sh/) harness combinations in one Git repository. Its
5	`pia` CLI selects a combo, safely materialises its configuration into private
6	runtime state, and launches the matching agent without putting credentials or
7	session history in Git.
8	
9	The design stays deliberately small: each combo contains a complete config
10	tree, derived combos are normal copies with explicit lineage metadata, and
11	parent changes are reviewed rather than merged implicitly.
12	
13	`pia` is written in [Node-native TypeScript](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v22.21.0/docs/api/typescript.html).
14	Node 22.19+ executes the erasable
15	`.ts` sources directly, so deployed checkouts need no build step or runtime
16	packages; TypeScript and Node type definitions are development-only tools used
17	by `npm run typecheck` and CI.
18	
19	## Quick start
20	
21	Requirements: Node.js 22.19 or newer, plus `pi` and/or `omp` for the combos you
22	want to run.
23	
24	```sh
25	git clone https://github.com/daviddwlee84/pi-agents.git
26	cd pi-agents
27	
28	# Optional for a development checkout; chezmoi deployments put bin/ on PATH.
29	npm link
30	
31	pia doctor
32	pia list --tree
33	pia apply pi/base --dry-run
34	pia run pi/base --
35	```
36	
37	No link is required to run directly from a checkout:
38	
39	```sh
40	./bin/pia --version              # macOS/Linux
41	```
42	
43	```powershell
44	.\bin\pia.ps1 --version         # Windows PowerShell
45	```
46	
47	```bat
48	bin\pia.cmd --version           # Windows cmd.exe
49	```
50	
51	When `bin/` is on `PATH`, all three environments use the command name `pia`.
52	The PowerShell launcher preserves literal argument boundaries and the child
53	exit code. The cmd launcher follows cmd.exe's normal quoting rules and is for
54	trusted interactive commands; programmatic callers with arbitrary input should
55	invoke `pia.ps1` through PowerShell. If an npm-installed harness is exposed as
56	a shim such as `pi.ps1`, `pia` invokes it through a fixed `PowerShell -File`
57	command and never enables child-process shell parsing.
58	
59	`pia run` safely applies the selected source before launch and stops on runtime
60	drift or an unowned collision. You can also save a default instead of naming
61	the combo every time:
62	
63	```sh
64	pia use pi/base
65	pia current
66	pia run -- --model provider/model
67	```
68	
69	Selection precedence is an explicit argument, then `PIA_COMBO`, then the value
70	saved by `pia use`.
71	
72	`pia` can generate native completion for every managed shell:
73	
74	```sh
75	pia completion zsh > ~/.zfunc/_pia
76	pia completion bash > "${XDG_DATA_HOME:-$HOME/.local/share}/bash-completion/completions/pia"
77	```
78	
79	```powershell
80	pia completion powershell | Out-String | Invoke-Expression
81	```
82	
83	Completion discovers combo directories directly, so `pia use <Tab>` reflects
84	newly derived or pulled combos without launching another Node process. The
85	provided chezmoi integrations generate/cache these scripts automatically.
86	
87	Human-readable output uses semantic terminal colours when the selected stream
88	supports them. `NO_COLOR` and `NODE_DISABLE_COLORS` disable colour;
89	`FORCE_COLOR` and non-zero `CLICOLOR_FORCE` can force it through a pipe. JSON,
90	completion code, versions, selected combo ids, and artifact paths always stay
91	plain for scripts.
92	
93	The compatibility snapshot for the current implementation is **Pi 0.84.4**
94	and **OMP 18.0.11**. Tests cover the wrapper's behavior and pinned session
95	fixtures; run `pia doctor` and a smoke launch when using a different upstream
96	version.
97	
98	## What is included
99	
100	- `combos/pi/base`: neutral upstream Pi configuration.
101	- `combos/pi/vanilla`: Pi with project/global resource discovery disabled by
102	  launch flags.
103	- `combos/omp/base`: neutral OMP native profile configuration.
104	- Strict source-to-runtime synchronisation with drift detection and dry runs.
105	- Per-combo or explicitly shared session storage, same-engine forks, and
106	  deterministic redacted handoffs across harnesses.
107	
108	Start with [combo authoring](docs/combos.md), then read
109	[architecture](docs/architecture.md),
110	[sessions and handoff](docs/sessions-and-handoff.md), the
111	[ecosystem snapshot](docs/ecosystem.md), and the optional
112	[chezmoi integration](docs/chezmoi.md).
113	
114	```sh
115	npm install --ignore-scripts   # development/type-check dependencies only
116	npm test
117	npm run typecheck
118	npm run check
119	```
120	
121	<!-- project-knowledge-harness:readme-roadmap -->
122	## Roadmap & lessons learned
123	
124	Future work is indexed in [TODO.md](TODO.md), with longer research under
125	[backlog/](backlog/). Past traps and their workarounds live under
126	[pitfalls/](pitfalls/).
127	<!-- project-knowledge-harness:readme-roadmap (end) -->
128
```
</details></tool-use>

1	# Architecture
2	
3	`pia` separates version-controlled intent from mutable agent state. The Git
4	repository is the source of truth for combo definitions; it is never an agent's
5	live home directory.
6	
7	## Data layout
8	
9	```text
10	pi-agents/
11	  combos/<pi|omp>/<name>/
12	    combo.json             declarative metadata
13	    agent/                 complete managed config tree
14	  schema/combo.schema.json
15	  bin/pia
16	  src/*.ts                 Node-native erasable TypeScript
17	
18	${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-~/.config}/pi-agents/
19	  selection.json           value saved by `pia use`
20	
21	${XDG_STATE_HOME:-~/.local/state}/pi-agents/
22	  manifests/               last-applied managed-file hashes and modes
23	  runtime/pi/<name>/agent/ Pi configuration runtime
24	  sessions/                isolated/shared session roots
25	  handoffs/                generated private Markdown artifacts
26	```
27	
28	`PIA_SOURCE_ROOT` can point the CLI at another checkout. `PIA_STATE_HOME`
29	replaces the entire state root. These overrides are useful for tests and
30	advanced setups; normal users should let the CLI derive both paths.
31	
32	For Pi, `pia` launches with `PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR` set to the combo's runtime
33	directory. For OMP, it uses a native profile named `pia-<combo-name>` and asks
34	`omp --profile ... config path` for the real location instead of assuming a
35	home or XDG layout. `PIA_PI_BIN` and `PIA_OMP_BIN` can override the executable
36	names.
37	
38	## Source and runtime contract
39	
40	Only files below a combo's `agent/` directory are managed. Downloaded packages,
41	credentials, sessions, caches, blobs, databases, and any other runtime-created
42	files stay outside Git or remain unowned in the runtime tree.
43	
44	The source tree must not contain credentials, `.env` files, session/package/
45	cache stores, or symlinks. On POSIX systems runtime directories are created
46	with mode `0700`; managed files use `0600` or `0700` according to their
47	executable bit. Windows does not expose equivalent POSIX mode enforcement
48	through Node, so runtime files inherit the user's profile ACL and drift checks
49	compare content rather than synthetic mode bits there. Writes and manifest
50	replacement are atomic.
51	
52	The source uses only TypeScript syntax that Node can erase without code
53	generation. Runtime execution therefore stays build-free; `tsconfig.json` and
54	the development dependencies exist solely for strict `tsc --noEmit` checking.
55	
56	Known runtime/credential paths are rejected structurally. `npm run check` also
57	runs gitleaks over combo content when the binary is available, while CI and the
58	existing pre-commit stack enforce the same secret scan before source is shared.
59	
60	Each manifest records its exact absolute target and, for every managed relative
61	path, the content hash, executable bit, and mode. `pia apply` classifies paths
62	as follows:
63	
64	| Source/runtime state | Result |
65	|---|---|
66	| New source path, unused target | Create it |
67	| Source changed, runtime still at last applied value | Update it |
68	| Runtime changed independently | Refuse the whole apply |
69	| Source and runtime both changed | Refuse the whole apply |
70	| Source removed, runtime unchanged | Remove the stale managed path |
71	| Source removed, runtime changed | Refuse unless forced |
72	| Target-only path never owned by `pia` | Preserve and omit from normal diff |
73	| New source collides with an unowned path or non-file obstruction | Always refuse |
74	
75	`--dry-run` returns the same plan without writing. `--force` makes source win
76	for previously managed drift and conflicts, including modified stale files; it
77	does not overwrite unowned collisions. This keeps force bounded by the prior
78	manifest instead of turning it into a recursive replacement operation.
79	
80	Use `pia status <combo>` for a summary and `pia diff <combo> --runtime` for
81	managed path details before applying.
82	
83	## Selection and launch
84	
85	A combo is selected in this order:
86	
87	1. The combo argument passed to the command.
88	2. `PIA_COMBO`.
89	3. The persistent value written by `pia use`.
90	
91	`pia run [combo] -- <agent arguments>` first performs the same safe apply, then
92	combines the combo's checked-in `launchArgs` with trailing arguments and
93	forwards the child process's exit code. Drift, conflicts, unsafe source files,
94	or unowned collisions abort before launch. A stale parent digest emits a warning
95	but does not block a standalone child combo.
96	
97	Wrapper-owned routing/session flags and secret-bearing flags are rejected from
98	`launchArgs`; runtime invocation remains explicit. Session storage is resolved
99	from engine, combo history policy, and canonical working directory. See
100	[sessions and handoff](sessions-and-handoff.md).
101	
102	## Why copies instead of inheritance
103	
104	Pi does not expose a stable, general-purpose config inheritance contract, and
105	OMP's layers do not cover every harness asset uniformly. `pia derive` therefore
106	copies a complete combo and records its parent digest. The child remains usable
107	and understandable on its own. Parent changes produce a lineage warning and a
108	review workflow, never an implicit merge at launch time.
109	
110	Declarative inheritance and three-way sync are intentionally deferred until
111	real usage demonstrates enough repeated maintenance to justify their conflict
112	rules. The research checkpoint is tracked in
113	[the backlog](../backlog/declarative-inheritance-three-way-sync.md).
114
```
</details></tool-use>

```text
1	# Pi harness ecosystem snapshot
2	
3	This page records the assumptions behind `pia`, not a permanent verdict on fast
4	moving upstream projects. The compatibility snapshot reviewed and represented
5	by the test fixtures is **Pi 0.84.4** and **Oh My Pi 18.0.11**, as of
6	2026-08-30.
7	
8	## Upstream Pi
9	
10	Pi supports a global agent directory, project-local `.pi` configuration, and
11	the `PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR` override. These primitives are sufficient for `pia`
12	to launch isolated full configurations, while repo-local settings and resources
13	can still participate according to Pi's trust and discovery rules. See Pi's
14	[settings](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/settings.md),
15	[environment variables](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/environment-variables.md),
16	and [packages](https://pi.dev/docs/latest/packages) documentation.
17	
18	Pi does not provide a single stable first-class abstraction that composes all
19	settings, skills, extensions, package references, prompts, and session policy as
20	a named inheritable profile. That is why `pia` switches the complete agent
21	directory and keeps combo inheritance explicit and copy-based.
22	
23	Two issue pages are easy to misread:
24	
25	- [#3590, layered config](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/3590)
26	- [#7813, multiple settings profiles](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/7813)
27	
28	Their closed status is easy to over-interpret, but each timeline contains the
29	GitHub Actions message that issues from new contributors are auto-closed
30	pending maintainer review. They are evidence that users asked
31	for these capabilities, **not** an explicit maintainer roadmap rejection. Any
32	future design review should re-check upstream rather than preserving either
33	interpretation as fact.
34	
35	## Oh My Pi
36	
37	OMP exposes named profiles through `omp --profile <name>` and has broader
38	configuration discovery and overlay behavior. A named profile relocates native
39	configuration and runtime resources, so `pia` uses an OMP profile named
40	`pia-<combo>` and resolves its actual path with OMP itself. See the upstream
41	[configuration and profile guide](https://github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi/blob/main/docs/config-usage.md).
42	
43	OMP's richer configuration system does not remove the need for a repository
44	contract: different resource types have different discovery rules, runtime
45	state must still stay out of Git, and a Pi combo should remain understandable
46	without translating it into OMP concepts. `pia` therefore presents the same
47	simple combo/source/runtime workflow for both engines and lets OMP own only its
48	native profile resolution.
49	
50	## MCP is an extension choice
51	
52	Do not describe `pi.mcp` as a Pi core package-manifest feature. The manifest
53	shape discussed in the original research belongs to an adapter/integration,
54	not upstream Pi's package contract. MCP support for a combo should identify the
55	specific extension it uses—for example the community
56	[`pi-mcp-adapter`](https://github.com/nicobailon/pi-mcp-adapter)—and keep that
57	adapter's configuration inside the combo like any other harness dependency.
58	
59	This distinction matters for portability: a combo that depends on an adapter
60	must pin and test that adapter rather than assuming another Pi installation can
61	interpret an undocumented `pi.mcp` field.
62	
63	## Why maintain another thin layer?
64	
65	There are many ready-made harnesses and profile managers. Use one of them when
66	its opinionated defaults already match the job. This repository is justified
67	when the goal is to:
68	
69	- keep experimental, learning, and production combos together;
70	- switch Pi and OMP through one predictable interface;
71	- review the exact Git-managed configuration before it reaches runtime;
72	- keep auth, sessions, packages, and caches private and mutable;
73	- reproduce selected behaviors from other harnesses without adopting all of
74	  their machinery.
75	
76	Research into [Claude Code](../backlog/claude-code-harness-to-pi.md),
77	[Codex](../backlog/codex-harness-to-pi.md), and
78	[OpenCode](../backlog/opencode-harness-to-pi.md) is intentionally deferred until
79	the base workflow has real usage data. Re-check upstream versions, docs, CLI
80	flags, and session formats before promoting any result to a production combo.
81
```
</details></tool-use>

```text
1	# Combos
2	
3	A combo is one complete, selectable agent setup. Its identifier is
4	`<engine>/<name>`, where the engine is `pi` or `omp`. Names are 1–60 characters,
5	start with a lowercase letter or digit, use lowercase letters, digits, dots,
6	underscores, or hyphens, and do not end in a dot. The shared restriction keeps
7	the generated `pia-<name>` value valid as an OMP profile.
8	
9	## Directory and metadata
10	
11	```text
12	combos/pi/research/
13	  combo.json
14	  agent/
15	    settings.json
16	    AGENTS.md
17	    skills/
18	    extensions/
19	```
20	
21	`agent/` mirrors the configuration files that should be managed at runtime. It
22	must be a complete, readable setup rather than a delta against another combo.
23	
24	A minimal `combo.json` is:
25	
26	```json
27	{
28	  "$schema": "../../../schema/combo.schema.json",
29	  "schemaVersion": 1,
30	  "description": "Research-oriented upstream Pi harness.",
31	  "maturity": "experimental",
32	  "launchArgs": [],
33	  "history": {
34	    "mode": "isolated"
35	  }
36	}
37	```
38	
39	The fields are:
40	
41	- `schemaVersion`: currently `1`.
42	- `description`: a short human explanation of the combo's purpose.
43	- `maturity`: `experimental`, `learning`, or `production`.
44	- `launchArgs`: non-secret agent arguments applied on every launch.
45	- `history`: `isolated`, or `shared` with a named same-engine group.
46	- `derivedFrom` and `parentDigest`: a paired lineage reference written by
47	  `pia derive`.
48	
49	Example shared history policy:
50	
51	```json
52	{
53	  "history": {
54	    "mode": "shared",
55	    "group": "daily-coding"
56	  }
57	}
58	```
59	
60	Sharing is still separated by engine and canonical project directory. It does
61	not make Pi and OMP JSONL files interchangeable. Group names follow the same
62	1–60 character/no-trailing-dot safety rule as combo names.
63	
64	Do not put auth tokens, API keys, `.env` files, sessions, blobs, package stores,
65	or caches in `agent/`. Reference packages from configuration; let the harness
66	install or cache them in runtime state.
67	
68	## Derive and maintain a combo
69	
70	Create a child from an existing combo:
71	
72	```sh
73	pia derive pi/base pi/research
74	```
75	
76	This makes a full copy, sets `derivedFrom`, and records a digest of the reviewed
77	parent. There is no live inheritance. Edit the child normally and commit it as
78	a standalone configuration.
79	
80	When a parent changes:
81	
82	```sh
83	pia lineage pi/research
84	pia diff pi/research --parent
85	# manually copy or adapt only the changes you want
86	pia lineage pi/research --ack
87	```
88	
89	`--ack` only records the current parent digest. It must be run after the review,
90	not as a way to hide an unresolved warning. Lineage must remain within one
91	engine and cycles are rejected.
92	
93	## Inspect and use combos
94	
95	```sh
96	pia list
97	pia list --tree
98	pia list --json
99	
100	pia use pi/research
101	pia current
102	
103	pia status pi/research
104	pia diff pi/research --runtime
105	pia apply pi/research --dry-run
106	pia apply pi/research
107	pia run pi/research -- <pi arguments>
108	```
109	
110	`pia run` can omit its combo after `pia use` or `PIA_COMBO`; an explicit run
111	argument always wins. The management command signatures shown here require
112	explicit combo IDs so mutations and diagnostics have an unambiguous target.
113	
114	If a managed runtime file was edited directly, normal apply fails without
115	changing anything. Review the diff and either carry the intended edit back to
116	`agent/`, or use `pia apply <combo> --force` to discard drift on paths that
117	`pia` previously owned. Unmanaged runtime files are preserved.
118	
119	`launchArgs` cannot contain wrapper-owned options such as profile, session,
120	cwd, config, resume/fork routing, or API-key flags. Put one-off agent options
121	after `--`; keep secrets in the harness's private auth mechanism or environment.
122	
123	## Command map
124	
125	In the table, `<session-selector>` means either `--latest` or
126	`--session <id-or-absolute-path>`.
127	
128	| Command | Purpose |
129	|---|---|
130	| `pia list [--tree|--json]` | Discover combos and lineage |
131	| `pia use <combo>` / `pia current` | Save or print the default selection |
132	| `pia derive <parent> <child> [--description TEXT]` | Copy a combo and record lineage |
133	| `pia lineage <combo> [--ack]` | Inspect or acknowledge a parent digest |
134	| `pia status <combo>` | Summarise source/runtime health |
135	| `pia diff <combo> [--runtime|--parent]` | Show managed runtime or lineage differences |
136	| `pia apply <combo> [--dry-run|--force]` | Safely materialise source configuration |
137	| `pia run [combo] -- <args>` | Safely apply, then launch the selected harness |
138	| `pia sessions <combo>` | List sessions visible to that combo |
139	| `pia fork <from> <to> <session-selector> -- <args>` | Native same-engine session fork |
140	| `pia handoff <from> <to> <session-selector> --goal TEXT [--no-run] -- <args>` | Redacted context transfer |
141	| `pia doctor [--json]` | Check binaries, versions, source safety, and helpers |
142	| `pia completion <zsh\|bash\|powershell>` | Emit native shell completion code |
143
```

415	  add("gitleaks", Boolean(commandExists("gitleaks")), commandExists("gitleaks") || "not found", "warning");
416	  for (const engine of ["pi", "omp"]) {
417	    const binary = engine === "pi" ? env.PIA_PI_BIN || "pi" : env.PIA_OMP_BIN || "omp";
418	    const probe = commandResult(binary, ["--version"], { env });
419	    add(engine, probe.ok, probe.ok ? (probe.stdout || probe.stderr).trim() : "not installed", "warning");

423	    for (const combo of combos) await scanTree(combo.agentDir);

426	    add("combos", false, errorMessage(error));

441	      const label = check.ok ? "ok" : check.severity === "warning" ? "warn" : "error";
442	      process.stdout.write(

444	        `${ui.muted(check.detail, stdoutStyle)}\n`,
445	      );

467	  if (command === "use") {

336	  if (typeof inputPath !== 'string' || inputPath.length === 0 || inputPath.includes('\0')) {
337	    fail('PIA_INVALID_PATH', `${context} must be a non-empty filesystem path`);
338	  }
339	  if (Buffer.byteLength(inputPath, 'utf8') > MAX_RELATIVE_PATH_BYTES) {
340	    fail('PIA_INVALID_PATH', `${context} exceeds ${MAX_RELATIVE_PATH_BYTES} UTF-8 bytes`);
341	  }
342	  return path.resolve(inputPath);
343	}
344	
345	function resolveWithin(root: string, relativePath: string, context = 'path'): string {
346	  const components = validateRelativePath(relativePath, context);
347	  const resolvedRoot = path.resolve(root);
348	  const resolvedPath = path.resolve(resolvedRoot, ...components);
349	  if (resolvedPath === resolvedRoot || !resolvedPath.startsWith(`${resolvedRoot}${path.sep}`)) {
350	    fail('PIA_PATH_TRAVERSAL', `${context} escapes its root: ${relativePath}`);
351	  }
352	  return resolvedPath;
353	}
354	
355	async function lstatMaybe(filePath: string): Promise<Stats | null> {
356	  try {
357	    return await fs.lstat(filePath);
358	  } catch (error) {
359	    if (errorCode(error) === 'ENOENT') return null;
360	    throw error;
361	  }
362	}
363	
364	async function readOrdinaryFile(
365	  filePath: string,
366	  context: string,
367	): Promise<{ data: Buffer; metadata: InternalFileMetadata }> {
368	  const noFollow = fsConstants.O_NOFOLLOW ?? 0;
369	  let handle: FileHandle | undefined;
370	  try {
371	    handle = await fs.open(filePath, fsConstants.O_RDONLY | noFollow);
372	  } catch (error) {
373	    if (errorCode(error) === 'ELOOP') {
374	      fail('PIA_SYMLINK_REJECTED', `${context} is a symbolic link: ${filePath}`);
375	    }
376	    throw error;
377	  }
378	
379	  try {
380	    const stat = await handle.stat();
381	    if (!stat.isFile()) {
382	      fail('PIA_NON_FILE_REJECTED', `${context} is not an ordinary file: ${filePath}`);
383	    }
384	    const data = await handle.readFile();
385	    const executable = (stat.mode & 0o111) !== 0;
386	    return {
387	      data,
388	      metadata: {
389	        sha256: sha256(data),
390	        executable,
391	        mode: desiredMode(executable),
392	        actualMode: stat.mode & 0o777,
393	        size: stat.size,
394	      },
395	    };
396	  } finally {
397	    await handle.close();
398	  }
399	}
